title: Bills vs Lions: Winners and losers for Buffalo against Detroit
summary: The Buffalo Bills earned a big win tonight, putting up 21 points early in the game before outlasting the Detroit Lions in a 41-31 victory. What better way to open the team’s new stadium than with a big victory over a solid NFC foe? Buffalo was in control right from the start, opening the scoring […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 07: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on September 07, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills earned a big win tonight, putting up 21 points early in the game before outlasting the Detroit Lions in a 41-31 victory. What better way to open the team’s new stadium than with a big victory over a solid NFC foe? Buffalo was in control right from the start, opening the scoring with a touchdown on their first drive. After forcing Detroit to punt on its first possession, the Bills scored again and they were off to the races. The Lions wouldn’t go down quietly, but when the clock hit triple-zero, Buffalo had the ball and the win, and the 2-0 start to the season. Much of tonight came up aces, but there were some negatives despite the big win. Here is our stock report for the evening—feel free to leave your suggestions in the comments below! _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up: Josh Allen Another game, another fantastic effort for Buffalo’s MVP. Allen started the game using his legs, running for 40 yards on a drive that ended with his one-yard touchdown rush. Allen added not one, not two, but three first half touchdown passes, as well, hitting Joshua Palmer for a 43-yard strike, Dawson Knox for a one-yard score, and Dalton Kincaid for a 16-yard score. Once again, Allen was efficient, but he did not fear pushing the ball downfield against a depleted Detroit secondary. In the second half, he kept the pressure on the Lions, leading scoring drives of 75 and 61 yards to seal the win. Overall, Allen finished the night with five touchdowns overall—three passing and two rushing. He completed 20-of-31 passes for 248 yards, adding 72 rushing yards on 11 carries. Horns Up: James Cook III It was a big first half for the NFL’s 2025 leading rusher. Cook totaled 101 rushing yards in the first half of action, and his best drive came at the most important time of the first half for Buffalo. After ceding a score to Detroit, which made the score 21-7, Cook gashed the Lions defense on the first three plays of the ensuing drive. He ran for 20 yards, 35 yards, and six yards on the first three plays of the drive, bringing the Bills all the way to the Detroit 13-yard line. One penalty and one play later, Allen found Kincaid to give the Bills a 27-7 advantage and the perfect answer to an opponent’s scoring drive. Cook had opportunities in the second half, as well, and he added a rushing touchdown of his own to punctuate the victory in the fourth quarter. He finished with 20 carries for 134 yards and a score. He also caught one pass for four yards. Horns Up: Dalton Kincaid Once again, the big tight end had a big day. He was open in space by design, but he also has shown a knack for finding the right space against zone defense, and with DJ Moore going down with an injury in the first half, it cleared the way for Kincaid to step up and lead the team in receiving. Well, maybe that’s not fair—he led the team in receiving last week, too—but without Moore to open things up for him, he still found space. If Kincaid can stay healthy all season, look out. That breakout we’ve hoped for might be upon us. He even looked great as a blocker, building on a strong game against the Texans to show that he has mastered what was one of the bigger holes in his game. Sure, it’s early, but Kincaid looks every bit the elite tight end Buffalo assumed they drafted in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He had seven catches for 95 yards, narrowly missing a second-straight 100-yard receiving day. Horns Down: Pass Defense I think that there are layers to this, so forgive me for nit-picking here. But, the coverage and the pass rush aren’t consistently marrying right now. That’s reasonable given that we’ve only seen two games in five days under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. However, there were concerns coming into the year that the Bills’ personnel didn’t necessarily fit the more man-heavy, pressure-oriented looks Leonhard wants to utilize, and through two games, some of those fears are coming to fruition. When Buffalo blitzes, there are too many openings and rushers aren’t getting home. When they don’t blitz, the front four is struggling to create consistent pressure. There are flashes of good, enough where I think it’s going to be great. But, for now, there is definitely room for improvement. Horns Down: CJ Gardner-Johnson I noticed Cole Bishop. I noticed Jordan Hancock. I noticed Damar Hamlin, too. I didn’t really see Gardner-Johnson much in coverage, nor did I see him much in run support. The defensive secondary in general hasn’t been great, but the safety play has been very hit-or-miss through two games. Gardner-Johnson had just one tackle in the game, and while he is a good veteran presence, he needs to make some plays on the ball to truly be an improvement over what the Bills had there last season. Horns Up: Disappointing Former Draft Picks Keon Coleman saw six targets, and he caught them all for 63 yards. DeWayne Carter made some plays in the run game, and he even looked spry on a few pass rush reps. Both players saw more time tonight thanks to injuries, as Coleman likely played more thanks to DJ Moore’s injury, and Carter stepped up when Ed Oliver went down with a hip injury suffered during warmups. Frankly, this might have been the best showing of Carter’s young career, and after missing all of last season due to a torn Achilles, it was nice to see the Duke product step up. Neither Coleman nor Carter needs to be a star for this to be a successful year for the Bills, but if they can put together solid outings like they did tonight, they could become part of a dependable depth squad for a team with immense potential. Tonight was a good sign for both players, and in turn, it was a good sign for the Bills overall. Horns Down: The Injury Bug Ed Oliver hurting his hip in warmups? Not great. DJ Moore hurting his shoulder during the game? Really not great. These things are inevitable, but they’re still not what anyone wants to see. Buffalo has ten days to rest before playing its next game against the Los Angeles Chargers. Hopefully, those ten days let the Bills see some better health before a big AFC matchup. Horns Down: Landon Jackson After some encouraging reps on Sunday, Jackson was bullied for much of the evening. He did manage two tackles, but he was also called for a tripping penalty late in the first half that gave the Lions an easy field goal before the half came to a close. Whereas DeWayne Carter seemed to boost his stock tonight, Jackson looked mediocre at best. Horns Unclear: You Make the Call What do we think, friends? On a short week, we couldn’t come up with some better branding, but I’m still open to suggestions about the name of the column and nominees for our stock up and stock down tonight. With apologies to the person who suggested just calling it “stock up/stock down” (I can’t remember offhand who it was), I just wanted to say that I initially leaned that way too. We can yell at clouds together. Go Bills!

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Detroit Lions, NFL Week 2 ‘TNF’ fan discussion
summary: Welcome to primetime, Highmark Stadium! To get Week 2 of NFL action underway, the Buffalo Bills host the Detroit Lions for the franchise’s first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. It’s been a long time coming, and the wait was made much sweeter with Buffalo winning its Week 1 road game against Houston Texans. […]
full_text: Welcome to primetime, Highmark Stadium! To get Week 2 of NFL action underway, the Buffalo Bills host the Detroit Lions for the franchise’s first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. It’s been a long time coming, and the wait was made much sweeter with Buffalo winning its Week 1 road game against Houston Texans. The win in Houston was quarterback Josh Allen’s first, and also the first for the franchise since the 2006 NFL season. Now, they look to start things off on the right foot where and when it counts in their new home. The hype has been building toward this moment for months, and One Bills Drive is ready to get the party off on the right foot. If you normally turn away at halftime, remember there’s the team’s first-ever major halftime performance by the band OneRepublic. Pomp and circumstance aside, tonight’s matchup is a massive game that should bring plenty of fireworks to the field. The last time these teams met, the Bills won a 48-42 barnburner at Ford Field. Running back Ty Johnson led Buffalo in receiving, catching all five of his targets for 114 yards. Johnson won’t play tonight, currently sidelined with a hamstring injury. Instead, look for Allen and the Bills to work the ball downfield to wide receiver DJ Moore and tight end Dalton Kincaid. Head coach Joe Brady still calls the plays, and you can bet he’s itching to get running back James Cook III going tonight. Cook was visibly upset on the flight home following a fumble in Week 1. As we know, fumbles are often difficult to predict, and Brady has given his vote of confidence in Cook. Will the Bills defeat the Lions to improve to 2-0? Buckle up for what should be a wild ride! With that, we turn things over to you, Rumblers! Here’s your open thread for Thursday Night Football on Prime . Remember, beginning this season we’re going to stick with one game thread, so sit tight in this space. As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills! title: Bills vs Lions: Ed Oliver a surprise inactive alongside Ty Johnson
summary: The Buffalo Bills open their brand-new stadium for real tonight, taking on the Detroit Lions in what should be an entertaining contest. Given the Bills’ Detroit roots — team founder and NFL Hall of Famer Ralph Wilson Jr. grew up in Detroit, and he maintained business operations in Michigan throughout his life—this is a fitting […]
full_text: MIAMI, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 17: Ed Oliver #91 of the Buffalo Bills reacts after a sack against the Miami Dolphins during the first quarter at Hard Rock Stadium on November 17, 2019 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills open their brand-new stadium for real tonight, taking on the Detroit Lions in what should be an entertaining contest. Given the Bills’ Detroit roots — team founder and NFL Hall of Famer Ralph Wilson Jr. grew up in Detroit, and he maintained business operations in Michigan throughout his life—this is a fitting matchup for the first regular-season game at new Highmark Stadium. After earning a hard-fought victory over the Houston Texans on Sunday, Buffalo enters this one relatively healthy. The same can’t be said for Detroit, who sports a banged-up unit following their 31-30 overtime victory against the New Orleans saints just four days ago. Detroit has already ruled out two starting offensive linemen, who join two starting safeties among the players who won’t participate tonight. Speaking of starting safeties, Cole Bishop popped up on the injury report this week for Buffalo, as he was listed as questionable entering play. We now have clarity on his status, as well as the other inactive players for both teams. Here is the full list. _____________________________________________________________________________ DT Ed Oliver Oliver was not listed on the Bills’ injury report this week so this is a surprise. He injured his hip during warmups according to the team. With a wet field and nine days to the next game, they are being cautious. He played more than 80% of the snaps last week. OLB Mike Danna was inactive last week and he gets the jersey tonight. RB Ty Johnson While the veteran was able to work more in practice drills this week, Buffalo will err on the side of caution and sit him down for one more week. Frank Gore Jr. is active after his second-straight week with an elevation from the practice squad. S Jalon Kilgore Like Johnson, Kilgore missed the first game of the year with an injury. WR Skyler Bell With veteran Greg Dortch elevated earlier today from the practice squad, Buffalo has once again chosen to deactivate their 2026 fourth-round pick. Dortch seems to have a hold on the punt-return gig as well as the second kickoff return spot, so his special teams versatility trumps Bell’s big-play potential for the time being. T/G Jude Bowry Speaking of inactive 2026 fourth-round picks, Buffalo’s other fourth-round choice in April is also a healthy scratch for the second straight game. Tylan Grable is the swing tackle behind Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown. G Ar’Maj Reed-Adams With ten offensive linemen on the 53-man roster, Buffalo has more than they need. Reed-Adams, a seventh-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, is a solid developmental prospect, but he’s a healthy scratch for now. Veterans Austin Corbett and Lloyd Cushenberry remain the reserve interior offensive linemen. DL T.J. Sanders Sanders missed Sunday’s game with a new injury, and while he was estimated to make two limited practices this week, he missed all of Tuesday’s work due to illness. Week 3 will be an interesting one for the defensive line, as Sanders will likely be healthy. Who, if anyone, will he replace on the gameday roster?

title: Panthers vs Falcons: Week 2 storylines to watch
summary: Hello CSR! I’m here to break down the biggest storylines to watch following an explosive but disappointing week 1 matchup against the Chicago Bears. The Panthers’ offense had its first week 1 coming out party in years, unfortunately the Bears’ party was much larger. Luckily, everyone else in the NFC South lost, including the Falcons, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 16: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Jonathan Bachman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! I’m here to break down the biggest storylines to watch following an explosive but disappointing week 1 matchup against the Chicago Bears. The Panthers’ offense had its first week 1 coming out party in years, unfortunately the Bears’ party was much larger. Luckily, everyone else in the NFC South lost, including the Falcons, so this is as good a time as ever for the Panthers to right the ship and improve on the things that did them in the first game of the season. Offense: More of that, please! If you looked at the Panthers offense during week 1 in isolation, you’d think the unit as a whole had a pretty complete game. Sure, there’s always those stops that happen in an NFL game, but even Bryce Young’s lone interception was basically just a decision to go after points in the waning moments of the first half. The offensive line was solid, Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan continued all of their momentum from 2025, and Bryce Young came out aggressive throwing the ball down the field and confident in his decision making. So while the loss was surely demoralizing, the offense cannot dwell on it and must simply come out swinging like they did against the Bears. There will be more opportunity for explosive plays down the field in the passing game, and while the Falcons did hold the Steelers to only 58 rushing cards, Jaylen Warren managed to average 4.6 yards per carry on 1o attempts against them while Aaron Rodgers wasn’t all that effective throwing the ball 40 times. The Panthers should be able to attack this defense in much the same way they attacked the Bears and see success. Defense: Less of that, please! Meanwhile, the Panthers defense surrendered 59 points against the Bears, while they ran for close to 300 yards against the unit and Caleb Williams absolutely balled out in the passing game. I wouldn’t expect the Falcons to have the same kind of game passing (more on that later), but Bijan Robinson could very easily give them major issues in the rushing game if this defense can’t lock in here. They need to maintain their assignments, especially on perimeter runs and QB scrambles. Princely Umanmielen, you gotta contain the QB dawg. But the biggest thing they must eliminate is mental mistakes that cost the defense easy field position. We cannot see defensive linemen jumping offsides on key plays or hitting the quarterback on 3rd and long and causing roughing the passer penalties. In the end, no matter how you felt about the Panthers defense on Sunday, there were several key preventable penalties that cost them the most in a game that was neck and neck going into the 3rd quarter. X Factor: Uhhh, which quarterback are they playing? Its been a wild week if you follow along with Falcons news on social media this week. As of right now, Cooper Rush is expected to be starting. But the Falcons coaching staff refuses to reveal their hand so throughout the week there’s been talk of Michael Penix potentially stepping in and starting this week. Both quarterbacks carry with them a vastly different game plan for the defense. The unit came out looking very unprepared at times against the Bears, and that can’t happen this week no matter who the QB is. What storylines are you watching this week, Panthers fans?

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: SOUTH BEND, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 12: Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa #27 of the Notre Dame Fighting Irish celebrates recovering a fumble during the second quarter against the Rice Owls at Notre Dame Stadium on September 12, 2026 in South Bend, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Notre Dame Fighting Irish linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa. Bio Viliamu-Asa (6’3”, 230 lbs.) was a five star recruit coming out of Bellflower, CA. After an ACL tear near the end of his freshman season in high school, he returned his junior year and dominated, earning the CIF Defensive Player of the Year on route to a MaxPreps National Championship. His senior year saw his dominance continue as he was named LA Times Player of the Year and was a Butkus Award finalist. Viliamu-Asa played in all 14 games for Notre Dame his true freshman season but didn’t really thrive until last season when he took over the starting role. Through the first 11 games of the season, he had accrued 48 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, three sacks, an interception, and a fumble recovery. Unfortunately, his season was once again cut short this time by tearing the ACL in his other knee. Viliamu-Asa did come back healthy in time for the season opener this year, logging five tackles and a fumble recovered in a 52-0 romp over Rice. Strengths/Weaknesses Viliamu-Asa has an incredible feel for the game, especially against the run. He diagnoses plays well and is a force when moving downhill towards the ballcarrier. He is also an accomplished blitzer, relying on impeccable timing to disrupt run and pass plays. While his athleticism won’t set records, he has the speed to make plays sideline to sideline and match well in pass coverage. Teams will also value his versatility: he has effectively lined up in the box, on the line, and in the slot for the Fighting Irish. The biggest question mark for Viliamu-Asa will be the medicals. He has torn the ACL in both knees at this point, and any lingering damage might scare teams away. He is also a little on the lighter side for an off-ball linebacker in the NFL. He’ll need to add some weight and strength to handle power backs at the next level consistently. Projection Viliamu-Asa will be a coveted player based on his run defense alone, but he has shown the ability to perform well against the pass. His positional versatility and overall impact is something teams covet at the linebacker position, especially as teams prioritize the running game more and more. If the medicals check out in the spring, he could definitely hear his name called on the first night of the Draft. With the poor defensive showing against the Bears, especially in the run game, the Panthers could be one of the many teams interested in Viliamu-Asa’s services next year. Pairing another do-it-all linebacker with Devin Lloyd could really help beef up the middle of the defense in Carolina. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Bears vs. Vikings: How Chicago will keep the momentum going
summary: The Chicago Bears are coming off an impressive, record-setting performance against the Carolina Panthers, but can they keep the momentum going this Sunday against a division rival, the Minnesota Vikings? On the latest Mac & Read show, Evan McLean and Ross Read preview Sunday’s game by spotlighting some of the key player matchups and also […]

title: PFF is wrong about more than just Caleb Williams
summary: The recent attention surrounding an elite performance by Chicago Bears’ quarterback Caleb Williams being graded as rather average by the organization Pro Football Focus has attracted a great deal of well-earned criticism, but it would ultimately be meaningless if it were a simple one-time mistake. It could be as insignificant as an interception thrown in […]
full_text: The recent attention surrounding an elite performance by Chicago Bears’ quarterback Caleb Williams being graded as rather average by the organization Pro Football Focus has attracted a great deal of well-earned criticism, but it would ultimately be meaningless if it were a simple one-time mistake. It could be as insignificant as an interception thrown in the final stages of a game that never even enters the stat line because of a penalty. However, it could also be indicative of an organization that has fundamental flaws in how it approaches and presents its work. Grading Quarterbacks Let’s get the obvious one out of the way. Imagine, for a moment, that you (the person reading this) are driving a perfectly lovely 2014 Honda Accord LX. Now, imagine that next to you is Michael Schumacher magically restored to his athletic peak in a custom-built Ferrari. You both have the same goal–make it across town as efficiently as possible without crashing. Do you think that you will make the same decisions? Do you think that you should make the same decisions? Even if you are a moderately talented driver, there are things Schumacher will be able to do easily that are not even options for you. Pro Football Focus, however, would grade your decisions by the same scale. A lot of quarterbacks have a Honda Accord for an arm, but Caleb Williams has a Ferrari, and they still insist on evaluating the throws he makes by the scale applied to other arms. There are moves he can make, decisions he can access, that simply are not reasonable considerations even for the majority of professional athletes. Josh Allen is another quarterback who fits into this same category, in that he has options to him at the position that are not available to a vast majority of players, and hence the system fails. Caleb Williams DOT to Cole Kmet for the TD 😮‍💨 Absolute seed in double coverage 🔥 (via @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/hUC5ka3bYn — Bleacher Report (@BleacherReport) September 13, 2026 However, I mentioned Michael Schumacher as the driver of this Ferrari, and that’s also relevant to the discussion. Because just as you or I could not drive the Ferrari nearly as well as a professional racecar driver, the average moderately-trained analyst cannot break down defensive tendencies and situations nearly as well as a professional quarterback being guided by Ben Johnson over a week’s worth of film review. Yet, again, PFF believes that they know better how to read defensive tendencies than the quarterback in the situation performing the review. Of course, someone moderately knowledgeable about football should spot a fundamental problem in my driving analogy, and it’s this–most of the time, the other cars on the road will not actively be trying to hinder your (or Schumacher’s) progress. I know it might seem otherwise (cough, Eisenhower Expressway, cough). Teams are actually engaged in a match against each other that is as much mental as it is physical, and aggressive play from the quarterback on a handful of throws can force a defense to react even if those individual throws for that individual play are not as effective. If I’m playing chess, I will gladly sacrifice a pawn to take a rook. If you are playing football, you might gladly take a deep shot where only your receiver can get it even if it doesn’t get a first down if it influences the defense to play the next series differently. The very act of grading a quarterback on a per-play basis ignores the degree to which football works on developing and exploiting tendencies across 60 minutes. Simply put, for all their talk about process , the process Pro Football Focus uses is fundamentally flawed. Drafting Next, however, it’s important to point out that Pro Football Focus fails in other areas. Twice, recently, I have evaluated which “big boards” do the best job of evaluating offensive linemen and edge defenders. With offensive linemen, I compared PFF to Daniel Jeremiah, Jacob Infante , Mock Draft Database’s Consensus Board, and Brandon Thorn. The study had more than a hundred offensive line prospects over three years of the draft. While I originally included PFF only for the sake of a different perspective, I found that Pro Football Focus was the least accurate of any public board I studied, and that only a third of their top prospects were selected near where they were drafted. They frequently disagreed with other boards and with the NFL itself in which players should be valued. Additionally, “when reviewed by a third-party evaluator once they entered the NFL, the prospects uniquely favored by PFF played worse than the players uniquely devalued by them.” In other words, PFF’s draft board preferences for offensive linemen not only did not resemble the players that NFL teams actually wanted to draft, but they also did not resemble the actual performance of those players once they got on the field. As I concluded at the time, “it’s worth asking if their grades are so inaccurate when checked at other times, how valuable can their in-season grades be?” When I pivoted to edge defenders, I also found a disconnect between which players were favored (or disfavored) by Pro Football Focus and which ones were actually productive on the field. This was a more limited study that compared singular measures of performance (such as combine metrics) and also ranking by board evaluators to see if there was any trait that aligned favorably with the performance of a new edge defender in terms of actually generating disruption, measured by pressures and also by disruptive plays (sacks, tackles for a loss, and defended passes). Of all individual public boards, PFF did the worst in terms of aligning their favored players with total pressures generated by edge defenders in their first two years. As I concluded in that article regarding draft prospects, if PFF is an outlier to other systems, it is likely PFF that is in error. Again, it is fine that they disagree in evaluation. However, if they consistently produce player evaluations that do not reflect the actual performance of the players, then what exactly is the value of their product? It’s the Process On a fundamental level, the product that Pro Football Focus puts out is nothing more and nothing less than the subjective evaluation of whether or not a given player tends to act the way that PFF itself thinks they should have acted. It’s an aesthetic score based on a set of normalized evaluators who are asked: “Does the performance look like we think it should look?” For those old enough to remember the media broadcasting of red carpet shows from the Joan Rivers era, PFF tells subscribers whether or not a given player matched the arbitrary fashion rules that they themselves generated. Matcha ✔️ Wired headphones ✔️ QB1 is ready pic.twitter.com/z5iVRpOlbx — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) September 13, 2026 In and of itself, there is nothing wrong with that. As an entertainment product, it’s fine. However, the problem comes from the way that PFF presents itself. By using a number scale (complete with decimal points) and presenting their work as “analytics”, implying a claim to objectivity, they risk engaging in pseudoscience. From Oxford Reference: One of the key differences between science and pseudoscience is that a scientific statement or theory is stated in such as a way as to be falsifiable. In contrast, pseudoscientific statements are usually not falsifiable using objective experimental or observational evidence. Pseudoscience provides no room for challenge and tends to dismiss contradictory evidence or to selectively decide what evidence to accept. The scores they give are not derived from objective measures but instead from vibes. Their methodology is proprietary, too, so it is not possible to have a third party check those vibes. Pro Football Focus seems to want the reputational benefits of claiming that their work is above reproach because it is “fact,” while not actually opening themselves up to the rigor of science by…

title: Are Bears’ Kyler Gordon and Jaylon Johnson receiving bad medical advice?
summary: The Kyler Gordon story just continues to get more and more bizarre, and it certainly took a wild turn this week thanks to Brad Biggs and Dan Bernstein. And this part of the story is not getting a tremendous amount of attention anywhere else. In Brad Biggs’ column, “10 thoughts on the week one win,” […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 06: Kyler Gordon #6 and Jaylon Johnson #1 of the Chicago Bears celebrate a third down stop against the Carolina Panthers at Soldier Field on October 06, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Quinn Harris/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kyler Gordon story just continues to get more and more bizarre, and it certainly took a wild turn this week thanks to Brad Biggs and Dan Bernstein. And this part of the story is not getting a tremendous amount of attention anywhere else. In Brad Biggs’ column, “10 thoughts on the week one win,” he mentioned that he called Montel Fleming, who is the man working with Kyler Gordon away from the facility. He said he answered the phone as “Dr. Moe,” and he discussed Gordon’s treatment plan with Biggs. Dan Bernstein, formerly of The Score and now of 312 Sports, did an entire podcast discussing Fleming further. You can see that video here . Between both of them working on this situation, a lot of alarm bells have gone off. We learned from Biggs that Fleming originally reached out to Jaylon Johnson through Instagram in 2021 and that Johnson was the one who suggested Fleming to Gordon. Since working with Johnson, Johnson has missed 21 games in five seasons. Through a background check, Bernstein learned that Fleming has no medical degrees of any kind; he has several different aliases (as many as 15) and countless addresses, as he has moved all over the country. Any of the websites you find that he claims he is associated with no longer exist or do not mention him on the site. He also has a criminal record, where Bernstein mentioned seven different “criminal entries” in his background profile. Fleming told Biggs that the Bears are too focused on the muscles and that Gordon’s issue is his alignment due to overcompensating from his injury. Fleming focuses on myofascia, which he states can help give the body a better range of motion. Fleming also stated that he works with a chiropractor. Bernstein did mention that he has no idea if the Bears are aware of Fleming, have vetted and approved Fleming, or generally what their stance is on Gordon (and Johnson) working with him. I am not a medical professional, and I certainly am not going to pretend to be one. I have no idea if Fleming’s techniques and concepts are sound. Admittedly, they might be. So I admit Fleming may be very good at this because I don’t have the knowledge to know one way or the other. However, I think it’s very fair to question a man with several aliases who consistently moves around the country, has no evidence anywhere that he has any formal medical training or any kind of medical practice, his websites are a dead end, and he only got involved with the Bears players as a random person who reached out to Jaylon Johnson on social media and not through any medical professionals. That is a lot of red flags. So we have Gordon, who is disagreeing with the Chicago Bears medical staff (that has been appropriately educated and trained in their respective fields) and taking the advice of a man who certainly shows a lot of signs of potentially being a charlatan. When you take all this information into account, you certainly have a better understanding of why Ben Johnson and Ryan Poles have said the things they have said about the situation publicly. This situation continues to be odd, and it certainly just took a turn down an even stranger path. Stay tuned. It will be interesting to see where this story goes next.

title: Week 2 NFL preview: Chicago Bears vs. Minnesota Vikings
summary: Get set for an absolute football chess match. On Sunday, we’re going to see Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson face off against Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Both coaches are some of the best in the league at scheming. The Bears are fresh off putting up 59 points on the Carolina Panthers. While […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates a fourth quarter touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Get set for an absolute football chess match. On Sunday, we’re going to see Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson face off against Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Both coaches are some of the best in the league at scheming. The Bears are fresh off putting up 59 points on the Carolina Panthers. While the Vikings sacked Jordan Love twice and forced two takeaways in a come-from-behind 39-22 win at home. It’s going to be a very interesting game. How many games do we think it will take to win on Sunday? I think if I had to put a number on it, it would be 28 points. The Vikings only scored more than 28 points last year. However, they scored 39 against Green Bay in week one. Let’s meet the Vikings. Minnesota Vikings SB Nation site: Daily Norseman Record: 1-0, first in the NFC North (tied) Game day, time, TV: Sunday, noon CT, FOX Spread: Bears -4.5 Bears all-time record against: 59-69-2, including 1-0 postseason Historical meetings: Week 2 of the 1964 season on Sept. 20. The Bears and Vikings traded scores in the second quarter. Frank Tarkenton hit Bill Brown for a 19-yard score. But Billy Wade answered, finding Rick Casares for a 51-yard touchdown. Next, Wade found Johnny Morris for a 13-yard score. Minnesota answered back before halftime with Hal Bledsoe hauling in a 34-yard touchdown from Tarkenton. In the second half Morris scored again on a 10-yard reception. Minnesota again answered with a Jerry Reichow 10-yard pass from Tarkenton. Wade scored on a one-yard run and in the fourth quarter, Joe Marconi rushed from three yards out for a score, too. The Vikings scored one more touchdown, a 26-yard pass from Tarkenton to Bledsoe, but Chicago won 34-28. Both QBs threw for 300 yards. Wade finished with 3 passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown. Morris had 10 catches for 135 yards and 2 touchdowns. Last meeting: Week 11 last season, the Bears went to Minnesota and squeaked out a 19-17 comeback win. The Bears led 16-3 heading into the fourth quarter and it felt like week one all over again. Set up by a 43-yard punt return, Jordan Mason scored from 16 yards out on a two-play drive for the Vikings to give them their first touchdown of the game. Cairo Santos missed a field goal on the next drive. Following a Minnesota punt, the Bears drove but ultimately punted back to the Vikings with just over 3 minutes left in the game. JJ McCarthy drove the Vikings down and hit Jordan Addison for a 16-yard score with just 50 seconds remaining. Devin Duvernay returned the ensuing kickoff 56 yards. Following three D’Andre Swift rushes, Santos hit a 48-yard walk-off field goal. Injury report – The Vikings listed five players on their Wednesday injury report Limited participation QB Kyler Murray (concussion) LB Blake Cashman (wrist) T Brian O’Neill (knee) OLB Andrew Van Ginkel (chest) Did not participate WR Jauan Jennings (NIR – personal) Offense: The Vikings are ranked third in points, but 29th in yards. Their passing offense ranks 29th and their rushing offense 18th. Kyler Murray is trending/not trending toward playing. In his place, Carson Wentz (63.2 pct cmp./133 yds./3 TD/0 INT) played well and led the Vikings late comeback. Justin Jefferson (8 rec./92 yds./2 TD) is among the best receivers in the league and Wentz (and Murray) are finally good enough for him to ball out again. Jordan Addison (42/610/2 in 2025) didn’t have a catch last week but is still the main No. 2. T.J. Hockenson (4/36/1) and Josh Oliver (2/22/0) were also in the mix. Jordan Mason (15 att./59 yds./1 TD) landed on IR this week with a thumb injury, leaving the veteran Aaron Jones Sr. (12/40/1) as the lead back. DeeJay Dallas (0 att in 2026, 1 catch – 4.3 YPC average in his career) will be the number two, according to coach Kevin O’Connell. Defense: The Vikings defense comes in ranked 12th in points allowed and 28th in yards allowed. Their passing defense ranks 30th and their rushing defense ranks third. Obviously, it’s a small sample size and somewhat skewed by the wild game they played against Green Bay in week one. One thing that’s consistent though, is defensive coordinator Brian Flores’s love of blitzing. Minnesota leads the league in blitz percentage and is third in pressure percentage. They blitzed seven more times than the second team (the Lions) and their percentage of blitzes was 71.7 percent, while Tampa Bay was second at 43.2 percent. The defensive line is led by EDGE rushers Andrew Van Ginkel (1.5 sk/` TFL/2 QB hits/1 FF/1 FR) and Dallas Turner (1 sk/7 QB hits/1 FF). Levi Drake Rodriguez (1 sk/1 TFL/2 QB hits) and Blake Cashman (0.5 sk/7 tkl/2 TFL/2 QB hits) also made some plays. The secondary features James Pierre (2 PD/1 INT/4 tkls) and Byron Murphy (1 PD/8 tkls) and Harrison Smith (1 tkl/1 PD/1 QB hits) are in the secondary, too. Key matchups: Ben Johnson vs. Brian Flores. Let’s not sugarcoat it. The players will execute the schemes, but this is about which coach can achieve the most schematic success against the other. Caleb Williams and the offensive line will have to be on top of their communication to make sure they know where the protections need to be and who is coming. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson have to bounce back from a rough week one outing with Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison coming to town. Key stats The Vikings allowed 28 or more points just twice last season – to the Chargers and Eagles. Last season the Bears scored 24 and 19 points against the Vikings. They lost the 24-point effort. Minnesota allowed just one of Green Bay’s four red zone trips to end in a touchdown. The Vikings scored on all four of their offensive red zone trips. The Bears are second in the league in pressure percentage, according to Pro-Football-Reference . The Vikings allowed 6.3 yards per play to Green Bay. Chicago allowed Carolina 7.7 yards per play. Carson Wentz is 4-0 in his career against the Bears with 5 touchdowns and 0 interceptions and a 91.0 rating.

title: Question of the Day: Will the Chicago Bears break the scoring record?
summary: Let’s just ask the question that’s on everyone’s mind this week. Before the season started, Ben Johnson stated that he wanted to break the all-time scoring mark, which was set by the 2013 Denver Broncos, who scored 606 points and averaged 37.9 points per game. Everyone blew off the comment as “Ben being Ben,” but […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-SEPTEMBER 14: Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson communicates from the sidelines during an NFL football game between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 14, 2025. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Let’s just ask the question that’s on everyone’s mind this week. Before the season started, Ben Johnson stated that he wanted to break the all-time scoring mark, which was set by the 2013 Denver Broncos, who scored 606 points and averaged 37.9 points per game. Everyone blew off the comment as “Ben being Ben,” but after scoring 59 points with no defensive or special teams touchdowns, suddenly everyone started talking around the league that perhaps Johnson might have a shot at this. Will the Chicago Bears break the all-time scoring record? Now the Bears get an extra game, so they don’t have to average quite as many points; 35.7 points per game gets them to 607 points and the record. Thanks to the 59-point outburst, the Bears now just need to average 34.25 points per game the rest of the way to get the record. Can they do it? How many points do you think they’ll finish the season with? Answer: I just want to run with this thing and go all-in and say yes, but it’s still so many points to score. One 17-point game basically just wipes out any chance they have at this thing. So no, I don’t think the Bears will break the all-time scoring record. But I do think there are several things that this offense will accomplish. The 1985 Bears hold the team record for most points in a season at 456. I think that record gets obliterated. I think the Bears easily score 500 points this season. I also think the Bears could have a top-ten offense all-time. To break into the top 10, the Bears would need to score 540 points in the regular season (not per game as previously reported). With the 59-point outburst, the Bears need to average 30.1 points per game the rest of the way to get there. I think that is certainly possible, and I would go as far as to say that’s probable. This Bears offense is going to put up some historic numbers; I’m confident about that, but I just don’t think that 607 points will be in the cards in 2026. What do you say, Bears fans? Do you think they can break the all-time scoring record? How many points do you think they will score? Sound off in the comments section!

This is a mark I think Caleb should grab this year but like Week 1 showed, this team still wants to run the football with authority. In the middle-middle, I’m bringing back the trackers for receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns to track how all the weapons are doing. Remember you can click on the graph to pull up catches. And finally, as a last minute edition, let’s track total team points against the franchise leading 456 from the 1985 team and the NFL record of 606 points from the 2013 Broncos. Obviously, the modern NFL schedule is 17 games where those teams only had 16 contests to rack up points, but that’s where we’ll start. If the Bears challenge those marks we can start to pull in the points per game. We’ll stick with the raw totals for now. Having laid out the tracker…what an incredible start. Caleb will pass Jim Harbaugh for 8th in passing touchdowns soon, hopefully this Sunday against the Vikings. This should be an incredibly fun season to track. If something new and interesting pops up throughout the year, we’ll add new elements.

title: 9 questions with Bengals WR Ja’Marr Chase
summary: We recently had a unique opportunity to chat virtually with Bengals star receiver Ja’Marr Chase. Fabletics and Chase’s new partnership with the activewear brand made this opportunity possible. In conjunction with The Orange and Black Insider podcast, its hosts Anthony Cosenza and John Sheeran, as well as with Cincy Jungle and A to Z Sports, […]
full_text: We recently had a unique opportunity to chat virtually with Bengals star receiver Ja’Marr Chase. Fabletics and Chase’s new partnership with the activewear brand made this opportunity possible. In conjunction with The Orange and Black Insider podcast, its hosts Anthony Cosenza and John Sheeran, as well as with Cincy Jungle and A to Z Sports, Fabletics gave us an opportunity to have a back-and-forth with the team’s star receiver. We fired off questions to “Uno” as the season kicked off, and he gave us his thoughts on a number of topics pertaining to the team. The Bengals are 1-0 and are seemingly heading in a great direction for the season. Chase is and will continue to be a major component of the team’s success. You’ve been very open about the expectations surrounding the Bengals this year. With the additions Cincinnati made on defense, particularly Dexter Lawrence, what feels different about this team heading into 2026 compared with the teams you’ve been part of in the past? JC: It just feels like we’re more complete. We know what we can do on offense, and adding guys like Dex on defense helps take us to that next level. He makes his presence known every day in practice. The foundation is there, now we’ve just got to go win. You’ve accomplished virtually everything individually that a receiver can accomplish, but the Super Bowl remains the obvious team goal. Has your mindset changed at all as you’ve gotten further into your career in terms of balancing individual success with that bigger goal? JC: At this point, winning is what matters. I want a Super Bowl. That’s always the goal. Everything else comes with that. You and Joe Burrow have been together since 2021, and your connection has obviously become one of the defining QB-receiver relationships in the NFL. Is there still a part of that relationship or your on-field chemistry that you feel you can take to another level in 2026? JC: For sure. There’s always more. Me and Joe have been doing this a long time, so we know what the other one is thinking. But we’re never satisfied. We can always get better, make more plays and keep pushing each other. That’s the fun part of the game. Joe Burrow said he’s getting 2019 LSU vibes from this team. What do you remember about the leadup to that season, and do you also feel something similar now with the Bengals? JC: Back then, we knew we had something special before everybody else did. It was just about going out and proving it. I feel some of that now. We know what we’ve got in this locker room. Now we’ve got to show it on the field. After a full training camp going up against DJ Turner II, how does he challenge you in practice and how do you feel you’ve helped each other get better? JC: DJ competes. He’s fast, he’s physical, and he’s going to make you work every rep. That’s what you want in practice. I make him better, he makes me better. We’re going at it every day. With Dohnte Meyers officially making the team, what has impressed you the most about him this offseason? JC: He comes in ready to work, competes and isn’t scared of the moment. I like that about him. He earned his spot. At this point in your career, defenses obviously know exactly what you’re capable of. What part of being Ja’Marr Chase on a football field has become more of a mental game for you — recognizing coverages, manipulating defenders, understanding what Joe is seeing — rather than simply relying on athletic ability? JC: It’s a lot more mental now. They know what I’m trying to do, I know what they’re trying to do. So it’s like, alright, who’s gonna win? I’m watching where the safety is, how the DB is playing me, where the help is coming from. Me and Joe usually see the same thing, so I already know where I need to be. Then it’s just setting the DB up. Make him think he’s got me figured out, then give him something different. That’s the fun part for me now. You think you know what’s coming? Cool. Stop it. Your Fabletics partnership is pretty different from a traditional athlete endorsement because you’ve had a significant hand in the actual creative process. What was something in the collection where you said, “That’s got to be changed,” and what did you ultimately get them to do? JC: I care about what I wear. On the field, in the gym, wherever. It’s got to look right and feel right. That’s what I like about working with Fabletics. I actually get to be in it. I’m not just putting my name on something. I’m wearing it, testing it, telling them what I think. For me, it’s always about fit, and I’m picky about that. Something can look good, but if I put it on and it doesn’t move right or sit the way I want, I’m gonna say something. But it’s also about having the right pieces, all the way down to the stuff people forget. Accessories are where a lot of brands stop paying attention. That’s where I pushed hardest. I wanted a skull cap. I wanted a balaclava. Things I’m actually reaching for in December in Cincinnati, not just things that look good in a photo. Fabletics ran with all of it, and now that’s some of the gear I’m most excited about. The phrase “Chasing No One” has been associated with your Fabletics collection. What does that phrase mean to you personally at this stage of your career? JC: I’m really just focused on being better than I was yesterday. That’s it. I’m not watching what everybody else is doing. I know what I can do, and I know I can still get better. So, I’m chasing the best version of me. Numéro uno. Our thanks to Ja’Marr Chase and Fabletics for this exclusive opportunity. We can’t wait to see all of the great things Chase will continue to do in 2026 and the years ahead! title: Nico Collins injury news means Mitchell Tinsley could play vs. Bengals
summary: As the Cincinnati Bengals get set to face the Texans, they may go up against a familiar face Sunday in Houston. On Wednesday, Pro Bowl wide receiver Nico Collins suffered a Grade 1 hamstring strain in practice. That led to him missing Thursday’s practice, and it looks like there’s a good chance he misses Sunday’s […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Mitchell Tinsley (82) catches a pass in the end zone for a touchdown in the fourth quarter of the NFL Week 12 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the New England Patriots at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Sunday, Nov. 23, 2025. The Bengals fall to 3-8 with a 26-20 loss at home. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co As the Cincinnati Bengals get set to face the Texans , they may go up against a familiar face Sunday in Houston. On Wednesday, Pro Bowl wide receiver Nico Collins suffered a Grade 1 hamstring strain in practice . That led to him missing Thursday’s practice, and it looks like there’s a good chance he misses Sunday’s game. Making matters worse for the Texans is that they’re already without wide receivers Tank Dell and Jayden Higgins. Now that Collins is potentially out, there’s a very real chance the Bengals will see former wide receiver Mitchell Tinsley on the field Sunday. Tinsley, who made the Bengals’ 53-man roster last year, was arguably the toughest cut the team had to make this year when it came time to make final cuts. Once Tinsley cleared waivers, he opted not to join the Bengals practice squad. Instead, Tinsley signed with Houston’s practice squad, and that decision could pay off this week with Houston hurting at wide receiver. If Collins is inactive, the Texans have only four other receivers on the 53-man roster, so at least one receiver would be assured of getting a gameday call-up from the practice squad, and possibly two. Will that be Tinsley? There are actually three other receivers on the practice squad — Josh Kelly, Daniel Sobkowicz, and Lewis Bond — so it’s not a done deal that Tinsley would be called up. Kelly, Sobkowicz, and Bond were all with the Texans this offseason and through training camp, so they could be ahead of Tinsley in the pecking order for a gameday call-up. Still, Tinsley not only made the 53-man roster last year, but also made several big plays in the regular season. He’s certainly someone to keep an eye on heading into the weekend. I expect Nico Collins to miss Week 2 with an acute grade 1 hamstring strain. He will be 50/50 in Week 3 and likely miss as well. It’s not worth the risk of progressing his mild grade 1 to a moderate grade 2. He had a grade 2 in 2024 and missed 5 weeks. title: Beyond the Box Score: Say what you want about Zac Taylor, but he’s striking the right chords so far this season
summary: Just before training camp got underway in late July, Bengals head coach Zac Taylor wrote on a board during a team meeting: The Bengals’ 2025 record— 6-11. Even after a great offseason on the field and from the front office that, from a fan’s perspective, put last season’s disaster in the rearview mirror, Taylor pushed […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 13: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals celebrates 33-27 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with fans after the game at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just before training camp got underway in late July, Bengals head coach Zac Taylor wrote on a board during a team meeting: The Bengals’ 2025 record— 6-11. Even after a great offseason on the field and from the front office that, from a fan’s perspective, put last season’s disaster in the rearview mirror, Taylor pushed the right button by reminding the players that last season wasn’t good enough. Let’s not forget that while a lot of players from last year aren’t here, a lot of last year’s team still is. That created the sense of urgency we saw throughout the offseason and training camp. That sense of urgency carried into the preseason and Week 1, when the Bengals beat the Buccaneers 33-27 to start the season 1-0. Some say Week 1 is a liar, and that may be true. However, I put a lot of stock in Week 1. It’s the first game of the season, and it sets the tone. Tampa Bay came into Sunday with five straight season-opening wins, the second-longest streak in the NFL behind the Philadelphia Eagles. Baker Mayfield had thrown nine touchdowns in Week 1 over his first three seasons with the Buccaneers. On Sunday, the Bengals became the first team since Week 16 of 2018 to have a scoop-and-score against the Buccaneers, snapped Tampa Bay’s five-game winning streak in Week 1, and held Baker Mayfield without a touchdown pass. They also forced and recovered three fumbles from Mayfield and recovered a fourth fumble from the Buccaneers. Zac Taylor had the Bengals ready to play. The Bengals’ defense, much-maligned over the last three years, was all over the field for the entire 60 minutes. They didn’t force a punt, but they forced four turnovers. That makes up for not forcing a punt. Before training camp, Taylor also challenged his coordinators to make sure they’re using their great talent accordingly. On Sunday, Al Golden’s defense sacked Mayfield four times and recovered four fumbles. They also held Tampa Bay to two field goals, including on a promising first drive for the Buccaneers. They even held the Bucs to just 282 total yards. They held just two teams under 300 yards last year: The 5-12 Cleveland Browns and the 3-14 Arizona Cardinals. The Bengals’ defense will also improve, and their leaders will make sure of it. For what it’s worth, the Bengals only punted once, and their offense, after a three-and-out on their first drive, scored on five of their next seven drives. One of those drives ran out the clock in the fourth quarter. After the Bengals’ first preseason game, Zac Taylor said in the locker room that they had to get better at finishing games with their four-minute offense. On Sunday, the Bengals ran out the final 3:14 of the clock on offense. They were aggressive, headlined by Burrow’s dart to a leaping Tee Higgins over the middle, and efficient, facing only one third down, which came when they were already in the red zone. Evan McPherson was named a captain on the Monday before the season started. On Sunday, McPherson made four field goals, including three in the second half. Two of those field goals were from at least 55 yards, including a 58-yarder at the start of the fourth quarter. Those two 55+ yard field goals accounted for six points. The Bengals won the game by six points. McPherson earned Week 1 AFC Special Teams Player of the Week for his performance. Taylor has his imprint all over this team. He called a great game on Sunday, has command of the locker room, holds his coordinators accountable, and has let go of any arrogance he may have had the last three years. Success can affect people in different ways. The Bengals got so close to winning the Super Bowl in 2021 and 2022. That may have given Taylor and the front office the impression they were set for the next several seasons. What followed, of course, was two straight 9-8 seasons with a playoff berth, but Taylor and the front office may have thought they had gotten unlucky with injuries and just needed to change a few things to get back into contention. Then 2025 happened. That humbled Taylor, the front office, and Joe Burrow, not to mention everybody on the roster who went through last year. What followed was an offseason that felt different. Zac Taylor sounded different. He sounded more urgent, recognizing the front office went all-in this offseason and sent a message: win this year, or maybe this is it for the Bengals’ head coach. Sunday after the game, Taylor gave Bengals’ director of player personnel Duke Tobin a game ball for his 200th win as a member of the Bengals. That shows respect and that there is alignment within the organization not seen since… maybe ever in the franchise’s history. This is a confident Bengals team, but it’s not an arrogant Bengals team. In 2021 and 2022, they went about business as a confident group, but arrogance eventually may have seeped in. That’s why this offseason offered the opportunity for a complete reset, and Zac Taylor looks and sounds like he did just that. Taylor is striking the right chords as a leader, and the players, including Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and Dexter Lawrence, are rallying around him. Urgency is at an all-time high, and the steady-handed, positive identity and culture Taylor created from the moment he arrived are driving it. Like the Bengals did this offseason, Taylor evolved as a leader, and it’s already paying dividends.

title: Bengals Film Room: Turnovers lead the way for revamped defense vs. Bucs
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 33-27 in a matchup between two teams desperate to return to the playoffs in 2026. The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles on Sunday. Each play led to the Bengals putting points on the board. On the Bengals’ first forced fumble, they trailed 3-0, fresh off an […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 33-27 in a matchup between two teams desperate to return to the playoffs in 2026. The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles on Sunday. Each play led to the Bengals putting points on the board. On the Bengals’ first forced fumble, they trailed 3-0, fresh off an offense that went 3-and-out to start the game. Initial pressure from Boye Mafe forced Baker Mayfield to step up into secondary pressure from Barrett Carter. As Carter got Mayfield in his grasp, Myles Murphy came from behind to hit Baker. The hit jarred the ball loose, and Demetrius Knight Jr. picked it up for the scoop-and-score. That play electrified the crowd and gave the Bengals an early 7-3 lead. A fantastic play from every angle pic.twitter.com/d7MnzfbWPX — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Bengals’ second forced fumble and recovery came on the Buccaneers’ very next possession. Bryan Cook came up and hit Bucky Irving, knocking the ball out. Boye Mafe combined with Cook on that hit, and Cook also had the awareness to recover the fumble. That play set the Bengals up in their own territory to begin the next drive. Ultimately, leading to a two-yard Mike Gesicki touchdown reception. Bryan Cook was feeling himself here, as he should. Great awareness from Mafe to recover the fumble. pic.twitter.com/GeEFJXg7Ff — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Buccaneers bounced back by driving down the field on their next possession. However, they would turn it over for a third straight time near the end zone. Dexter Lawrence pushed the guard directly into Baker Mayfield’s lap, nearly coming up with his first sack as a Bengal. A holding penalty went uncalled, and Mayfield escaped Lawrence’s grasp and took off toward the goal line. This time, Barrett Carter made the play, knocking the ball out of Baker Mayfield’s hands before he could score the touchdown. Bryan Cook recovered it in the end zone. The Bengals then went on a 12-play, 80-yard touchdown drive capped by a Chase Brown run. While we were robbed of a Sexy Dexy celebration, we will take the third turnover of the first half all day long. pic.twitter.com/nL3Ak1RWhO — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 The Bengals’ fourth and final forced fumble and recovery came in the fourth quarter. Holding a 10-point lead, Boye Mafe was able to get the sack-fumble on Mayfield. TJ Slaton came up with the fumble recovery, which ultimately led to another Evan McPherson field goal. The Bengals 4th forced fumble and recovery of the day was caused by Boye Mafe. Mafe was highly impressive generating pressure throughout the game on Sunday. pic.twitter.com/yi25Q1gVuS — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 14, 2026 Just an impressive performance by the Bengals defense overall. Playing opportunistic defense, making the hustle plays to create turnovers, and players having the awareness to recover each one of them shows a defense that has the talent to keep improving throughout the season. A great debut for the revamped defense on Sunday.
author: Dale Altman

title: Browns signing one of Shedeur Sanders’ favorite receivers, reportedly
summary: The never-ending roster process of the NFL is why we are cautious about not calling the initial 53-man roster “the final 53-man roster,” as it used to be referred to. Cleveland Browns GM Andrew Berry is always looking to improve the roster, from the top to the bottom, and is unafraid to make moves, even […]
full_text: Sep 16, 2023; Boulder, Colorado, USA; Colorado Buffaloes wide receiver Xavier Weaver (10) and quarterback Shedeur Sanders (2) and running back Kavosiey Smoke (8) and wide receiver Jimmy Horn Jr. (5) before the game against the Colorado State Rams at Folsom Field. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The never-ending roster process of the NFL is why we are cautious about not calling the initial 53-man roster “the final 53-man roster,” as it used to be referred to. Cleveland Browns GM Andrew Berry is always looking to improve the roster, from the top to the bottom, and is unafraid to make moves, even some that are unpopular . On Monday, the Browns made eight roster moves , including placing RB Dylan Sampson on injured reserve. A majority of those moves involved the practice squad, a unit that Berry uses to evaluate players as much as reinforce the 53-man roster. According to a report, Cleveland is now bringing in WR Jimmy Horn Jr. , former college teammate of QB Shedeur Sanders : Sources: The #Browns are expected to sign former #Panthers WR Jimmy Horn Jr. The former Colorado standout was college teammates with Shedeur Sanders and now reunites with him in Cleveland. pic.twitter.com/7BcsQWTeiC — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) September 17, 2026 With Horn passing through waivers, it is likely that he will be signing to the Browns practice squad. Horn spent his final two college seasons with Sanders at the University of Colorado, where he caught 95 passes for just over 1,000 yards with seven touchdowns. Horn actually outproduced Heisman Trophy winner Travis Hunter in 2023, before Hunter’s trophy-winning season in 2024. Last year, with the Carolina Panthers, Horn played in 13 games, contributing 11 receptions for 108 yards. Horn also returned seven kicks for Carolina, Cleveland’s Week 3 opponent.

full_text: With Week 2 of the NFL season set to kick off, several games beyond the Cleveland Browns’ matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers could catch the attention of Browns fans. Of the various matchups, which games should Browns fans be paying the closest attention to? The Los Angeles Rams, fresh off their Week 1 loss and DE Myles Garrett going on injured reserve after surgery , look to stave off an 0-2 start against the New York Giants on Monday Night Football. A loss could dramatically impact Cleveland’s future draft options. The Cincinnati Bengals and Houston Texans will face off at 1:00 PM EST on Sunday. This game, in particular, could provide a clearer picture of where two important AFC teams currently stand. The Texans are coming off a tough loss to the Buffalo Bills and will be hoping to prove something in Week 2. They will want to show that they are real contenders in the AFC. The Bengals are coming off a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and will be looking to get off to a fast start this season. While it is still early in the season, this matchup could indicate some things about teams that could make a postseason run this year. The Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs will be facing off on Sunday Night Football this week, another matchup that could be meaningful for the AFC picture this season. The Chiefs are coming off of a big 31-10 win against the Denver Broncos, who almost made it to the Super Bowl last season. The Chiefs will be hoping to show they are still the leaders in the AFC as Patrick Mahomes is returning from his injury. The Colts are coming off of a tough loss to the Baltimore Ravens, but certainly could still be in the mix this season. title: The Cowboys defense needs to lean into Caleb Downs
summary: For a while it seemed like everybody sort of forgot about Caleb Downs. This seemed impossible right after the Dallas Cowboys drafted him. Downs was the story for the team, so much so that wars were being fought on the internet about how a veteran on the team should forfeit his jersey number so that […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Downs #13 of the Dallas Cowboys during the game against the New York Giants on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For a while it seemed like everybody sort of forgot about Caleb Downs. This seemed impossible right after the Dallas Cowboys drafted him. Downs was the story for the team, so much so that wars were being fought on the internet about how a veteran on the team should forfeit his jersey number so that Downs could have the one that he wanted. However you felt about that, the Downs hype sort of cooled as training camp wore on. To be clear this wasn’t about Downs in any way, but other storylines developed. The Cowboys have a lot of new faces on their team this season, specifically on the defensive side of the ball, and as football fans were are often distracted by the shiniest object at any given moment in time. Downs reminded everyone who he is during the season opener, though. The Cowboys need to lean into Caleb Downs We have speculated/known for a long time that the Cowboys are going to use Downs in a variety of ways. To be clear this is a good idea. He is enormously talented and can do tons of different things. Benefit from that however you can. Last week is a good example of this (it is admittedly the only actual example from his career to date, obviously). Dallas lined Downs up in the slot on 29 of his 60 defensive snaps (including 26 snaps when the team was in nickel), all data here is from NFL Pro , and gave him three pass rush attempts on New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart. That last bit is particularly important. Downs is a defensive back. He is not a pass rusher. His true value may not wind up being in the slot anyway. We are still figuring this out. But consider that of his three pass rush attempts that Downs generated a pressure on each of them. He had the sack and forced fumble that everybody saw, and according to Zebra Technologies it was actually the fastest sack that any player in Week 1 recorded (2.49 seconds). You don’t have to get home every time, though. If you are generating pressures then you are causing disruption which the rest of the team stands to benefit from. This was the first game in which a Cowboys defensive back recorded at least three pressures in a game since Donovan Wilson did it in Week 3 of 2022, coincidentally also against the Giants. This isn’t to say that Downs has to have a certain number of pass rushes a game, but it is to say that he has to do everything. Play nickel. Rush the passer. Drop back and play safety. It may seem intense to assign this much responsibility to a rookie, but if there were ever one who has earned that so early on it is him. Plus, why throw out some hypothetical point in time where it is believed he will be more “ready” than he is now? Does anyone seriously believe that he can’t handle that type of responsibility/usage now? There are a number of ways to lean into Downs as noted, but the point is that each and every one of them has to be explored and as often as possible.

title: 2026 Week 2 rooting guide for Cowboys fans
summary: While the Cowboys didn’t handle their own business last Sunday night, they weren’t the only projected NFC contender with a bad season opener. In addition to hoping Dallas corrects course in Week 2, what else can we root for in this week’s schedule? Last week, the preseason favorite Los Angeles Rams were dominated at home […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Dallas Cowboys fans can only watch as the New York Giants control the ball in the final minutes of their loss at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, September 13, 2026. (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images) While the Cowboys didn’t handle their own business last Sunday night, they weren’t the only projected NFC contender with a bad season opener. In addition to hoping Dallas corrects course in Week 2, what else can we root for in this week’s schedule? Last week, the preseason favorite Los Angeles Rams were dominated at home by the 49ers and lost Myles Garrett for at least a month. The Packers were the only NFC North team to lose a game, getting blown out by the Vikings and… Carson Wentz?! Will Week 2 go more according to the oddsmaker’s script, or will we be reevaluating our predictions for the NFC? For the Cowboys’ sake, let’s hope last week was the outlier. In addition to Dallas righting the ship against the Commanders, what else should Cowboys fans be rooting for in Week 2? NFC East teams Titans d. Eagles Rams d. Giants Until we’re much further down the road, it’s hard to imagine ever rooting for one of our division rivals to win. That’s especially true here: both Philly and New York are 1-0, and their opponents are relatively irrelevant to Dallas. The Rams losing last week only makes it easier to root for them, even if they’re still a top threat for playoff seeding. Unfortunately, Tennessee might be one of the worst teams in the league this year. So if they hang a loss on Philadelphia, even as the home team, it will be a huge upset. NFC vs. NFC Falcons d. Panthers Vikings d. Bears Cardinals d. Seahawks Some of this may be splitting hairs, but we expect Carolina, Chicago, and Seattle to be more competitive overall this season than their Week 2 opponents. These picks are about those projected contenders taking losses, which will hopefully help Dallas later with playoff seeding. You never know how a September result could help decide who gets a bye week, home game, or some other postseason bonus. NFC vs. AFC Bills d. Lions Jets d. Packers Ravens d. Saints Browns d. Bucs Dolphins d. 49ers It’s a heavy interconference slate this week, and we can freely root for the AFC in every matchup. About the only time we’d root for an NFC team to win one of these is if it helped us with a future draft pick, like whenever the Steelers or Texans face an NFC opponent. But outside of those, or perhaps some rare scenarios that present themselves later this season, NFC losses are always preferred. AFC vs. AFC Patriots d. Steelers Bengals d. Texans As we just mentioned, monitoring the Steelers and Texans’ games is relevant for Dallas because of the 2027 draft. We own the Steelers’ fourth-round pick from the Broderick Jones trade, and the Texans’ seventh-rounder after sending them Nate Thomas. Scenarios may present later where we’d prefer that Pittsburgh or Houston win, like when the Steelers play the Eagles in Week 11. The Texans will play every NFC East team this year, and we’d certainly prefer losses for our division foes to a higher seventh-round pick. But for now, against other AFC teams, our rooting choice is clear.
