title: How the Cowboys can best use CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens
summary: It seems so easy. The Dallas Cowboys employ one of the better quarterbacks in the NFL in Dak Prescott as well as perhaps the best wide receiver duo across the league in CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Boom. Done. Anyone can call plays. Just get them the ball, right? That is sort of how we […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 17: (L-R) George Pickens #3 and CeeDee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys celebrate a touchdown during the second quarter against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on November 17, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images It seems so easy. The Dallas Cowboys employ one of the better quarterbacks in the NFL in Dak Prescott as well as perhaps the best wide receiver duo across the league in CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Boom. Done. Anyone can call plays. Just get them the ball, right? That is sort of how we all tend to look at this kind of thing, but obviously there is more nuance to this idea, especially as the duo accrues more games together and defenses can devise plans to slow them down, or stop them outright. Last week’s season-opening loss was hardly the most impressive game that Lamb and Pickens have ever played together, but perhaps there is something that can be learned about what happened. And specifically what didn’t. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens can overwhelm defenses The old adage is that you can’t double both of the star pass-catchers on a given team. If one is drawing double coverage then the other has a larger opportunity, theoretically speaking, to capitalize. Living inside of this sort of argument, imagine if they lined up next to each other. Imagine if you were on one side of the defense and they were within about an arm’s reach of each other. Right off of the line of scrimmage, once the ball was snapped, it would be a bit overwhelming for you and your defensive teammates to figure out how to keep everything in front of you. This idea was highlighted a bit during this week’s insights inside of NFL Pro . It is important to note that the season is as young as it possibly can be which means that the sample size is as small as it possibly can be. Still, we are building this plane as we fly. Consider that last week the Cowboys ran 32 offensive plays where Lamb and Pickens were on opposite sides of the formation. It makes sense to do this. Spread the wealth, so to speak. In total, nine of these 32 plays led to conversions for a first down and the Cowboys averaged 4.6 yards per play on them. But what about plays where they lined up on the same side of the formation? There were only three plays of this variety, again a super small sample size, but the Cowboys converted all three of them for first downs. They averaged 6.3 yards per play on them, a clear difference. Beyond this being a super small sample size, there are a number of factors that could have led to this difference. The takeaway should not be: “ I’ve seen what I need to see. Lamb and Pickens should line up on the same side of the formation all of the time!“ But is it fair to ask the question as to whether or not that should happen at a higher rate? Even a slightly higher one? At the very least in the interest of gathering more data? The Cowboys operate a lot out of 11 personnel and have a third receiver in Ryan Flournoy who is capable of succeeding in his own right. And to the old adage referenced above, if the Lamb and Pickens side of the formation is drawing exorbitant levels of coverage then the other side would surely be all the more exposed, no? It is an idea worth considering. Surely Brian Schottenheimer has kicked it around in his mind, too.
author: RJ Ochoa

title: History says Cowboys can bounce back against the Commanders
summary: Week 1 didn’t go according to plan for the Dallas Cowboys. A 28-20 defeat to the New York Giants leaves Dallas looking for its first win of the season, but there may not be many opponents Brian Schottenheimer’s team would rather see coming through the doors of AT&T Stadium than the Washington Commanders. Washington is […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Jake Ferguson #87 of the Dallas Cowboys catches a touchdown against Quan Martin #20 of the Washington Commanders in the first quarter of a game at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 1 didn’t go according to plan for the Dallas Cowboys. A 28-20 defeat to the New York Giants leaves Dallas looking for its first win of the season, but there may not be many opponents Brian Schottenheimer’s team would rather see coming through the doors of AT&T Stadium than the Washington Commanders. Washington is also 0-1 after losing 24-22 to the Philadelphia Eagles, meaning Sunday’s home opener already carries some extra importance. One NFC East team will leave the game 0-2. We look at the reasons to be positive for this week’s game. The first reason to be positive about this game is Dak Prescott has owned Washington (we concede he also owned the Giants previously). Prescott has faced the Commanders 15 times in his career and has a remarkable 13-2 record. In those games he has thrown for 3,716 yards, 32 touchdowns against only five interceptions, with a 107.4 passer rating. That is already impressive, but his record against Washington when the game is played in Dallas is even better. Prescott is a perfect 7-0 at home against Washington. Across those seven games he has completed 68% of his passes, thrown 20 touchdowns without a single interception, and produced a 126.4 passer rating. Washington visited AT&T Stadium last October and Dallas hammered the Commanders 44-22. Prescott completed 21 of 30 passes for 264 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions, finishing with a 130.4 passer rating. Dallas produced 409 yards of offense and scored on three of its four trips inside the red zone. And it wasn’t just Prescott who enjoyed that matchup. Javonte Williams rushed for 116 yards and a touchdown, averaging a whopping 6.1 yards per carry. CeeDee Lamb caught five passes for 110 yards and a touchdown, while George Pickens added 82 receiving yards. Then there was Jake Ferguson. Ferguson caught all seven passes thrown his way and scored two touchdowns. Washington simply couldn’t stop all of Dallas’ weapons at the same time. That becomes especially interesting after what happened to Washington against Philadelphia on Sunday as tight ends seem to be the Commanders kryptonite. Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert caught four passes for a team leading 77 yards and scored two touchdowns against the Commanders. One of those went for 43 yards. Jalen Hurts finished the game with three touchdown passes and no interceptions. Ferguson therefore enters this game knowing both that he has already hurt Washington around the goal line and that Philadelphia just found success attacking the same defense with its tight end. There are also positives Dallas can take from the Giants loss despite the final score. The biggest one came after halftime. Dallas only had two offensive possessions in the entire second half because New York controlled the clock for so long. The Cowboys scored a touchdown on both of them. One was a 12-play, 75-yard drive finished by a Williams touchdown run. The next time Dallas got the football, Prescott quickly drove the offense down the field again and found Williams for a 17-yard touchdown reception. In other words, Dallas’ offense finished the game by scoring touchdowns every time it touched the ball in the second half. Williams also finished Week 1 with two total touchdowns, one rushing and one receiving. CeeDee Lamb scored Dallas’ other touchdown, while Prescott threw two touchdown passes. The final offensive numbers were disappointing because Dallas simply didn’t have the football enough, but there were signs late in the game that the unit was beginning to find a rhythm. If that continues into the home opener, Washington could have a difficult afternoon. There were also flashes from the Cowboys’ rebuilt defense that deserve attention. Rookie safety Caleb Downs recorded his first NFL sack, blasting Jaxson Dart and forcing a fumble that New York recovered. Quinnen Williams then created Dallas’ first takeaway of the season when he forced another fumble that Shavon Revel recovered. Those individual plays matter this week because Washington’s offensive line is already missing its most accomplished blocker. Five-time Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil is on injured reserve after suffering a torn triceps. Washington has moved Brandon Coleman back outside to replace him. Defensive tackle Jer’Zhan Newton is also on injured reserve, as is cornerback Trey Amos. Tunsil’s absence in particular gives Dallas’ defensive front an opportunity. The Cowboys didn’t produce consistent enough pressure against New York, but Quinnen Williams showed that he can wreck a play, Downs showed Christian Parker is willing to send pressure from the secondary, and Dallas now gets to attack a Washington offensive line without its star left tackle . Jayden Daniels also didn’t exactly explode out of the blocks in Week 1. Against Philadelphia, Daniels completed only 18 of 34 passes, a completion rate of 52%, for just 164 passing yards. He did throw two touchdowns without an interception, but much of Washington’s passing production arrived during its late comeback attempt. Dallas has also shown before that it can make Daniels uncomfortable. The Cowboys don’t need their rebuilt defense to suddenly become perfect. They simply need more of those disruptive plays and, most importantly, need to get off the field so Prescott and the offense have more opportunities. Washington also came out of Week 1 with some new injury concerns. Tight end Chig Okonkwo left the Philadelphia game with a hamstring injury, while linebacker Frankie Luvu and special teams standout Tyler Owens also suffered injuries. Their availability for Dallas will become clearer later this week. Luvu’s situation is particularly worth monitoring. He is one of Washington’s most important defensive players and part of a pass rush that Dallas will need to account for with Tyler Smith still on injured reserve. The final reason to be positive is that Dallas had to open its season on the road in a primetime divisional game. Now the Cowboys return to AT&T Stadium for their home opener, against an opponent Prescott has never lost to at home. Washington, meanwhile, has to play its second consecutive divisional road game after beginning the season in Philadelphia. The Commanders go from Lincoln Financial Field straight into another difficult NFC East environment while Dallas gets its first home game of the year. That’s an extremely tough condition for the Commanders to be in.
author: Mike Poland

title: Cowboys LB DeMarvion Overshown’s health continues to be a major concern
summary: DeMarvion Overshown is one of the most talented players that the Dallas Cowboys have on either side of the ball. When he’s on the field, he has the ability to move sideline-to-sideline with his speed and athleticism, he can rush the passer if need be, and as a former safety, he has the ability to […]
full_text: DeMarvion Overshown is one of the most talented players that the Dallas Cowboys have on either side of the ball. When he’s on the field, he has the ability to move sideline-to-sideline with his speed and athleticism, he can rush the passer if need be, and as a former safety, he has the ability to make plays in coverage. Those are excellent traits to have for any linebacker, and he simply makes the Cowboys’ defense better when he’s in uniform (except on this past Sunday night). However, as the old saying goes, a player’s best ability is availability. In that department, Overshown hasn’t had the best of luck. In fact, it’s been a constant struggle for him to remain healthy, and it started as soon as he was drafted. When Overshown was selected in the third round with the 90th overall pick in 2023, the buzz was huge around Dallas. Unfortunately, it ended almost as soon as it started as he wouldn’t even play a snap in his rookie season due to tearing the ACL in his left knee that August in the preseason. The Cowboys still managed to go 12-5 and made the playoffs, but there’s no telling how better their defense would have been with him on the field. The 2024 season saw Overshown take the league by storm. Although the Cowboys weren’t good as a team, Overshown proved that he had what it takes to be an effective player. He racked up 90 tackles, eight tackles for loss, five sacks, five quarterback hits, one interception (returned for a touchdown), four pass breakups, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. As great as his performance was, Overshown missed the last month of the season as he tore the ACL, MCL, and PCL in his right knee. This forced him to miss the first 10 games of the 2025 season. He was activated in Week 11 against the Las Vegas Raiders, and logged 28 tackles in the six games he played in. Once again, he had to miss a little bit of time as he was out for the final two games with a concussion. Dallas has only played one game so far in 2026, but Overshown is expected to miss 1-2 weeks with a hamstring issue. Luckily, the time frame isn’t long, but it’s just the latest in a long list of injuries for Overshown. As good of a player as Overshown is, it just seems like they’ll always be something he has to deal with. It’s a very frustrating thing for Overshown and the Cowboys, especially considering that their defense has been a major issue over the past few seasons. Also, he is in a contract year, and another injury-plagued season will force the Cowboys to have to take a serious look at his future with the organization. The hope is that his current injury will be the only thing he deals with after he returns in the week or two. If not, Overshown could be playing elsewhere in 2027. Of course, nobody wants that to be the case, but it’s a possibility that could become a reality. What’s your take BTB? Will Overshown ever shake off the injuries and become the player we saw in 2024?
author: Matthew Lenix

title: Plenty of blame to go around after Cowboys loss in Giants game
summary: Well, that wasn’t much fun. After all the offseason and preseason hype, the Dallas Cowboys put a whole lot of same old, same old on the field in falling to the New York Giants. Disappointment is the mood of the week. We hope they can turn things around against the Washington Commanders, but things went […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Jaishawn Barham #55 of the Dallas Cowboys during the game against the New York Giants on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Well, that wasn’t much fun. After all the offseason and preseason hype, the Dallas Cowboys put a whole lot of same old, same old on the field in falling to the New York Giants. Disappointment is the mood of the week. We hope they can turn things around against the Washington Commanders, but things went so badly in so many ways. Our Sean Martin and Tom Ryle look at what they each felt was the biggest letdown. Tom – For me, it was the defense. Ever since last season ended with a whimper, a consensus has grown that all this team really needs is to put an average defense on the field, and we should be able to amass enough wins to get back to the playoffs. To a certain extent, we did this to ourselves. We saw draft picks, trades, and cap space poured into the defense, and a shiny new defensive coordinator brought in to get more out of them. Surely that would lift this team from the depths of the worst NFL defenses. None of it paid any dividends we could see. As our Dan Rogers pointed out so well, the Cowboys only managed six offensive series on the night, and just two after halftime. The Giants played a highly effective game of keepaway. Dallas held the ball for under 24 minutes. No matter how good your offense is, it is almost impossible to do much when most of the game it is just watching from the sidelines. Sean – I don’t do personal anecdotes all that often, but this time I really feel like it’s important to provide context on this disappointing loss in the swamps of Jersey. Even as someone that said almost all offseason leading up to this game that I see it as one of the most even Cowboys-Giants matchups in a long time. It brought me right back to the feeling of growing up a Dallas fan in Jersey and sweating out these rivalry games knowing what it would mean at school if the Cowboys lost. I’ve even been open about wanting this level of competitiveness back in the rivalry, as opposed to the game being devalued a little during the past dominance by the Cowboys. Well, Brian Schottenheimer’s team got the test I guess it needed right off the jump, and failed miserably to rise to the occasion and prove they’re ready to truly be competitive this year, or show improvement in any of the areas we expected. Since Schotty is the man still in charge of the play-calling on offense, I’m going to continue with my gripes about the offense. We had to “wait all day for Sunday night” to start off this season, creating opportunity to watch other teams play first, like the Bears scoring 59 points to a team that beat the Cowboys last year or the Vikings going from Kyler Murray to Carson Wentz and still dropping 39. Looking back on these games and others after the Cowboys managed just 20 points with a killer interception in there too, it feels like every advantage we’re supposed to be talking about this offense having is the opposite of what’s actually working elsewhere around the league. Explosive runs from backs that can punish defenders on the second and third level with speed? The Cowboys don’t have Jaydon Blue or Malik Davis anymore, and while we’re on it couldn’t get Javonte Williams going either. Passing out of condensed formations with more usage for tight ends than wide receivers? Nope, the Cowboys are built to spread it out, and while we’re here this time, didn’t do nearly enough creative things to free up CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens. These players are good enough to get open anyway, which they did a little bit, and then both dropped the ball. To make matters even worse the Giants offense was actually better in a lot of these areas going against the Cowboys defense. For me, the pressure is firmly on for this Commanders game because of it, and that’s from someone that anticipated a possible loss to the Giants – the way it actually unfolded was still that bad. Sorry for the long therapy session Tom, but like I said, Cowboys-Giants has always been personal. Forget bringing back memories of the 2025 Cowboys defense getting shredded, Jaxson Dart was reminding me of the way Eli Manning used to rip Cowboys fans’ hearts out. And this time instead of having a good Tony Romo performance to match, we got four quarters of Prescott needing to be near perfect without enough help. Anyway, back to you. Tom – Oh, I never said I wasn’t disappointed in the offense, with all the implications it has for the rest of the season. You can almost see when Dak feels like it is all on his shoulders, because he starts trying to do just a little too much. But it wasn’t just the rest of the offense that was dropping that load on him. I think the biggest problem was that the supposedly new look defense under Christian Parker looked, well, just like the one Matt Eberflus fielded. Dallas couldn’t buy a stop, with New York converting nine of eleven third downs. (As a side note, one reason I am more upset with the D than the O is that the Cowboys went eight for eleven, normally a sign of a successful attack.) Many of those conversions were demoralizing. Nineteen yards on 3rd and 10. Sixteen on 3rd and 9. Thirteen on another 3rd and 9. And plenty of short conversions as the Giants were quite efficient on early downs. Meanwhile, facing Jaxson Dart, who is known to be more than willing to use his legs to pick up yards, Dallas seemed completely unprepared for him to take off with the ball. He would wind up as the second leading rusher for New York with 54 yards on ten carries, including a 22 yard scamper. With Cam Skattebo as the lead dog, the Giants would run for a total of 165 yards. That kind of ball control is how you win games. Dart did not have to be dominant through the air, never playing from behind. It all adds up to a defensive showing that would have fit in perfectly with last year’s Cowboys team. And that is frankly disturbing after all we thought we had coming. Sean – Disappointment all around at being 0-1 on the season and 0-1 with a divisional loss that was there for the taking at that. Amazingly, you could almost make a case the Cowboys were closer to winning in Philadelphia last year then they were at New York this time around. We’ve already covered how we didn’t see any of the signs of progress we wanted yet, and in some ways there was even regression. The preseason is over and the offense will need to start playing like it too, getting after that ever so familiar Dan Quinn defense in week two.
author: Sean Martin

title: Cowboys vs Commanders: 2 players Dallas should use more in Week 2
summary: Not much went right for the Dallas Cowboys in their Week 1 loss to the division rival New York Giants. While the game ended 28-20, the play on the field suggested the contest was never really that close. With another divisional game on the schedule this Sunday against the Washington Commanders, Dallas will need to […]
full_text: Not much went right for the Dallas Cowboys in their Week 1 loss to the division rival New York Giants. While the game ended 28-20, the play on the field suggested the contest was never really that close. With another divisional game on the schedule this Sunday against the Washington Commanders, Dallas will need to change some things to avoid falling to 0-2. With that thought in mind, today we look at two players the Cowboys should use more in Week 2. 1) TE Brevyn Spann-Ford Last week the Cowboys made a fairly surprising move, signing 26-year-old tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford to a three-year extension totaling $18M. Investing this kind of money in a young tight end shows the Cowboys believe he can be an impactful piece in their offense this year and beyond. Spann-Ford saw limited opportunities in Week 1 against the Giants, playing just 13 offensive snaps, just eight of which ended up being pass plays. This week against the Commanders, Dallas needs to give Spann-Ford a more significant role and see if he can help out their offense. Jake Ferguson has been cemented as Dallas TE1 for quite some time now, but the former Pro Bowler has been fairly unimpressive of late. Dating back to Week 6 of the 2024 season, Ferguson has averaged 7.2 Y/R with an average of 5.4 Y/Tgt over that 25-game span. Ferguson’s YAC skills and ability to make plays down the middle of the field have been missing for a while now, and it’s been evident. While Spann-Ford is unproven, in his limited playing time he’s shown an ability to make an impact when given opportunities. On 20 career catches, Spann-Ford has averaged 9.6 Y/R. The 6’6 tight end has the same ability Ferguson once did to stretch the middle of the field and make teams worry about his big-play ability. Dallas needs to give the former undrafted free agent more opportunities on Sunday and see if he can bring a missing ingredient to their offense. 2) CB Cobie Durant It may seem crazy to say, but at this point in time, Cobie Durant is without a doubt Dallas’ best cornerback on the roster. Throughout training camp, Durant shined time and time again, and that play carried into Week 1 against New York. The former Los Angeles Ram finished the game with a 77.2 Pro Football Focus coverage grade, allowing just one reception on three targets for 18 yards. Last Sunday, Durant played 50 total defensive snaps, 26 of which came in pass coverage. The 28-year-old saw some of his snaps taken by second-year corner Shavon Revel Jr., who played 20 defensive snaps with nine coming in coverage. While Revel is certainly important to the Cowboys’ future, there is no world in which Dallas should be taking Durant off the field to give him snaps. If the Cowboys want to get Revel opportunities, they should be looking at taking snaps away from DaRon Bland instead of Durant. As long as he is healthy, Cobie Durant needs to be on the field for every defensive snap Sunday against the Commanders.
author: Matthew Holleran

title: Broncos players take ownership after ugly loss to Kansas City
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Teams face adversity. It’s not a matter of if, but when. For the Denver Broncos, it just happens to come a little earlier than some (most) would have liked. But how the Broncos respond to the beatdown at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday will reveal what kind […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos reacts after a play against the Kansas City Chiefs during the fourth quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Teams face adversity. It’s not a matter of if, but when. For the Denver Broncos, it just happens to come a little earlier than some (most) would have liked. But how the Broncos respond to the beatdown at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday will reveal what kind of makeup they have. To add to the motivation, Denver faces the Jacksonville Jaguars, a team that thoroughly whipped it 34-20 a season ago. The good news is the Broncos have been in this position before under Sean Payton, going 4-8 in and struggling in September games heading into Sunday. Week 2 work. 💪 pic.twitter.com/f0wwVGVDI2 — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 17, 2026 “I learned a long time ago, you never play as bad as you think and you never play as good as you think,” Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media on Thursday. “So for us, it was the case of we didn’t play as bad as what we thought. We just there at the end of the game, we didn’t make third-down conversions. We felt like it was 7-7, 14-7, and 21-7 for a long time in the game. So it was reachable, and we were in it for a while. “We just didn’t help ourselves by any means. You watch the film, and there are a couple good things and then all of a sudden we’re back because of a penalty or something. You just can’t win in this league like that. So, overall, we’re not going to press the panic button, and we’re not freaking out. We’re not starting from scratch or anything. We’re still in a good spot, and we just didn’t play great by any means, and we’ve got to play better.” The first step to correcting what went wrong against the Chiefs is the work at practice this week. As Nix said after the game on Monday, it was a “nasty wake-up call.” After that, it’s about the players doing their job, doing the little things, and executing. “We all know we are a very talented team, no question about it,” Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said to the media. “That’s why I feel like everybody has us on the high horse and stuff like that. That comes with a certain privilege. But if you don’t show up each and every week, you’re going to get humbled quickly. Every week is a new challenge. “We all know that as a team, but we just have to focus on getting better day-by-day and honing in on the small details. I think that’s what’s going to separate us. It’s still early in the year. Going into our second game, we know what we need to correct. Like I said before, every week’s a new challenge. You have to bring the intensity no matter what.” If used properly, being served some humble pie can be a good thing. “I think the biggest thing is learning from our mistakes from what we saw on film,” Broncos receiver Courtland Sutton said to the media on Thursday. “There were things that we did well, things that we didn’t do well. Being able to build on what we did well, make that last longer throughout the game, and minimize our mistakes. I would say one of the things I’ve seen from the team over the past few days, since the game, is an attitude of accountability, an attitude of wanting to get better and improving so that we can maximize these days leading up into Jacksonville.” Teams face adversity; it’s a matter of how they respond. Denver gets its first test on Sunday. What can certainly help the Broncos is playing at home. “A big spark,” Nix said when asked about the spark Broncos Country could provide. “There’s nothing like a home-field advantage, nothing like playing at home. I know, as an away team, what it’s like to go and play in a loud environment. It’s definitely not easy. There are a lot of variables and things that go into it, a lot of communication tactics. It’s just not easy, and that’s what the crowd does. The crowd makes it not easy for them. “So hopefully we’ll have, like we always do, a sellout, hopefully we’ll have a loud environment, and I expect it to be a really fun time being the home opener. I expect it to be loud. Essentially, what it is, it’s a playoff game. So I expect it to be that kind of environment, sort of like we had at the end of the season last year.” Bronos links
author: Ian St. Clair

title: Denver Broncos: An easy to solution to ‘rage baiting’ is to play better
summary: An interesting thing happened today that I would classify as abnormal in the NFL world — as far as the Denver Broncos are concerns anyway. The team played terrible and were lackluster during a blowout road loss in Week 1, which led a lot of fans and bloggers to bemoan specific issues like missed tackles. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs stiff arms Alex Singleton #49 of the Denver Broncos as he runs with the ball during an NFL football game on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images An interesting thing happened today that I would classify as abnormal in the NFL world — as far as the Denver Broncos are concerns anyway. The team played terrible and were lackluster during a blowout road loss in Week 1, which led a lot of fans and bloggers to bemoan specific issues like missed tackles. It would appear Alex Singleton’s agent had a problem with that and took to X to air out that dirty laundry. I didn’t personally partake in whatever triggered this response, but my advice to Paul would be to inform his clients that the best way to avoid rage baiting is to just play better. Show heart. Play hard. Look like you care. All three of those things didn’t seem to show up on Monday night and that’s likely why fans are irritated this week. We can handle a bad game. It’s the lackluster effort that triggers the negative reactions you didn’t like. Many of us probably thought it would be hard to beat Kansas City in their house. None of us expected to see such pitiful effort to make tackles drive after drive. On to the next one, though. Please! title: Broncos vs. Jaguars: 3 Things to Watch for in Week 2
summary: The Denver Broncos follow up their Week 1 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs by hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. The Jaguars were just one of three teams to deliver the Broncos a defeat last season. In a way, this matchup has the allure of a revenge game. Most importantly, the opportunity to get […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - DECEMBER 21: Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars and Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos interact after an NFL football game at Empower Field At Mile High on December 21, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos follow up their Week 1 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs by hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. The Jaguars were just one of three teams to deliver the Broncos a defeat last season. In a way, this matchup has the allure of a revenge game. Most importantly, the opportunity to get back on track and avoid going 0-2 to start off the 2026 season. Here are three storylines I’m going to keep a close eye on throughout the game. Will the Broncos show signs of life on offense? I figured there would always be a little bit of a learning curve for Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb and the Broncos’ offense this season. That happens with change. However, I didn’t expect them to be as flat as they were on Monday Night Football versus the Chiefs. There was no dedication to the run. Their passing attack was a joke. It’s almost impossible to win a football game when both phases on offense look that bad. In last year’s defeat to the Jaguars, Bo Nix had to throw 47 times. That’s a recipe for failure and can’t happen if Denver wants to win on Sunday. The Broncos went just 5-of-14 on third down and were 1-of-3 on fourth down conversions in that matchup, on top of turning the ball over twice. They need to establish the run. Feed J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and give Jonah Coleman an opportunity to shine. Nix and the wide receivers need to be on the same page. Jacksonville’s defense is quite opportunistic and winning the turnover battle will be an absolute must to get to 1-1 on the season. Can the defense embark on a drastic turnaround on a short week? The defense gave up numerous big plays that resulted in touchdowns for the Chiefs. Kenneth Walker II had one of the best games of his career and the defense looked like they completely had forgotten how to tackle. It was certainly embarrassing to watch, but not as bad as the 70-point shellacking the Miami Dolphins gave Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players in 2023. Last December, the Jaguars put up 34 points on the scoreboard—the most of any opponent in ’25. That loss, just like the Chiefs, was humbling for Denver. Jacksonville converted over 50-percent of their third downs and had several long touchdown drives. Whether it was on the ground or through the air, Liam Coen’s gameplan against the Broncos’ defense in key situations was virtually flawless. On a short week, Joseph and the defense don’t have a lot of time to fix things. Going up against Trevor Lawrence, who is playing some of the best football of his career, poses a significant challenge for them. They will have to be at their best to limit his top-tier playmaking ability. Great teams rebound and respond to adversity: Will Denver do that? One game isn’t indicative of how the remaining sixteen will play out. That being said, I’m concerned about what’s to come and the team’s potential this season after their disastrous showing at Arrowhead on MNF . The Broncos won fourteen games last year. And in some ways, I think they may have overachieved. Your mileage may vary. All things considered, I certainly didn’t expect them to win that much in ‘26. They’ve got a first-place schedule and a lot of teams got better over the course of the offseason. Regression, in some fashion, happens quite often in the NFL. The Jaguars will be a formidable foe for Denver. In the weeks to come, the Broncos will go up against a bunch of quality teams. Sure, the Broncos have started off slow in Head Coach Sean Payton’s time with the team, but this certainly isn’t the time to do that. To be the best, you have to beat the best. To be a Super Bowl competitor, you have to win against good teams. And that’s what the Jaguars are—a really good football team. Will Denver rise to the occasion and get back to a .500 ball club or will they fall into a two-game hole to start the season. We will find out on Sunday.

title: How the Denver Broncos can defeat the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 2
summary: The Denver Broncos host the Jacksonville Jaguars for their Week 2 matchup. After a blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1, the Broncos are looking to rebound quickly and avoid going 0-2 to begin the 2026 regular season. Last year, the Jaguars were just one of three teams to hand the Broncos […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - DECEMBER 21: Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen looks on during a game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on December 21, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Denver Broncos host the Jacksonville Jaguars for their Week 2 matchup. After a blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1, the Broncos are looking to rebound quickly and avoid going 0-2 to begin the 2026 regular season. Last year, the Jaguars were just one of three teams to hand the Broncos a loss. They will certainly be a tough opponent for Denver on Sunday. It won’t be easy, but here are a few ways they can achieve a much-needed victory. The Broncos can’t let Trevor Lawrence have another big game Last week, I was concerned about how Denver would perform against the Chiefs revamped rushing attack. Kenneth Walker II ended up having a field day against the Broncos’ defense. This week, I’ve got my eye zoned in on Jacksonville’s aerial attack. There were a lot of quarterbacks who impressed in Week 1. One of best was Trevor Lawrence who went 18-of-23 for 238 yards and had 4 touchdowns against the Cleveland Browns. In last year’s matchup, the Broncos were able to sack Lawrence five times. However, they weren’t able to create any turnovers he scored four total touchdowns in the Jaguars’ 34-20 victory against Denver last December. The Broncos’ secondary must find a way to limit his impact. One key area of focus will be on third down. Jacksonville converted eight of fifteen opportunities against Vance Joseph’s defense in ‘25. The defense absolutely has to get off the field on third down—especially if their offense continues to struggle converting them and extending drives. It’ll be tough, but the Broncos have to establish the run In last year’s loss to the Jaguars, quarterback Bo Nix aired out the ball 47 times. That was the second most attempts in a game last year trailing the miraculous comeback victory against the New York Giants in Week 7. Last season, Denver notched 101 yards on the ground on 17 attempts in their loss to Jacksonville. However, over half of those yards were on just three carries. On Monday Night Football , Denver failed to establish the run. We all saw what happened due to that. No excuses this weekend. They have to do their best to do that on Sunday. Unfortunately, the Jaguars sported the NFL’s best run defense in 2025 and is poised to fare well with that in ‘26 as well. It’s important to note Denver’s offense was without J.K. Dobbins for last year’s matchup. With him back in the lineup and the addition of Jonah Coleman, I do expect Denver’s rushing game to be more successful this time around. But that means they have to be committed to the run. Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb can’t ignore making the run game a focal point of their offensive gameplan. Nix’s play in the season opener wasn’t up to par. He has to be better, but he also needs a run game to help take the pressure off his shoulders. The Broncos can’t be their own worst enemy Everyone across Broncos Country saw how outclassed Denver was by Kansas City on Monday Night Football . Kudos to Andy Reid and his coaching staff for a dominant gameplan. Shame on the Broncos for consistently shooting themselves in the foot. It’s been a while since Denver suffered such a humbling defeat. It should be a wakeup call for the team. What we witnessed on Monday certainly didn’t meet the high standard the Broncos themselves this offseason. The execution on offense just wasn’t there. Several of their top playmakers, including Jaylen Waddle, were absolutely invisible. On defense, they couldn’t find a way to stop the run or tackle. Numerous missed tackles resulted in multiple touchdowns for the Chiefs. It’s mind-boggling they looked that unprepared out the game. And those penalties? Yikes. The Broncos had their struggles with them last year and this preseason. Sadly, it looks like that bad trend is showing up early this season. They’ve got to put a stop to it and play more disciplined.

title: NFL picks and predictions: Broncos vs. Jaguars and the rest of Week 2
summary: Welcome back to the second installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 1, I was 11-5 with my predictions. Not too shabby, but a few of the outcomes were a bit of a surprise—but that is what makes football fun. Let’s see how I do with my Week 2 slate […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Denver cornerback Pat Surtain II (2) waves to fans following the conclusion of the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to the second installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 1, I was 11-5 with my predictions . Not too shabby, but a few of the outcomes were a bit of a surprise—but that is what makes football fun. Let’s see how I do with my Week 2 slate of picks. Detroit Lions at Buffalo Bills — Thursday Night Football Both the Lions and Bills were able to hold off their opponents and eek out close victories in Week 1. In my opinion, this has the fixings of a high-powered offensive matchup. I believe we will see a lot of points on the scoreboard. Can Jahmyr Gibbs be stopped? Can Josh Allen keep the connection to DJ Moore strong? Those are things I’ll be watching closely. This is tough to predict, but I’ll take Buffalo at home in this one. Winner: Bills Carolina Panthers at Atlanta Falcons — Sunday (Early Game) This NFC South matchup features two teams who started their seasons off with a loss. The Falcons fell short in a one score game to the Pittsburgh Steelers, while the Panthers had 59 points dropped on them by Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears. I don’t feel very confident about this pick, but I’m taking Carolina on the road with the Falcons poised to start Cooper Rush again. Winner: Panthers Houston Texans at Cincinnati Bengals — Sunday (Early Game) Two potential playoff contenders go head-to-head in this one. The Texans fell short to the Bills in Week 1, while the Bengals were able to topple Tampa Bay in a thrilling game. Early word on this game is quarterback Joe Burrow is dealing with some back issues which may hinder his ability to be at his best against a Texans defense known for bringing pressure. If so, that could be an issue. I’m thinking the Texans bounce back this weekend and come up with a big victory on the road. Winner: Texans Philadelphia Eagles at Tennessee Titans — Sunday (Early Game) Every week there are games on the docket that don’t require much analysis. Long story short, Cam Ward and the Titans offense will likely struggle immensely against Philadelphia and Vic Fangio’s defense. They didn’t look good at all against the New York Jets last weekend. Winner: Eagles Green Bay Packers at New York Jets — Sunday (Early Game) The Jets are coming off a win over the Titans, whilst the Packers had a hard time protecting Jordan Love who took a beating in their loss to the Minnesota Vikings. I’m concerned about their ability to run the football which was an issue going up against Brian Flores’ defense. Can their offense be more cohesive this weekend against the Jets and will their offensive line step up and give Love the time he needs to succeed through the air? They’ll have to or they’ll wind up being 0-2 to start the year. I think Green Bay finds a way to win on the road. Winner: Packers New Orleans Saints at Baltimore Ravens — Sunday (Early Game) Close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades, but the Saints gave it all they had in their Week 1 overtime loss to the Lions. Unfortunately for them, they have a tough opponent on the road in the Ravens, who manhandled the Indianapolis Colts in Week 1. I’ll diverge here for a change and go with a home team for only the second time thus far. Winner: Ravens Minnesota Vikings at Chicago Bears — Sunday (Early Game) I love a good NFC North rivalry matchup and this one centers around two teams whose offenses really impressed in Week 1. It sounds like Carson Wentz is likely to start for the Vikings after Kyler Murray exited the game against Green Bay early on with a concussion. Though I’m not sure Wentz and Minnesota’s offense can keep up with Caleb Williams and the Bears who were on fire last week scoring 59 points. I think the Bears win this matchup. Winner: Bears Cleveland Browns at Tampa Bay Buccaneers — Sunday (Early Game) You can count on less than one hand the number of times you will see me pick the Browns to win a game this season. This Sunday against Tampa Bay isn’t going to be one of them. Winner: Buccaneers Pittsburgh Steelers at New England Patriots — Sunday (Early Game) The Steelers barely beat a bad Falcons team while Drake Maye struggled immensely against the Seattle Seahawks in the regular season opener. I’m still high on Maye’s ability as a quarterback and think he will have a much stronger performance against the Steelers in Week 2. I’ll take New England at home to get back to .500 on the season. Winner: Patriots Las Vegas Raiders at Los Angeles Chargers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The Chargers losing in epic fashion to the Arizona Cardinals was one of my Ls in my Week 1 picks. I didn’t see that one coming. Meanwhile, the Raiders were able to handle the Miami Dolphins thanks to a strong rushing attack. Can Ashton Jeanty have similar success going up against the Chargers? That will be a must if they want to win. However, I think Justin Herbert will have a rebound game and avoid going 0-2—putting both these AFC West teams at 1-1 to start the ‘26 season. Winner: Chargers Jacksonville Jaguars at Denver Broncos — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Jacksonville impressed with a Week 1 victory while Denver was dominated by the Chiefs on Monday Night Football . Broncos Country isn’t going to be happy with me picking against our team, but the Jaguars were one of just three teams to deliver Denver a loss in 2025 and have a very good team. I’m not very optimistic Denver can right all their wrongs quickly on a short week. I’m taking Jacksonville here. Sorry friends. Winners: Jaguars Washington Commanders at Dallas Cowboys — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The loser of this NFC East matchup will be the bottom dwellers of the division to start the season. The Commanders played the Eagles tough and the Cowboys struggled to establish the run against the New York Giants. In order to win this weekend, Javonte Williams needs to have a much better game. They can’t put it all on the arm of Dak Prescott to lead them to victory. I’ll go with my gut and choose Dallas. Winner: Cowboys Miami Dolphins at San Francisco 49ers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The 49ers toppled the Los Angeles Rams down under in Australia and the Dolphins lost to the Raiders. I think it’s a relatively safe bet to take Kyle Shanahan’s squad to go to 2-0 on the year hosting Miami. San Francisco all the way. Winner: 49ers Seattle Seahawks at Arizona Cardinals — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Okay, so the Cardinals surprised most all of us and beat the Chargers. That being said, there really isn’t a good reason to believe lightning will strike twice. The odds of them being the victors against the defending Super Bowl Champions? Not good. I’ll be taking the Seahawks. Winner: Seahawks Indianapolis Colts at Kansas City Chiefs — Sunday Night Football These teams both had strong performances from their running backs in Week 1, but Kenneth Walker II was on a different planet with the way he ran roughshod over the Broncos’ defense. I expect Andy Reid and the Chiefs to keep their ground game strong against a Colts defense who gave up nearly 200 yards on the ground to the Ravens in Week 1. Winner: Chiefs New York Giants at Los Angeles Rams — Monday Night Football The John Harbaugh era started off with a bang with the Giants toppling the Cowboys in Week 1. The Rams’ season started off on a low note being walloped by the 49ers in Australia. Even worse? Myles Garrett will be out for the foreseeable future after having knee surgery a few days ago. My heart wants me to pick the Giants for a feel-good story here, but my mind has settled on Sean McVay and the Rams rebounding and earning a dub in preimtime. Winner: Rams

title: Questions still linger for Broncos after Week 1 loss to Chiefs
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country. Monday’s loss to the Kansas City Chiefs was a gut punch for the Denver Broncos. Losses to division rivals always sting, but how badly they were defeated still sticks in my craw. That wasn’t something I—or most any of you—expected at all. How the Broncos respond this weekend against the Jacksonville […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Brandon Jones (22) of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after the Kansas City Chiefs' 31-10 win at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. Monday’s loss to the Kansas City Chiefs was a gut punch for the Denver Broncos. Losses to division rivals always sting, but how badly they were defeated still sticks in my craw. That wasn’t something I—or most any of you—expected at all. How the Broncos respond this weekend against the Jacksonville Jaguars remains to be seen. A sign of a great team is being able to bounce back after adversity. On Sunday, we will have a better idea of what kind of team this year’s Broncos are. Later today, I’ll have a few articles discussing the upcoming matchup against the Jaguars. For this morning, I thought I’d offer up some reflection and random thoughts I had after trying to digest the manner in which the Broncos lost. Feel free to let me know what you think about these questions in the comments section. How much is Denver’s defense missing Jonathan Franklin-Myers and Jonathon Cooper? Denver’s defensive performance against the Chiefs on Monday Night Football was concerning to say the least. They were outclassed and outmatched by Andy Reid and his staff who were able to concoct a great offensive gameplan. It’s hard to single out any particular player or reason for their rough evening. Most everyone on that side of the ball had some issues. I still can’t comprehend how the tackling that bad. But that got me thinking even more—would things have been different if Franklin-Myers and Jonathon Cooper had been starting? The lack of execution was across the board, but I honestly felt like their presence was missing a great deal. Sure, it’s only one game. Though without those two, the run defense seemed to struggle immensely and the pressure on Mahomes—even with short throws—just wasn’t consistent. I think it’s safe to say there is a pretty big dropoff from the aforementioned to the players Denver has trying to replace them. I’ll be keeping my eye on this as the next few games transpire to see if it was just an aberration, or something that could be an ongoing issue for the team moving forward. How long will it take for the Broncos’ offense to get better? There is no doubt Denver is a much-improved franchise now before Head Coach Sean Payton and his staff took over. It’s been a terrific turnaround even with the stench of the loss to the Chiefs still lingering. However, slow starts have been a common theme for the Broncos in that timeframe. This past Monday was emblematic of the early season offensive struggles over the past few seasons. There wasn’t enough emphasis on the run and too much of a burden put on Bo Nix’s shoulders. I’m still bullish on Nix’s potential and think he has a great shot at taking a leap in Year 3. Nevertheless, his outing versus Kansas City was one of the worst games of his career. Though I’ll say the offensive line didn’t look that impressive and contributed to some of his lackluster play. I felt that the interior combination of Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg struggled when confronting Steve Spagnuolo’s interior and blitz pressure packages. At right tackle, I was underwhelmed with Mike McGlinchey who seemed to have issues holding his own one-on-one in pass protection against the Chiefs’ edge rushers. The Broncos’ offensive line has performed well the past two years. Even so, a part of me wonders if defensive coordinators across the league now have a bit of a blueprint to attack some of their weaknesses. There’s no doubt Denver’s linemen have to perform better on Sunday versus the Jaguars to give Denver an honest chance at winning. As always, thank you for reading. title: What hope is there in the Detroit Lions defense?
summary: If you were looking for a silver lining in the Detroit Lions’ defensive performance against the Buffalo Bills in their 41-31 loss on Thursday night, you’d have to squint pretty hard to see it. You may have to hallucinate, to be honest. The Bills racked up 446 yards of offense for an average of 6.5 […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills consoles Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions after the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you were looking for a silver lining in the Detroit Lions’ defensive performance against the Buffalo Bills in their 41-31 loss on Thursday night, you’d have to squint pretty hard to see it. You may have to hallucinate, to be honest. The Bills racked up 446 yards of offense for an average of 6.5 yards per play. For reference, the best offense in the NFL last year averaged 6.2 yards. Josh Allen finished with a 121.4 passer rating, the Bills ran for 203 yards at 5.6 yards per carry, and they punted only twice—once after a dropped third-down conversion and another time after a second-down drop. In the end, the Bills posted an astronomical 0.44 EPA/play (highest of any game so far in 2026) and 59 percent success rate (second). Whatever the Bills wanted to do on Thursday night, they did. “We’ve got to clean up a lot of things on defense right now, particularly on the backend,” coach Dan Campbell said after the game. The understatement of the night. So where does Detroit go from here? Where is there any semblance of hope on defense after following up a disastrous second half against the Saints with an even more futile performance against the Bills? Lions coach Dan Campbell was asked what gives him optimism this can get turned around this early in the season. “I think this front—we’ve got some juice up front, man,” Campbell said. “I think we’ve got a mix of guys that can apply pressure that can stop the run and that relieves a lot of stress on your backend.” The Lions did apply a fair amount of pressure to Allen on Thursday night. They sacked Allen twice, tallied eight quarterback hits, and finished with a pressure percentage 34.2%—comfortably above the league average. But that hardly seemed to take any pressure off the back end, which was plagued by missed assignment, failed communications, and blown coverages. “We had a couple of busts—we had more than a couple of busts on the backend for touchdowns in the pass game that really hurt us,” Campbell said. “We had a couple of busts in the run game, too, our fits. We’re fitting the wrong gaps or not where we’re supposed to be. We’ve got two guys in one gap, and (James) Cook is busting these runs.” Campbell remains hopeful that time on task will help them play cleaner football. “The more those guys play together, the better they’ll get,” Campbell said. “The more that we really digest what we’re trying to do to opponents or what we feel like we need to do any given week, I think will help those guys, and their confidence will grow and we’ll get better.” Another reason Campbell has hope is that they can finally dig into correcting the film. Prior to Thursday, Campbell admitted the short week really prevented them from correcting their errors made against the Saints in Week 1. With another set of data points and a long weekend to digest and self-diagnose, they can really start the big adjustments. “Now we can really digest—okay, this is our two-game snapshot, this is what you are, this says what you are,” Campbell said. “And we can really deep-dive these players, what they do best, what they don’t do or need help in, and we’ll move on from that.” While there is undoubtedly some truth to the Lions’ defensive mistakes being internal and correctable, it is a eerily familiar refrain from the defensive meltdown at the end of last season. It may be early in the season with plenty of time to improve, but Detroit will need to be much more effective at fixing their mistakes than they were in 2025.

title: 3 winners, 8 losers from Detroit Lions’ loss to Buffalo Bills
summary: This was always going to be a tough matchup for the Detroit Lions. On a short week and playing the Buffalo Bills on their newly opened home turf, Detroit was in for a battle. When the short week meant losing two starting offensive linemen for the game, things got worse. When the defense gave up […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Deone Walker #96 of the Buffalo Bills deflects a pass by Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images This was always going to be a tough matchup for the Detroit Lions. On a short week and playing the Buffalo Bills on their newly opened home turf, Detroit was in for a battle. When the short week meant losing two starting offensive linemen for the game, things got worse. When the defense gave up four touchdowns in a row in the first half, well, it was all downhill. The score ended up being 41-31 for the Bills, with Detroit putting up an effort in the second half. However, their defense dug them a hole too deep to overcome. Few offenses can make up a deficit like that. The Lions drop to 1-1 on the season, but with the New York Jets up next, they are in a good position for a rebound performance. That being said, there are problems that need urgent correcting. If not, even the worst teams on paper could defeat this Lions team. Loser: Kelvin Sheppard, DC There is no easy way to put it: it was a disastrous performance from Kelvin Sheppard’s defense. The Lions had plenty of sub-par performances (more on that later), but the main problem is that Sheppard looked outclassed. For all the critics talking about the Lions playing too much man coverage, Thursday night showed that their zone defense is somehow worse. Bills defenders were open all night, thanks largely to miscommunications from the secondary and questionable play calling from Sheppard (why are their defensive backs playing so far off on third-and-short?). When the Lions dialed up a blitz, nobody got home. When they tried to spy Josh Allen, he beat them. Almost every single defensive play was a failure in design, coaching, and execution. Firing Sheppard will be a hot topic among the Lions community, but not only is this too soon (it is only Week 2 against an elite offense), it probably does not solve the problem either. Who would replace him? There is no miraculous defensive mastermind that can step in and lead this group. Getting Brian Branch or Kerby Joseph back or trading for Joey Porter Jr. would certainly help on paper, but the pressure is on Sheppard to show he can orchestrate a competent defense. Loser: Dan Campbell, HC This quote at halftime stuck with me—not because I disagree with it, but because I should be agreeing more with it: "The little shit is killing us right now." – Dan Campbell — Pride of Detroit (@PrideOfDetroit) September 18, 2026 Campbell is 100-percent right: the little [things] are killing this team. Whether it is missed assignments, misplays, or untimely penalties, the Lions shot themselves in the foot a lot on Thursday. If anything, it is impressive that the game ended up being as close as it was. The Lions looked completely unprepared and, dare I say, unmotivated against one of the best teams in the league. For a team that prides itself on being competitive, where was the competitiveness this night? My biggest gripe with this quote is that it is not enough . Sure, the little things are killing this team, but how about your defense that is incapable of making a stop without the opposition messing up on their own? This game was not a failure of a bunch of small things. It was a fundamental failure of half of this roster. Maybe this is just coach speak, but I certainly hope there is understanding that the Lions are severely underperforming, and that reflects heavily on Campbell’s leadership. We cannot be focused on cleaning up small mistakes when the big ones are the root of their struggles. On the Titanic, you can’t complain about a paint scratch when the iceberg is sinking the ship. Winner: Aidan Hutchinson, DE Hutchinson is the best player on the Lions defense and it is not even close. On nearly every snap, he is giving his all and making an impact. Any time the Bills offense stalled, Hutchinson was at the center of it—pressuring Josh Allen, wrapping up runners, holding the edge (unlike many his defensive teammates). On a night when the defense was horrible, Hutchinson was a rare exception. He finished the night with one sack and nearly had a second if not for an incredible play from Allen. Normally, a dominant defensive end like Hutchinson would take over a game. Yet when the secondary is struggling to cover for even a split second, it wounds up not mattering. Losers: Secondary (minus D.J. Reed) People will be quick to fault the entire secondary for this awful performance, but we should at least exclude Reed from the group. Is he an elite lockdown corner? No. Is he a liability? Far from it. On a night when Josh Allen threw the ball 31 times, Reed was rarely targeted—he is doing his part, not to mention being a strong run defender. The problem is everyone else in the secondary. Rock Ya-Sin continues to struggle (putting it mildly), and he even exited this game with an injury. Teams will continue to pick on him and win. As for the safeties, Chuck Clark was okay, but the play of Thomas Harper and Avonte Maddox was felt in a negative way. Both safeties looked discombobulated on numerous snaps, failing to pass off coverage or outright missing their assignment. Worse for Maddox, he left the game in crutches . The Lions flat out cannot go on a playoff run with a secondary playing like this. At this rate, I’m not sure if the return of Joseph and Branch even fixes the problem. Losers: Larry Borom, Juice Scruggs, and Ben Bartch, OL The injury replacements looked like injury replacements. After a solid Week 1 outing from Bartch and Scruggs, the two linemen struggled mightily on Thursday night. Their pass protection was awful for most of the game, with Goff having to weather inside pressure on a frequent basis. Scruggs was also responsible for a penalty on a false start. Borom was the worst of the trio. Filling in for Blake Miller, who likely would have suited up if it was not a short week, he was easily the weakest link of the line. In pass protection, he was on skates. In run defense, he was generating zero push. Worse yet, he was flagged twice, penalties that killed drives. For a player brought in to solidify the swing tackle spot, he has yet to prove he is an upgrade over Dan Skipper. The Lions offense was surprisingly effective for how bad the offensive line was. Hopefully they can put together a more rounded offensive performance when their usual starters return to full health. Winner: Jared Goff, QB Goff was quietly superb against the Bills. Some people will argue he padded his stats with garbage time, but he was genuinely on point for most of the night. He stayed turnover-free, navigated many collapsing pockets, and delivered some strikes amid tight windows. He finished with 327 yards and four touchdown passes to little fanfare. He and Amon-Ra St. Brown once again flexed their chemistry, the only shame is that it took until the second half for it to materialize. Early on, the offense was stalling, but it was not his fault—too often the offensive line was resulting in negative plays, either via penalty or sack. Borom, in particular, was getting beat like a drum off the right side, but Goff largely weathered the storm. Despite pressure from the interior, he was able to stay upright and make plays when it counted. If the Lions had any type of competent defense, this would have been viewed as a heroic outing from Goff. I have a lot of confidence in the offense going forward despite some recent speedbumps. At the end of the day, the Lions have a great quarterback at the helm. Loser: Jack Campbell, LB Fresh off an All-Pro season and a sizeable $81 million contract, Campbell is not living up to expectations. He had a poor game against the New Orleans Saints last week, but he was dreadful against the Bills. In particular, his coverage took a nose dive. The Bills were exploiting the Lions linebackers in cover with their tight…
