title: 5 takeaways from Detroit Lions’  41-31 loss against Buffalo Bills
summary: Coming off an overtime victory over the New Orleans Saints, the Detroit Lions had to move on quickly. The Lions had to not only shift focus to the next game, but also travel to Highmark Stadium, home of the Buffalo Bills, one of the top teams in the AFC. Buffalo also came off a thrilling […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Bradley Chubb #9 of the Buffalo Bills sacks Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming off an overtime victory over the New Orleans Saints, the Detroit Lions had to move on quickly. The Lions had to not only shift focus to the next game, but also travel to Highmark Stadium, home of the Buffalo Bills, one of the top teams in the AFC. Buffalo also came off a thrilling win over the Houston Texans and needed to defend its new home turf on “Thursday Night Football”. The game felt over just as it began, as the Bills drove down the field with ease to go up 7-0. The Bills’ defense was stout and continued to dominate the Lions’ offense, and after just five minutes in the second quarter, it was 21-0. Detroit tried to make it a game and scored to close the gap, but every time they got close, Buffalo pulled away. Detroit’s efforts came too little too late, and it was an embarrassing loss on national television. Here are my five takeaways from the Lions’ 41-31 loss against the Bills in Week 2. Defense looked unprepared The Bills finished the game with 446 yards, rushing for 203 and throwing for 243. Quarterback Josh Allen made the Lions’ defense pay on the opening drive, rushing four times for 40 yards and a touchdown, making it look easy. The Bills offense only got stopped twice, moving the ball however they wanted for all four quarters. Penalties (more on that later), missed assignments, and too many easy plays by the Buffalo offense hurt Detroit. Detroit looked unprepared and still seemed to be recovering from the previous week’s game. Buffalo also had a short week, but their defense made far fewer mistakes than Detroit’s. Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard had a rough game, and it seemed like he didn’t have his guys prepared. It was an awful game from that entire side of the ball, players, and coaching. Burn the tape and use the time between now and Week 3 to improve and make sure this isn’t a recurring theme. Offensive line held together by gum It’s Week 2, and the Lions already have three backups playing on their offensive line. We knew center Cade Mays would miss the first four games, but other injuries hit Detroit. Left guard Christian Mahogany left Week 1 early with a hip injury and didn’t return. Rookie right tackle Blake Miller played the full game but didn’t practice all week with a knee injury and was ruled out. That meant left guard Ben Bartch and right tackle Larry Borom would get their first start in Detroit, joining center Juice Scruggs, who got his first start last week. Three players with little practice with the other lineman next to them, and this is the result you’re going to get. The good news is that Miller’s injury shouldn’t be long-term, and Mays could debut in the next month. It sucks seeing the line struggle again, but this isn’t a long-term issue, just a week where Detroit had to put something together quickly. When you have little time to build that chemistry, this is the result you’re going to get. This is the worst game Detroit will play this season I don’t want to discredit any optimistic fans who believed the Lions could win this game. Playing on a short week, after having to play in overtime, with a banged-up offensive line, both starting safeties on IR, and having to travel on the road in your opponent’s first game in their new stadium, that’s a very tall ask for your team. I’m not making excuses for how the team played; they played awful. I’m just saying the Bills are the toughest team the Lions will play this year, and it was in the worst situation possible. Detroit’s next three games: home against the New York Jets, away against the Carolina Panthers and Arizona Cardinals. All three of those games are easier than the Bills, and that’s without safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, along with Mays. Those three could return starting Week 5, but I believe with a Week 6 bye week, they’ll return Week 7 against the Green Bay Packers. When those three players return, the team will change on both sides of the ball. The secondary will get much-needed help, and that should give the defensive line more chances to get to the quarterback. The offensive line will be a big upgrade with Mays, and by then I think Miller and Mahogany will be back, so the whole gang can finally play together as a unit. This team has an easy schedule and few injuries; there’s no way they play this way against another team this year. The only other difficult game (and by difficult I mean against a top-end team) is against the New England Patriots in Germany. If Detroit loses that game and splits all three divisional games, 12-5 is a solid season and easily gets them in the playoffs. Gibbs continues to be the workhorse for the offense Last week, Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs had a career-high 29 carries as he was the lifeblood of the offense. Not much changed this week as Gibbs remained their heartbeat, finishing with 16 carries for 52 yards and six catches for 61 yards and a touchdown. Even when Detroit was down 21-0 early, they still relied on Gibbs to move the chains. Gibbs is an important piece for this team, but when you’re down by 21 points, someone in the receiving game needs to step up who isn’t your running back. The Lions needed him to score on their opening drive, but as the game went on, others stepped up like wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and tight end Sam LaPorta. This game proved one thing: no matter what, Gibbs is the focal point of the offense and the team will rely on him to carry the workload if needed. If this game was closer, I believe Gibbs would’ve gotten more touches on the ground, but as the game dragged on and time was running out, the Lions offense had to let it rip. Penalties added insult to injury Buffalo was dominating Detroit, and any time it felt like the Lions would catch a break, they hurt themselves with penalties. Whether it’s a holding in the secondary that costs an interception or a false start that wipes out a first down, Detroit kept making the game tougher on themselves. The Lions finished with 10 penalties for 58 yards, and as Lions head coach Dan Campbell said at halftime of the broadcast, “The little shit is killing us.” When you aren’t playing your best, the worst thing you can do is hurt yourself and make life harder. The Lions couldn’t afford to make mental mistakes against the Bills, but they kept doing so. If they clean up their act, this game could’ve been a one-score game, and Detroit may have pulled off the upset. They had eight penalties last week against the Saints, now averaging nine flags a game. You can’t win many games if you are almost averaging double-digit penalties.
author: Brandon Knapp

title: Lions, Bills recap: Detroit’s defense obliterated by Josh Allen in 41-31 loss
summary: The Detroit Lions finished Week 1 by letting Saints quarterback Tyler Shough carve through their defense. On Thursday night against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills, they picked up right where they left off. For the entire night, they had no answers to the Bills’ high-octane offense. They couldn’t stop the run. They couldn’t stop […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills throws a pass against the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions finished Week 1 by letting Saints quarterback Tyler Shough carve through their defense. On Thursday night against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills, they picked up right where they left off. For the entire night, they had no answers to the Bills’ high-octane offense. They couldn’t stop the run. They couldn’t stop the pass. Buffalo essentially did whatever they wanted all night in the opener of Highmark Stadium. Meanwhile, the offense had its moments. But much like Week 1, there were too many self-imposed mistakes, along with poorer play on Detroit’s patchwork offensive line. The final score was a tough-to-swallow 41-31 loss to the Bills. There will be serious questions about whether this defense can turn things around after two very discouraging performances to open the year. Here’s how Thursday night played out. First quarter The Bills won the toss and elected to receive, giving Josh Allen the opportunity to strike first. After a penalty on the kickoff, the Bills were forced to start at the 15-yard line. But the Bills were able to quickly get into Lions territory. Despite an early Aidan Hutchinson sack, Allen found some success scrambling. He picked up 13 yards on one play, then 12 more when Detroit lost contain. A 13-yard pass to Khalil Shakir and 10-yard run put Buffalo near the red zone. Another Allen scramble put the Bills on the goal line, then he plunged into the end zone for a 1-yard touchdown. 7-0 Bills. Of course @JoshAllenQB scores the first touchdown at Highmark Stadium!! 📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/kQphVyhZZc — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026 Jared Goff and the Lions offense needed to retaliate in order to not fall behind too much too quickly. Instead, they went three-and-out. After two unsuccessful plays, Jared Goff took a coverage sack. The Bills defense collapse the pocket for the sack! DETvsBUF on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/7mri0gBDgm — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 The Lions defense had a chance to get off the field quickly, forcing the Bills into a third-and-6 on their first series of downs. But Allen found Keon Coleman for an easy 7-yard pickup. Then Allen split the Lions’ zone to find Dalton Kincaid for a big 25-yard gain. Detroit was then able to get into a third-and-11 to finally get off the field… except the Lions had a coverage bust, and Allen found Joshua Palmer for an easy 43-yard touchdown. 14-0 Bills. WIDE OPEN‼️ 📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/uEiPEzlOfq — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026 Detroit tried to pull out of this nightmarish start with the help of Jahmyr Gibbs, who kicked off the ensuing drive with a 16-yard run followed by a 9-yard run. But Goff was sacked on second-and-1 by Greg Rousseau. Greg Rousseau gets to Goff! DETvsBUF – on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/RyyZG8pTKL — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 Then Juice Scruggs sent the third-down snap too high, and Goff had to fall on it to end their drive. To add insult to injury, former Lions wideout Greg Dortch returned the ensuing punt 25 yards all the way to the Bills’ 43-yard line. The rout was officially on, as the first quarter came to a merciful end. Second quarter Allen went right back to work with completions to Kincaid and Keon Coleman for 12 and 22 yards to open the second quarter. Josh Allens finds Keon Coleman for their 14th first down of the first half 😮 DETvsBUF – on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/M0ASu7aH3H — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 Again, the Lions had an opportunity to get off the field on a third-and-6, and while it initially looked like rookie defensive lineman Skyler Gill-Howard had caught an interception off a deflection, Lions cornerback Rock Ya-Sin was called for holding on the play, negating the turnover and setting up a first-and-goal for the Bills. On the next play, Lions safety Avonte Maddox suffered an injury and was carted to the locker room . He was listed as questionable to return with a foot injury. A few plays later, Allen hit Dawson Knox for a 1-yard touchdown. 21-0 Bills. DAWSON. KNOX. 📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/Yilrw54xH8 — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026 The Lions countered with their best drive. Highlighted by a third-and-7 conversion via a run, Detroit was able to get into Bills’ territory. Then Goff extended the drive with a tight throw to Gibbs for 8 yards on a third-and-4. An 11-yard catch from Amon-Ra St. Brown—his first target and catch of the game—set Detroit up for their first red-zone trip of the night. Then Goff found Gibbs for an 11-yard touchdown catch to stop the bleeding. 21-7 Bills. Goff to Gibbs for the score pic.twitter.com/81Pfhuw7WO — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 18, 2026 Detroit’s defense got a rest, but they didn’t come out looking any different. James Cook ripped off a 20-yard run to start the next drive, then followed it up with a 35-yarder. James Cookin' for 35 yards DETvsBUF – on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rNtH0sn6vo — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 Bills receiver DJ Moore suffered an injury on Buffalo’s red zone trip, but Allen went right back to Kincaid for a 16-yard touchdown, a 27-7 Bills lead, and a fourth first-ahlf touchdown for Allen (missed extra point). FOUR touchdowns for Josh Allen before the half 🔥 DETvsBUF – on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/lI4OWKUnvL — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 Detroit desperately needed points to end the half, but a critical error on Juice Scruggs stalled the drive. The Lions were facing a third-and-inches, and Scruggs false started. Then, on third-and-6, Goff was sacked after trying to escape interior pressure. That gave the Bills yet another opportunity to add to their 20-point lead before halftime. But three straight incompletions from Allen led to the Bills’ first punt of the game. That left one more opportunity for Detroit to cut into the lead before halftime. Goff found LaPorta for 12, St. Brown for 22, and Jameson Williams for 16 to get into field goal range. Tack on a tripping penalty on the Bills, and Jake Bates had an easy chip-shot field goal to make it 27-10 Bills as time expired. Third quarter Detroit got a big play to start the second half, with Goff connecting with St. Brown for a 22-yard gain on third-and-3. St. Brown. First down. DETvsBUF – on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/YPig1P2FbV — NFL (@NFL) September 18, 2026 But after an incomplete pass and 0-yard run from Gibbs, Detroit faced a third-and-10. St. Brown caught a 5-yard pass, setting up a fourth-and-5. Detroit had little choice but to go for it from the Bills’ 40-yard line, and Goff found LaPorta for a big 18-yard gain. LaPorta picks up the fourth down conversion pic.twitter.com/10CzemtLEU — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 18, 2026 A few plays later, Goff hit St. Brown on a 2-yard touchdown pass to make it 27-17 Bills. That's a Saint score to start the second half! pic.twitter.com/eHA0PfcqCQ — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 18, 2026 The Bills offense wouldn’t be denied, though. Though the Lions made them work harder for it, Buffalo converted a third-and-1, third-and-2, and another two third-and-1s to move into field goal range. Then they finally hit on a big play, finding Kincaid in a soft spot of the zone for 23 yards—setting up a first-and-goal. A few plays later, Allen ran it in on a 1-yard, play-action touchdown. 34-17 Bills. THAT'S. OUR. QUARTERBACK. 📺: @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/ANUdd4NZQm — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026 Detroit attempted to answer, and hit on a big play of their own—a 34-yard post route to St. Brown. That would be the final play of the third quarter. Pickup of 34 for Amon-Ra to close out…

(Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions’ first big litmus test of the season is a big one. Reed #4 of the Detroit Lions walks off the field after an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. title: Detroit Lions fans pick winner of Lions at Bills in Week 2
summary: Earlier this week, we published our latest SB Nation Reacts survey, sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, and asked Detroit Lions fans two questions: Confidence dipped ahead of Week 2 after the Lions stumbled late in the game vs. the Saints and needed overtime to secure the win, but the majority of fans are […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; A Detroit Lions fan shows his sprit during a game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Earlier this week, we published our latest SB Nation Reacts survey, sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , and asked Detroit Lions fans two questions : Will the Lions beat the Bills in Week 2? (weekly question) Are you confident the Lions are headed in the right direction? (recurring poll) Confidence dipped ahead of Week 2 after the Lions stumbled late in the game vs. the Saints and needed overtime to secure the win, but the majority of fans are doing their best not to overreact to a single September game. That confidence dip has also carried over to the game predictions survey, as most fans expect the Lions to struggle in Buffalo on Thursday night. Let’s take a look at the results of this week’s polls: Let’s take a closer look at the comment section of our original article and The Feed post to see fans’ explanations for why they voted the way they did (lightly edited for clarity). Best of “right direction” comments : presde : “Very confident. I know everyone talks about the Lions’ escape, but the physicality in the trenches was back. All the mistakes will get cleaned up, and if this team stays healthy, who knows how far they go.” Xlgrev : “Extremely confident. This is how the modern NFL typically goes. There are rarely blowout wins, and each game has swings of momentum. The good teams figure out a way to win and the not so good teams (Packers) figure out a way to lose.” Best of “Week 2” prediction comments: Oldmanlion : “My heart always says yes. My head… it’s going to be tough.” Justwantwins : “I suspect this game will come down to whoever has the ball last” critical perspective : “I don’t have this one going our way. title: Detroit Lions re-sign Levi Onwuzurike, elevate 2 OL for Bills game
summary: The Detroit Lions have made their final roster moves in preparation for Thursday night’s game against the Buffalo Bills, and none of them are particularly surprising. First, the Lions have signed defensive tackle Levi Onwuzurike from the practice squad to the 53-man roster. Last week, the Lions cut Onwuzurike and signed him to the practice […]
full_text: From left, Detroit Lions center Seth McLaughlin (65), center Cade Mays (64) and guard Tate Ratledge (69) practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions have made their final roster moves in preparation for Thursday night’s game against the Buffalo Bills, and none of them are particularly surprising. First, the Lions have signed defensive tackle Levi Onwuzurike from the practice squad to the 53-man roster. Last week, the Lions cut Onwuzurike and signed him to the practice squad. While no formal explanation was given by the team, there is a pretty common strategy that the Lions appear to have implemented. Vested veterans see their entire annual salary become guaranteed if they’re on the 53-man roster during the team’s Week 1 game. The Lions avoided this last week by playing Ben Stille over Onwuzurike. Now that Onwuzurike is on the roster, he’s eligible to play on Thursday, but his salary won’t be guaranteed. The other two moves the Lions made were temporarily elevating two offensive linemen from the practice squad: Seth McLaughlin and Devin Cochran. These moves were expected, because the Lions have already declared two offensive linemen OUT for this game due to injury: starting left guard Christian Mahogany and starting right tackle Blake Miller. McLaughlin and Cochran will not only give Detroit better depth along the offensive line, but their addition also pushes Detroit’s game-day roster to eight offensive linemen, allowing the team to keep an extra player eligible to play—moving from 47 players to 48. So with the Lions’ 53-man roster back to 53 players, plus the two practice squad elevations for the Bills game (55 total players), the Lions will have to declare seven inactive players for Thursday night to get down to 48. Two of those are already known, with Mahogany and Miller out.

Detroit Lions (1-0) at Buffalo Bills (1-0) Spread BUF -4.5 · Total 54.5 · Implied BUF 29.5 / DET 25.0 Week 1: Buffalo 36-31 at Houston: Josh Allen 20-of-29, 334 yards, 2 pass TD, 2 rush TD Detroit 31-30 (OT) over New Orleans: Jahmyr Gibbs 29-156-2 rushing; Amon-Ra St. Brown 10-67-2; Jared Goff 26-of-39, 206 yards, 2 TD. FPTS game script: Buffalo is favored by 4.5 at home and should stay balanced. Detroit already throws more than expected; trailing would push that further. That script is the whole game. If Buffalo gets ahead, Allen can pick spots in the two passing mismatches below. If Detroit stays within one score, Gibbs and the Lions’ anti-blitz / run edges become live. The five FPTS Data matchup edges Each row is unit vs unit. Rank 1 is best. The bar leans toward the team that owns the gap. Two Buffalo passing edges, three Detroit counter-edges. That is a shootout profile with a home-favorite tilt, not a one-sided smash. 1. Intermediate passing: BUF #1 vs DET #25 (+24) This is the largest bar on the graphic and the cleanest “why Buffalo is favored” number. Allen’s Week 1 tape already pointed here. He averaged 11.5 yards per attempt and 11.5 air yards per attempt , with 38.5% of throws traveling 15+ yards and 26.9% traveling 20+. First-down dropbacks jumped to 48.1% after sitting at 39.2% last year. On first-down passes he went 8-of-12 for 186 yards. Brady’s Bills are no longer a “run first, then throw” offense; they are throwing in-structure and down the field earlier. Detroit is missing the two players who police those windows. Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch are both on PUP and ineligible until Week 5. New Orleans’ Tyler Shough just went 35-of-56 for 410 yards and 3 TDs . Detroit allowed 378 net passing yards in Week 1, last in the league. Intermediate in-breakers, play-action crossers, and TE seams are the exact throws a safety-less Lions defense will struggle to wall off. How Buffalo should attack it: play-action from under center and 13-personnel (Buffalo used 13-personnel on 40.4% of snaps in Week 1, highest in the NFL), then hit Dalton Kincaid and DJ Moore on intermediate crossers and seams. Kincaid went 5-for-6 for 130 yards and 5.91 yards per route. Moore was 5-for-8 for 100 yards and a TD , plus a 46-yard PI. Those two are the primary beneficiaries of this +24 gap. 2. Deep passing: BUF #5 vs DET #24 (+19) Same defense, longer throws. Allen went 11-of-14 on throws of 10+ yards against Houston and posted a 12.8-yard aDOT. Brady ran play-action on 40.5% of dropbacks. Detroit’s deep-pass rank (#24) plus missing safeties is an invitation to take shots, especially early, when Buffalo is still on schedule. Watch DJ Moore and Keon Coleman on go/post concepts, and Allen himself if the pocket breaks. The Lions’ front can still generate pressure, Aidan Hutchinson had 2 sacks in Week 1, but once Allen escapes, Detroit’s current secondary is not built to cover the second play. 3. Beating the blitz: DET off. #9 vs BUF blitz D #30 (-21) This is Detroit’s best passing answer. Buffalo’s blitz EPA rank of 30th says the Bills have been getting cooked when they send extra rushers. Goff has lived on that look for years: quick game, choice routes, and St. Brown sitting in the hole the blitzer vacated. St. Brown saw a league-high 14 targets in Week 1 (10-67-2), including 54.5% of third-down targets and 57.1% of red-zone targets. If Jim Leonhard’s new 3-4 front gets impatient on a short week, Goff’s anti-blitz profile is the punishment. Caveat: Detroit’s offensive line is banged up. LG Christian Mahogany (hip) and RT Blake Miller (knee) are out; C Juice Scruggs is limited. If those spots don’t hold up, Buffalo can get home with four and never need the blitz this graphic flags as a weakness. That is the swing factor for whether this -21 gap actually shows up. 4. Two-TE / 12-personnel: BUF 12P off. #27 vs DET vs 12P #9 (-18) This one is easy to misread. Buffalo loves heavy personnel . Week 1 was loaded with 13-personnel (three TEs), and Dan Campbell specifically called out Buffalo’s three-TE versatility, one blocker, one matchup piece, one hybrid. But FPTS is grading 12-personnel EPA , and Buffalo’s 12-personnel offense ranks only #27. Detroit’s defense against 12P ranks #9. So: Buffalo can line up heavy, but Detroit has been good at defending two-TE looks specifically. The implication is not “don’t use tight ends.” It is “Buffalo’s efficiency edge is not coming from 12p smash-mouth.” The efficiency is coming from intermediate/deep passing out of those looks, and from 13p motion that stresses linebackers. Kincaid still plays; the graphic is saying Detroit can handle base 12p run/play-action better than it can handle Allen’s intermediate game. 5. Run game: DET rush off. #9 vs BUF run D #26 (-17) Gibbs is the reason Detroit can stay in this game. Week 1: 29 carries, 156 yards, 2 TDs , plus 5 catches for 30 yards, 34 touches, 186 total yards. He took 91.9% of backfield touches. Isaiah Pacheco is on IR. This is no longer a Gibbs/Montgomery split. Detroit was under center on 75% of snaps (second in the league) and posted a 51.5% rush success rate , way up from 37.6% in 2025. Buffalo just allowed 124 rushing yards to Houston, including 60 and 3 scores from David Montgomery. ILB Terrel Bernard (calf) and DL TJ Sanders (knee/illness) are on the injury report. If those two are limited, Gibbs’ #9 rush EPA against a #26 run defense is the most transferable Lions edge on the sheet. James Cook is still Buffalo’s balancer (13-57 rushing in Week 1, 88.9% of backfield touches), but the mismatch FPTS is highlighting is Detroit on the ground, not Buffalo. How the script should actually play out If Buffalo leads early (the base case): Allen lives in the +24 intermediate and +19 deep gaps. Detroit is forced into the “already throws more than expected, trailing pushes that further” script. Goff volume rises, St. Brown and Sam LaPorta (8 targets, 82.9% route share in Week 1) become PPR engines, and Detroit needs the anti-blitz edge to hit. The total (54.5) is in play because both defenses leaked 30 in Week 1. If Detroit stays on schedule: Gibbs and under-center 12/13 looks keep Buffalo’s offense off the field. Buffalo only ran 52 plays in Week 1. Detroit ran 73 . That pace gap is how an underdog with a worse passing defense still covers and potentially pulls off the win. The -17 run-game gap is the path to +4.5. The hidden overlay: personnel and absences Lions safeties Branch and Joseph out through Week 4. That amplifies Buffalo’s two passing edges beyond what a generic L5 rank already shows. Lions OL availability will decide whether Goff can actually beat the blitz/rush. title: Detroit Lions vs. Buffalo Bills Week 2 preview: 6 key stats
summary: Two high-powered conference contenders meet Thursday night when the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills open the new Highmark Stadium after both coming off Week 1 barnburners. The last time these two squads faced off, in Week 15 of 2024, they combined for 90 points. After the Bills scored 36 against the Texans and the Lions […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 15: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) scrambles and is hit by Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (46) during the Detroit Lions versus the Buffalo Bills game on Sunday December 15, 2024 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Two high-powered conference contenders meet Thursday night when the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills open the new Highmark Stadium after both coming off Week 1 barnburners. The last time these two squads faced off, in Week 15 of 2024, they combined for 90 points. After the Bills scored 36 against the Texans and the Lions reached 31 thanks to overtime against the Saints, this week’s total has climbed to 54.5—the highest for two teams playing on short rest since 2022. Given the expected fireworks, the Lions will need to keep pace with the fire-breathing beast that is Josh Allen, and they’ll be doing so without three starting offensive linemen in Blake Miller, Cade Mays, and Christian Mahogany. Finding ways to mitigate what Buffalo does best offensively while allowing Detroit’s offense to run the ball like it did in Week 1 against the Saints (33 carries for 165 yards) and play more consistent complementary football will be what gives the Lions a fighter’s chance in this primetime heavyweight fight. Below are my six key stats and matchups for the Lions’ big road tilt. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. Mafia Mash Last season, the Bills offense had its way with teams on the ground as the best rushing offense in football. Buffalo led the NFL with 547 rushing attempts, 2,714 rushing yards, 30 rushing touchdowns, and 0.105 EPA per rush while ranking second with a 47.3% rushing success rate. It was an attack under then-offensive coordinator and now head coach Joe Brady that helped James Cook earn second-team All-Pro honors. The Bills relied on their horses up front and their physicality to define a downhill rushing attack that was both prevalent and successful utilizing inside zone and man/duo concepts. Last season, Buffalo had a 26.5% inside zone run rate (sixth) and 19.0% man/duo rate (25th), averaging 4.6 yards per rush on inside zone (tied-fourth) and 5.3 yards per rush on man/duo (second) as its bread-and-butter, similarly executed run-game concepts. That remained prevalent against the Texans in Week 1, with Buffalo posting a 42.9% inside zone rate (third) and 14.3% man/duo rate (17th). However, the Bills weren’t nearly as successful with the physical, vertical-displacement run designs that worked so well last season, generating only a 33.3% success rate (23rd) on those runs in Week 1. The Texans weren’t able to fully capitalize on taking away the run game, but doing so is still critical for the Lions. As a less dominant pass-coverage unit than Houston, Detroit needs to force Buffalo to play one-handed and rely more heavily on only stopping Josh Allen’s arm and improvisational skills in obvious passing situations. What changed for the Bills this year? Offensive line coach Aaron Kromer retired this offseason, and Alec Anderson replaced Saints free agent loss David Edwards at left guard. He’ll join re-signed center Connor McGovern and recently extended right guard O’Cyrus Torrence as the bruisers on the interior of the trenches. Buffalo will also want to get extra bodies on the field, leading the NFL in Week 1 with a 40.4% 13-personnel rate, with the Rams being the only other team even above 20%. That makes it imperative for Detroit’s point-of-attack defenders up the middle—Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and the other role players in the spine of the defense—to remain stout and give the Lions better chances of getting Buffalo off the field. That’s especially true against those condensed, scale-tipping heavy personnel groupings when the Bills deploy the likes of tight end Jackson Hawes. The Lions’ Week 1 performance against these types of runs was incredibly reassuring. Detroit allowed only 38 yards on 14 such carries for 2.7 yards per attempt (sixth) and just a 14.3% success rate (third) against the Saints. The Lions have invested heavily in those interior trench players, and making sure everything is placed on Josh Allen’s shoulders is a necessary first requirement when facing this juggernaut offense. Otherwise, Detroit risks finding itself in the ultimate pick-your-poison situation. Bomb Squad Next on the Detroit Lions’ defensive checklist for the jauntin’ Josh Allen is disarming his reinvigorated explosive nature. Too often under Kelvin Sheppard, the Detroit Lions’ pass defense has resembled SWAT detective Harry Temple in the movie Speed , played by Jeff Daniels. A routine third- or fourth-and-long has resulted in Detroit getting blown to smithereens 20-plus yards downfield. Last week against the Saints, the Lions’ second-half defense allowed Tyler Shough to average 9.0 yards per attempt with an 8.8-yard aDOT, 309 catchable air yards, and five explosive passes—four of which traveled 20-plus air yards. The last time these two teams played, Josh Allen rocket-launched his way to 10.6 yards per attempt, a 9.7-yard aDOT, 249 catchable air yards, and seven explosive passes, including four that traveled 20-plus air yards. When it came to those deep shots last season, Allen still ranked second with 75 attempts of 20-plus air yards, but Buffalo’s success and reliance on them declined. Allen completed only 34.7% of those passes (26th), while his overall aDOT dwindled to 7.3 yards (tied-24th). That all changed last week against the Texans. On Sunday, Allen was back in risky business, ranking second in the league at 11.1 yards per attempt with a league-leading 12.8-yard aDOT—his highest since 2022—along with the third-most catchable air yards (223) and five explosive completions. He also tied Shough for the league lead with four completions on passes traveling 20-plus air yards. A healthy Dalton Kincaid (career-high 130 receiving yards in Week 1) and the addition of DJ Moore (100 receiving yards) opened up plenty for the Bills’ passing attack. Kincaid was essentially a power slot in Week 1, aligning detached on 72.5% of his snaps and out wide on 37.5% of offensive snaps, both comfortably higher than last season’s rates. He hauled in all four of his targets traveling 10-plus air yards, including two of 20-plus, becoming the first Bills receiver to record 100-plus downfield receiving yards in a game since late 2024. Moore, meanwhile, had seven targets of 10-plus air yards, resulting in four receptions for 93 downfield receiving yards—his most since late in the 2023 season—while aligning out wide on 76.7% of his snaps. The duo of Kincaid and Moore represents the pair of offensive skill threats that most threaten the Lions’ ability to control this game. How Sheppard approaches pass coverage—whether again relying on an onslaught of blitzes and possibly leaning more into zone coverage—will be telling. How Detroit deploys its matchups against tight ends will be an interesting development, potentially with Christian Izien serving as the key to unlocking that element in his Lions debut. Just as important will be how D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin handle Moore downfield and what level of help they receive from the safeties, while potentially seeing more Thomas Harper than Chuck Clark to account for Buffalo’s downfield attack and the need to put an umbrella over the offense. Frisky Fourth Down Duo In a high-stakes, high-scoring matchup where every possession matters, both coaches will likely be aggressive about keeping their offenses on the field. Their fourth-down decision-making last season certainly supports that, with both teams consistently looking to maximize drives. summary: The Green Bay Packers’ Thursday practice came with some good news and some bad news. The good news is that rookie second-round cornerback Brandon Cisse, who got the start at left cornerback in Week 1, is now completely off the injury report after leaving Sunday’s loss early with cramps. For anyone who saw Carrington Valentine’s […]
full_text: (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ Thursday practice came with some good news and some bad news. The good news is that rookie second-round cornerback Brandon Cisse, who got the start at left cornerback in Week 1, is now completely off the injury report after leaving Sunday’s loss early with cramps. For anyone who saw Carrington Valentine’s short but impactful handful of snaps (derogatory) that will be music to your ears. The bad news is that defensive lineman Javon Hargrave, who came into the year dealing with a knee injury, was also listed as a limited participant for Wednesday’s practice due to a concussion. On Thursday, his status was downgraded to being a non-participant. Before practice on Thursday, head coach Matt LaFleur said that both Hargrave and Lukas Van Ness (another player with a surprise concussion status on Wednesday) were in the league’s concussion protocol due to contact they sustained in Sunday’s game, not Wednesday’s practice (usually when a player gets injured midway through a practice, his status is listed as limited for that day). For whatever reason, though, Hargrave’s health seems to be trending in a downward direction. The only other non-participant on Thursday was defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), who was inactive for Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings. The limited participants for Green Bay today were left guard Aaron Banks (knee), right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt (ankle), edge defender Barryn Sorrell (foot) and linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles), along with Van Ness. Banks and Hopper were not active last week due to injury, but the rest of the players on the list were able to finish Week 1’s action (as was Hargrave). Banks’ situation is still touch and go, but it seems like the group of Bako-Bewele, Wyatt and Sorrell should be able to suit up on Sunday, with Hopper (missed last week), Hargrave (concussion) and Van Ness (concussion) being the question marks and Brinson likely to miss action. On the Jets’ end of the injury report, starting linebacker Jamien Sherwood (knee) and second-round rookie cornerback D’Angelo Ponds (calf) went from limited participants to full participants over the last two days. Sherwood played last week against the Tennessee Titans, but Ponds was inactive for the game. Edge rusher Will McDonald IV (ankle) popped up on the injury report for the first time this week on Thursday, after not being listed on the injury report at all yesterday. Apparently, he suffered an injury that led to him being a limited participant today. We’ll keep you updated on New York’s designated pass-rusher when we hear news there. Rookie first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle), starting safety Minkah Fitzpatrick (groin), edge defender Joseph Ossai (foot) and running back/returner Kene Nwangwu haven’t practiced with the team this week. Cooper and Fitzpatrick left the game early last week, while Ossai and Nwangwu weren’t healthy enough to be activated. If you want a full breakdown of the Jets’ personnel going into Week 2, including how injuries come into play with the team, you’re going to love this article that we published earlier today . title: Packers have a sneaky interesting tight end room
summary: The Packers’ tight end room is quite a bit different than we expected this season, and quite a long way from the ultimate goal the team had when it spent two top-100 picks at the position in 2023. Drafting Luke Musgrave and Tucker Kraft that year was supposed to produce a two-headed tight end juggernaut, […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Tucker Kraft #85 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers’ tight end room is quite a bit different than we expected this season, and quite a long way from the ultimate goal the team had when it spent two top-100 picks at the position in 2023. Drafting Luke Musgrave and Tucker Kraft that year was supposed to produce a two-headed tight end juggernaut, but that’s not what we’ve got. While Kraft might be the best thing going at the position in the NFL right now, Musgrave has never really lived up to his potential and is currently on the Physically Unable to Perform list. This wasn’t how it was supposed to be. But the Packers have still backdoored their way to an interesting tight end room for 2026, and it’s a lot of fun in its own right. Kraft, of course, is a one-man juggernaut, so the Packers still hit at least part of their 2023 goal. In Week 1, Kraft had an average target depth of 11.8 yards, a career high by far and the sixth highest in the NFL among tight ends with at least three targets. This in his first game back from his torn ACL. Not too shabby! I wish we could have sprinkled at least one rushing attempt in there , too, but you can’t have everything, I guess. Kraft is joined by Jonnu Smith, the epitome of a late-camp signing. Nobody should read into his big-time reception in Week 1 as evidence of future highlights, but it’s funny to note that he produced a longer catch (43 yards) in one game with the Packers than Luke Musgrave did in his entire Packers career (35 regular season games). But more importantly, Smith gave the Packers 32 snaps on Sunday, lining up in-line, in H-back/wing looks, in the slot, and out wide. That’s valuable versatility, and if he can do that in addition to providing the occasional catch, he’s more than worth whatever the Packers paid for him. Mark Redman and Josh Whyle fill out the rest of the room, and both of them were nearly as versatile as Smith. Both Redman and Whyle took snaps aligned as fullbacks, and Redman did some particularly nice work as a traditional in-line Y as well. It all adds up to a tight end room that’s versatile and interesting, if not particularly explosive as receivers outside of Kraft’s general excellence and Smith’s fluky play. Though max-protection plans surely had something to do with it, the Packers ran 31 plays with two or more tight ends on the field in Week 1 per Sumer Sports (21 in 12 personnel and 10 in 13). That will fluctuate week to week and probably won’t be as high when the Packers aren’t facing a blitzaholic madman, but it still seems like a good indication that tight ends are going to be a big part of the Packers’ plans this year. And fortunately, they’ve got the guys to make it happen.

title: Green Bay Packers sign OL Cordell Volson
summary: Bill Huber of Sports Illustrated is reporting that the Green Bay Packers signed offensive lineman Cordell Volson to their practice squad on Thursday, one day after Volson — and only Volson — worked out with the team. So far this season, Volson is the seventh outside signing brought in for the Packers’ practice squad, and […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bill Huber of Sports Illustrated is reporting that the Green Bay Packers signed offensive lineman Cordell Volson to their practice squad on Thursday, one day after Volson — and only Volson — worked out with the team. So far this season, Volson is the seventh outside signing brought in for the Packers’ practice squad, and the addition of Volson fills Green Bay’s practice squad roster moving forward. Here is what we wrote about Volson yesterday , when it was reported that he was brought in: Volson was picked in the fourth round out of North Dakota State back in 2022. Over his rookie contract, he played 50 games (48 starts) with the Cincinnati Bengals at guard. He didn’t play at all during the 2025 regular season, though, because he had a season-ending surgery on his right shoulder. After the completion of his rookie contract, he signed a one-year, $3.2 million contract with the Tennessee Titans this offseason, which included $2 million in guaranteed money. He did not make it through final cuts with the Titans, so he’s now a free agent. For what it’s worth, Volson worked out with the Dallas Cowboys last week, who ultimately ended up signing former Pro Bowler Laken Tomlinson to their practice squad. Going into camp, it was projected that Volson was going to be the Titans’ starting right guard, but rookie fifth-round pick Fernando Carmona Jr. ended up winning the job. Volson had a 29.1 grade in true pass protection sets in the 2024 season per Pro Football Focus, the last year in which he was active for a regular-season game. The following players have now been brought in from the outside to fill out Green Bay’s practice squad: QB Kedon Slovis (via Cardinals) RB Damon Bankston (via Giants) WR Quincy Skinner Jr. (via Jets) OL Cordell Volson (via Titans) DL Eric Johnson II (via Falcons) S Khalef Kailassie (via Vikings) K Lenny Krieg (international exemption, had spent three days in Green Bay this summer) That leaves us with 10 players who are currently on the Packers’ practice squad who were members of the 91-man active roster before cutdowns: RB Pierre Strong Jr. WR Isaiah Neyor TE Drake Dabney OL Dalton Cooper OL Josh Gesky OL Dillon Wade ED Nyjalik Kelly ED Arron Mosby LB Kristian Welch CB Domani Jackson There’s a bit of a bloat at the offensive line position, but I don’t think Green Bay fans will be complaining about that after the game we just saw in Week 1 . Below are the full roster counts for the Packers, once you combine the 53-man roster and 17-man practice squad: QB: 3 RB: 5 (1 exempt) WR: 8 (1 IR-DFR) TE: 5 (1 PUP) OL: 14 DL: 8 (1 PUP) ED: 6 (1 IR-DFR, 1 PUP) LB: 6 CB: 6 S: 5 K: 2 P: 1 LS: 1 If nothing else, there’s a big number of offensive linemen in practice for Green Bay moving forward. If I were to guess, they’re probably going to move off of one of them the next time they need to add numbers at another position. The names below are a rolling list of players who have been brought in for tryouts or visits since the cutdown deadline: QB Jack Plummer QB Cam Miller RB Phil Mafah (signed by Giants) RB Damon Bankston (signed by Packers) RB Ian Wheeler WR Nick Nash WR Bryce Oliver (signed by Texans) WR Quincy Skinner Jr. (signed by Packers) TE Cody Hardy OL Cordell Volson (signed by Packers) DL Zxavian Harris ( they got in trouble for this ) DL Eric Johnson II (signed by Packers) DL Jalen Hunt ED Cruz Smith ( international exemption player from Australia, per sources ) CB Ambry Thomas S Sanoussi Kane S Kahlef Hailassie (signed by Packers) S John Saunders Jr. (signed by Jets)

full_text: (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The victim in Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs’ legal matter requested a permanent seal of discovery evidence after Jacobs pleaded no contest to charges of battery and criminal damage to property last week. According to FOX 11 News in Green Bay , Judge Marc Hammer, who is overseeing this case, denied the victim’s motion for a permanent seal due to a paperwork issue. Per the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel , the request was “not in the proper format for the Brown County court system,” and the judge encouraged her legal team to refile the request. According to the documents provided to FOX 11 News, the motion was declined on Tuesday and was officially filed on Thursday. Below was the justification for keeping evidence from entering the public sphere, from the perspective of the victim’s representation: The Court finds that public disclosure of the Discovery Material would threaten or substantially impair ANM’s privacy, dignity, personal security, emotional well-being, or ability to participate safely in the criminal-justice process. This protection is not to impede any legitimate law-enforcement function, criminal prosecution, judicial proceeding, or disclosure otherwise required by law, but to prevent unnecessary public dissemination of information that identifies ANM, reveals intimate or sensitive details of ANM, or creates a material risk of harm. ANM is an acronym used for the anonymous woman identified as Jacobs’ girlfriend. At the moment, the next hearing in this case — where we might see the judge making a ruling on the refiled paperwork from victim’s team — is set to overlap with the same day as a nationally televised Packers game, as Green Bay will host their first home game of the year against the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday, September 24th. Evidence, particularly a video, is becoming a crucial piece of this story, as the police report stated that a forensics analysis team was able to recover footage from a camera in Jacobs’ garage that shows part of “the altercation.” Per the police report, the running back “grabbed [victim] and threw her to the ground and she struck her head” while she tried to leave Jacobs’ residence via the garage after a dispute that originated over text messages. The police report states flatly that she is seen on the ground in the garage and that “approximately 40 seconds later, Jacobs returns to the garage and appears to damage ANM’s phone.” What is unclear, because of the wording of the police report, is whether or not “the altercation” includes the portion of the dispute where Jacobs had a physical interaction with his girlfriend. Fueling the fire for interest in the video is that the NFL is reportedly attempting to acquire the video prior to making a ruling on Jacobs’ return to the field. At the moment, Jacobs is on the commissioner exempt list, essentially a purgatory situation as it stands right now. He’s not officially suspended by the league, and any time on the commissioner exempt list will essentially function as time served toward a suspension — if the NFL suspends him — but the league has yet to make a decision on whether they will suspend Jacobs or for how long. Jacobs’ legal team asked for a temporary order to seal evidence , which is why the video evidence is still sealed today. For whatever it’s worth, Jacobs’ request was filed on September 10th — the day of his no contest plea — while the victim’s original request was filed on September 15th. Below was the justification that Jacobs’ representatives filed with the court for the evidence being sealed: The Court finds that public disclosure of the Discovery Material would threaten or substantially impair Defendant’s and [the victim’s] privacy, dignity, personal security, emotional wellbeing, or ability to participate safely in the criminal-justice process. This protection is not to impede any legitimate law-enforcement function, criminal prosecution judicial proceeding, or disclosure otherwise required by law, but to prevent unnecessary public dissemination of information that identifies [the victim], reveals intimate or sensitive details of [the victim] or the Defendant, or creates a material risk of harm. The timing of the NFL’s punishment for Jacobs and the potential release of a video is important to the league, as Ray Rice took the NFL to arbitration over his indefinite suspension in 2014. Initially, the league only suspended Rice for two games, but after the video of his domestic violence incident went public, the NFL pushed him more severely. In the end, it was ruled that the league only had one opportunity to suspend the running back for a single personal conduct violation, because Rice never misled the NFL, and he was paid back for the game checks that he missed while on suspension. The NFL learned the hard way back in 2014 that they only get to use the suspension button once per case, as long as they aren’t misled, and can’t just use the temperature of public perception to a video to justify added punishment. Because of that Rice ruling in 2014 and the situation surrounding the video evidence in this case, the league’s announcement of a potential Jacobs suspension is taking some time. — Update: The lawyers for the victim have resubmitted their proposal, according to WBAY in Green Bay .

title: Green Bay Packers News: Can the Packers offensive line bounce back against the Jets?
summary: Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love was hit 15 times and sacked four times in Sunday’s 39-22 loss to Minnesota (OC Adam Stenavich actually counted 18 hits). While blitzing at an unheard of rate, the Vikings pressured Love on nearly 55% of his dropbacks. For Packers fans, the second half of that game was one […]
full_text: (Photo by USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co) Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love was hit 15 times and sacked four times in Sunday’s 39-22 loss to Minnesota (OC Adam Stenavich actually counted 18 hits). While blitzing at an unheard of rate, the Vikings pressured Love on nearly 55% of his dropbacks. For Packers fans, the second half of that game was one long “oh no” moment. Is this what our OL will look like all year? Did it not get better, but worse? But context matters. Brian Flores created a uniquely difficult assignment in a particularly hostile environment. That doesn’t excuse everything. Stenavich acknowledged that communication and mental errors caused breakdowns, while Matt LaFleur said the Packers need to establish continuity up front. You think? The Packers may get a slight personnel boost Sunday. Left guard Aaron Banks, who missed the Minnesota game with a knee issue, returned to practice Wednesday and is working his way back toward game readiness. Banks has been a disappointment when compared to the contract he signed last year, but his return to the lineup would still represent an upgrade in experience and ability. Looking ahead: the Jets aren’t very good, but they don’t exactly offer a soft landing. Last week, they held Tennessee to 195 total yards, and generated three sacks. They have an edge group that Green Bay knows it shouldn’t overlook. So, can the Packers bounce back? Great question! The truth is that the answer has to be yes. A repeat of Minnesota’s 15-plus-hit performance would suddenly turn an already challenging schedule into an even steeper uphill climb. The remedy? Quit being cute with your starters. Start your best 5. Clean up communications. Try to stay healthy. If those boxes get checked, and the offense in general continues to land explosive plays, Week 1 looks more like an isolated example of how bad it could get rather than a true forecast for the rest of the schedule. Hopefully, Sunday provides a much clearer indication of if it’s the former or the latter. Confidence meter: how I feel about Packers’ OL bouncing back vs. Jets The Green Bay Packers’ offensive line was beaten to a pulp by the Vikings. Will it bounce back on Sunday and will it be good enough for the Packers to be a playoff contender? ICYMI: How would you fix the offensive line? Let’s discuss! If you have any ideas on how to solve Green Bay’s issues up front, let us hear them. Cooper was ‘lights out’ in week one Despite the loss, Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon made it clear that Edgerrin Cooper excelled, and that his stock remains firmly up. Packers WR Jayden Reed responds after disappointing loss Jayden Reed was seemingly absent from the offense in week one. That’s not something the fourth-year wideout is worried about going forward. On this week’s UnPack pod, the guys identify which conclusions they’re jumping to after a hard-to-watch season opener for the Packers in Minnesota. title: Packers Film Room: Week 1 pressure of the week
summary: In the last article, we covered the week 1 blitz of the week. In this article we’ll cover the pressure of the week. The difference between two is simple, a blitz sends five or more rushers at the quarterback. A pressure can be generated without a blitz and it can involve simulated pressures and creeper […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Edgerrin Cooper #56 of the Green Bay Packers sacks Carson Wentz #11 of the Minnesota Vikings in the fourth quarter of a game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the last article, we covered the week 1 blitz of the week . In this article we’ll cover the pressure of the week. The difference between two is simple, a blitz sends five or more rushers at the quarterback. A pressure can be generated without a blitz and it can involve simulated pressures and creeper pressures. Pressure is also loosely something used to describe what happens to a quarterback as soon as he’s throwing the ball (a hit, hurry, or sack). Creeper and sim pressures are ways defenses disguise pressure by sending different rushers than the front initially shows, while dropping a would-be rusher into coverage — keeping the same number of rushers (usually four) as a standard down, but changing who’s doing the rushing. Simulated pressure A sim pressure shows blitz-like pressure — often with multiple defenders walked up near the line — but ultimately rushes a “normal” number of players (typically four), just not the four the offense expects. The defense drops a lineman or an edge player into coverage and replaces him with a blitzing linebacker or defensive back. It’s designed to confuse protection (it simulates a blitz look pre-snap and alters the offensive line slide protection without actually bringing extra numbers). It creates free access or leverage against the protection’s blocking rules. Creeper pressure A creeper is closely related but usually refers more specifically to bringing an off-ball defender (linebacker or DB) while dropping a down lineman or edge rusher into a shallow coverage zone (often a “spy” or hook/curl zone). The name comes from the rusher “creeping” up late or from depth rather than lining up on the line pre-snap, making it harder for the quarterback and O-line to identify pre-snap. Creepers tend to emphasize disguise and late movement more than the wholesale front-to-coverage swap that defines a sim pressure. In practice, the two terms overlap a lot in modern usage (Fangio-tree defenses especially), and people often use “sim” as the umbrella term with “creeper” as a specific flavor of it — a same-number pressure where the exchange rusher comes from depth or off the ball rather than off the edge. Wasp creeper “Wasp” is a simulated pressure to the weak side that attacks the A-gap with the Jack linebacker. In Fangio’s terminology, of which Jonathan Gannon is a part of, the “Jack” refers to the linebacker most teams would call the Will, or weak-side ILB. On Wasp, the Jack linebacker shoots the A-gap on his side while the Nose occupies the A-gap on the opposite side or the center. If the offense lines up 3×1, the defense rotates into a strong-side Cover 3; if it’s a 2×2 look instead, the defense plays Quads (Quarters) coverage, which has the option to bracket down into Palms (2-Read). Facing a 3×1 double-slot alignment, the defense calls Wasp paired with cover-3 behind it. The offense counters with four verticals, a concept designed to attack the weaknesses in cover-3. Here, the Vikings motion from a 2-back back field (the 3×1 side) to a 2×2 just before the snap. The coverage most likely would have shifted from cover-3 to quarters here. At the second level, the Safeties will read the release of the tight end and opposite #2 receiver. If the tight end releases, like he does here, the safety will get over the top of a potential vertical. If the tight end were to stay in and block, there’s no more vertical threat and the safeties would redirect their eyes to the far side to wall off any crossing routes. The routes barely develop here as linebacker Edgerrin Cooper sprints through the A-gap and sacks Carson Wentz as he barely hits the top of his dropback, forcing a 6-yard loss. Cooper gets a free run thanks to the nose tackle and defensive tackle occupying the center and left guard. Unfortunately on this drive, the very next play resulted in an illegal contact penalty after Wentz was sacked by Cooper and Devonte Wyatt. A couple of ticky-tack penalties called on the Packers defense kept this drive alive and moving down the field until the Vikings eventually scored what would end up being the game-winning points.

title: Packers vs. Jets preview: A crash course on New York’s personnel
summary: It’s time to stop licking our wounds, and time to focus on the Green Bay Packers’ next opponent. To set the table for some of the analysis that will come out later this week, let’s talk about the New York Jets’ roster and their starting players — as the Packers hope to best them to […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time to stop licking our wounds, and time to focus on the Green Bay Packers’ next opponent. To set the table for some of the analysis that will come out later this week, let’s talk about the New York Jets’ roster and their starting players — as the Packers hope to best them to avoid an 0-2 start. Last week, the Jets ran for 152 yards in a fairly low-scoring 23-10 game against what looks to be a very poor Tennessee Titans. For what it’s worth, they held quarterback Cam Ward to just a 34.4 QBR in Sunday’s win. Skill Players QB Geno Smith RB Breece Hall WR Garrett Wilson WR Adonai Mitchell WR Isaiah Williams TE Mason Taylor TE Jeremy Ruckert On film, quarterback Geno Smith looked spry — more like the Seattle Seahawks version of himself than what we saw with the Las Vegas Raiders last year. Obviously, New York’s number one running back is Breece Hall, but expect former Badger Braelon Allen to get some touches throughout the game, too. Running back Kene Nwangwu, best known for his contributions as a returner, missed Week 1 (he was listed on the injury report as doubtful), and he was listed as a non-participant in practice on Wednesday . Rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. is expected to miss several weeks with an ankle sprain, a pretty big blow for the Jets, who are already down a projected starting receiver in Tim Patrick — who is on the injured reserve with a groin injury. At the moment, New York’s third receiver appears to be Isaiah Williams, a third-year undrafted free agent who is already on his third NFL team. Frank Reich is a demon pic.twitter.com/9FnVGNHO2H — Jalen Brunson enthusiast (NBA CHAMPIONS) (@GothamCityM) September 14, 2026 Because of the issues at receiver, don’t be surprised if the Jets lean into their tight ends in this game, which would put the Packers’ base 3-4 defense on the field more frequently. New York’s most-used tight ends were Mason Taylor and Jeremy Ruckert in Week 1, but first-round pick Kenyon Sadiq, Jelani Woods and fullback Andrew Beck (a former Packer) also got playing time. In fact, the Jets had the bright idea to play all five of them on the field at once in the red zone in Week 1, featuring Sadiq (who got a rushing touchdown on another play) in the backfield. Offensive Line LT: Olu Fashanu LG: Dylan Parham C: Josh Myers RG: Joe Tippman RT: Armand Membou The Jets’ tackles are young, but you’ll recognize an old name in the middle of the offensive line: former Packer Josh Myers. I’m sure that if the Packers struggle at any point with their own offensive line, we’ll be hearing a lot of would-have, could-have, should-haves about Myers on Sunday. Defensive Line David Onyemata Harrison Phillips T’Vondre Sweat The Jets talked a lot about running a 4-3, 3-4 hybrid this offseason, but they almost exclusively played a 3-4 defense in base in Week 1. Their new-look defensive line mostly featured David Onyemata (a free agent signing) and T’Vondre Sweat (a trade) on the line of scrimmage. For what it’s worth, rookie Darrell Jackson Jr., who was a draft crush of many, was New York’s fifth-most-used defensive lineman last week. Edge Defender David Bailey Kingsley Enagbare This was supposed to be a four-man rotation, but edge defender Joseph Ossai missed last week’s game with a plantar fascia injury and started this week as a non-participant in practice. Without Ossai, it’s really a three-man unit with first-round rookie David Bailey, former Packer Kingsley Enagbare and Will McDonald IV spearheading the unit. Yes, McDonald, who was taken two picks after Lukas Van Ness, has been relegated to a backup role going into Year 4 of his NFL career. Off-Ball Linebacker Demario Davis Jamien Sherwood This one is pretty straightforward, as these players are every-down players for the Jets. Demario Davis is the team’s veteran presence at 37 (!) years old, while Jamien Sherwood is New York’s run-and-chase linebacker. There’s been mixed results on the Sherwood front after the team signed him to a three-year, $45 million contract that helped reset the off-ball linebacker market for non-Pro Bowlers in the 2025 offseason. Cornerback Brandon Stephens Azareye’h Thomas Jarvis Brownlee Jr. (slot) Rookie second-round pick D’Angelo Ponds missed last week’s action with a calf injury after being listed as doubtful going into the weekend. For what it’s worth, Ponds was also a limited participant in practice on Wednesday, as it’s unclear whether or not he will play this week. With Ponds out (and a major injury at safety), the outside cornerbacks right now are Brandon Stephens and Azareye’h Thomas, with Jarvis Brown Jr. playing in the slot. Safety Dane Belton Andre Cisco Starting safety Minkah Fitzpatrick left Week 1 early with a groin injury and is expected to miss several weeks, meaning he obviously won’t play against the Packers. Without Fitzpatrick, the safeties were Dane Belton and Andre Cisco, two journeyman players. — In kicker news, the Jets had to call up veteran Jason Sanders from the practice squad for Blake Grupe last week. The two are in a kicking competition right now, and it’s not clear who will be on the field against the Packers on Sunday.

title: Value of Things: By the numbers
summary: With a week of football in the books, we can begin to tackle what we currently are seeing in this year of football. On a long enough timeline, the survival rate drops to zero. Every year of football stands on its own and one of the biggest mistakes people make is that they assume because […]
full_text: With a week of football in the books, we can begin to tackle what we currently are seeing in this year of football. On a long enough timeline, the survival rate drops to zero. Every year of football stands on its own and one of the biggest mistakes people make is that they assume because things happened a certain way last year that they will happen the same way this year. of course, that is both positive and negative as we will find out. So, these numbers will build and will begin to make more sense as the season goes along. What we do here is take some basic rankings from both teams and evaluate how each team is going to try to maximize those to win the game. Additionally, we are going to track something this year as an alarming trend that has been going on for several seasons now. Yes, each year does stand on its own, but we do see some distinct patterns that pop up. The Numbers Texans Bengals Rushing Yards For 13th 19th Passing Yards For 8th 9th Rushing Yards Allowed 8th 10th Passing Yards Allowed 29th 17th Additionally, we are going to track how many catches and yards primary tight ends get against the Texans defense. Dalton Kincaid finished week one with five catches for 130 yards. Dawson Knox also had one catch for seven yards, so Bills’ tight ends combined for six catches and 137 yards. Obviously, that is likely considerably more than the average tight end comes up with. Stay tuned. How will the Bengals offense attack the Texans? This one is obvious beyond measure. The Bengals are not a good running football team likely because they have never had a good offensive line. They rely on two premium wide receivers and a premium quarterback to get things done. However, Mike Gesicki (their tight end) actually led them in receiving last week. Those looking for an easy prop bet the cash in on would be wise to take the over on receptions and yardage for him in this game. I don’t think he will go off like Dalton Kincaid, but with Henry To’o’to’o on the shelf, coverage will likely fall on whoever takes his slot or Reed Blankenship. That’s a scary proposition either way. The Texans secondary has to keep safeties back to guard against the deep ball to Chase and/or Higgins. That means a heavy dose of Joe Burrow coming in this one. How will the Bengals defense attack the Texans? The Bengals look improved through one week, but a lot of that was opportune turnovers. The key to beating the Texans is to take advantage of their struggles in pass protection. Fortunately, it looks like the run blocking is improving, but there are still lapses in the passing game that crop up in key moments. C.J. Stroud has shown that ball security is sometimes an issue, so the strip sack looks like their path to glory if it is going to come at all for the Bengals. How will the Texans offense attack the Bengals? I would expect something similar to last week where the Texans try to control the clock through ball control. That means a heavy dose of David Montgomery and Woody Marks. This is particularly true with Nico Collins possibly being limited or out due to his hamstring injury. The Texans depth at tight end could lend itself to a ton of 13 formations where you utilize three different tight ends for blocking and/or receiving. Either way, DeMeco Ryans isn’t going to suddenly sling it around the yard unless the Texans are coming from behind. If they got an exact replica of week one for seventeen weeks they would take it and run. How will the Texans defense attack the Bengals? The good news is that the Bengals offensive line isn’t as talented as the Bills offensive line. The bad news is they Bengals have more explosive weapons to keep track of. This is a risk/reward scenario waiting to happen. If the Texans defense can get to Burrow five or six times on Sunday then it could be a great week. If they have a similar week as week one then it could be another disappointing day. Matt Burke may have to dial up the pressure a little more to force the issue. If they can slow down Chase Brown then it could be an easier path to victory for the Texans defense.

title: Texans fans already waiting for next season?
summary: Will the Texans beat the Cincinnati Bengals this weekend? We spent all off-season believing the Houston Texans defense would carry this team to great heights. We also believed the offense was still a long way from prime time. Last weekend, against the Buffalo Bills, our defense surrendered the most points they’d given up in a […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: David Montgomery #32 of the Houston Texans celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Xavier Hutchinson #19 against the Buffalo Bills during the fourth quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images Will the Texans beat the Cincinnati Bengals this weekend? We spent all off-season believing the Houston Texans defense would carry this team to great heights. We also believed the offense was still a long way from prime time. Last weekend, against the Buffalo Bills, our defense surrendered the most points they’d given up in a game since the 2023 season. Meanwhile the offense put up 31 and came within one play of 37 and a win. Josh Allen got an elusive W at NRG , Andre Johnson criticized C.J. Stroud for pouting and Henry To’oTo’o went on injured reserve. Thankfully Nick Caserio has assembled a solid Houston Texans depth chart to weather the injuries. But they need to slow down already. Houston’s secondary, especially newly added safety Reed Blankenship, got smoked like a Rudy’s brisket time and again. The only real bright spot to the game was David Montgomery, who racked up 3 scores in his H-Town debut. Then, Wednesday delivered another hit: Nico Collins suffers (yet another) hamstring injury at practice Texans WR Nico Collins injured his hamstring at Wednesday’s practice, met with doctors after and they “don’t believe it’s serious,” per source. Yet Collins’ status for Sunday’s game vs. the Bengals is in jeopardy. pic.twitter.com/Quo1m4C56H — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 17, 2026 The Texans are now down both of their starting wide receivers, with Jayden Higgins already on IR and Collins battling what’s becoming an annual hamstring concern. It’s only week two and the Texans 53 man roster is already down 3 starters. The team did not look well prepared when they took the field last weekend. The most legendary receiver in team history publicly bashed the quarterback for “bad body language”. Seems like everything is going wrong – if you’re only looking for what’s falling apart that is. Houston Texans Andre Johnson on @lgndtlk and what he dislikes about CJ Stroud… Thoughts? pic.twitter.com/KpHiimlFN9 — Kyle Leiblein (@KyleLeiblein) September 15, 2026 Are the wheels already off the bus? Should every Texans fan panic? Is it time to start praying for the 2027 season? Well, before we pack it in and find another pastime, let’s look at the W-L stats for the Texans in opening games. 2025 season – Loss (finished 12-5) 2024 season – Win (finished 10-7) 2023 season – Loss (finished 10-7) 2022 – Tie (finished 3-13-1) Week one’s record over the last 5 seasons isn’t exactly a solid predictor of the how the team finishes. Unless they tie. Which means there’s no reason to get down this soon, despite what many might believe. In fact, the Texans have gone 0-3 to start the season and still made the playoffs. Twice. So, believe that. David Montgomery running for the record books Nothing like a debut as a “secret superstar ” to start things off on the good foot, right? NFL Communications Houston running back David Montgomery recorded three scrimmage touchdowns (two rushing, one receiving) in his Texans’ debut in Week 1. He had 79 scrimmage yards (60 rush, 19 rec.) & 3 TDs (2 rush, 1 rec.) in his Houston debut, becoming 8th player in SB era with 3+ scrimmage TDs in 1st game with new team. Aims for his 3rd in row vs. Cincinatti with 70+ scrimmage yards. Had 71 scrimmage yards (65 rush, 6 rec.) & rush TD in his last game vs. Cin. (10/5/25 w/ Det.) With at least two scrimmage touchdowns on Sunday against Cincinnati (1 p.m., CBS), Montgomery can become the sixth player ever with at least five scrimmage touchdowns in their first two games with a new team, joining Dutch Sternaman (six scrimmage touchdowns with the Decatur Staleys), Jahvid Best (five with Detroit), Kareem Hunt (five with Kansas City), Bob Shaw (five with the Chicago Cardinals) and Billy Sims (five with Detroit). And, as we’ve known all along, a solid run game helps the passing game. Last week, the embattled Stroud put up great numbers, despite the final play, with a 106.7 passer rating. The Bengals Joe Burrow did, not so well, with a rating of 89.5. If Demeco Ryans and defensive coordinator Matt Burke can get the D to play to their potential, this weekend should bring a whole different story. Particularly since the Bengals are not on par with the Josh Allen led Bills. #GoTexans

title: Indianapolis Colts Injury Report: Thursday Week 2
summary: The Indianapolis Colts released their Thursday injury report for Week 2 of the NFL season against the Kansas City Chiefs. Wide receiver Alec Pierce (heel() missed practice Thursday. Pierce had been a full participant the day before. Pierce could be resting and trying to manage the workload on his heel or the worst case scenario […]
full_text: The Indianapolis Colts released their Thursday injury report for Week 2 of the NFL season against the Kansas City Chiefs. Thursday's practice report for #INDvsKC . pic.twitter.com/KFdAVxzwBh — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 17, 2026 Wide receiver Alec Pierce (heel() missed practice Thursday. Pierce had been a full participant the day before. Pierce could be resting and trying to manage the workload on his heel or the worst case scenario could be he could have aggravated his heel injury. Either way it’s not looking great for the Colts WR1 moving forward. Wide receiver Ashton Dulin (ankle) missed back to back practices and looks set to miss this weeks game against the Chiefs. Dulin who had taken on a bigger workload on offense with Pierce’s injury and a key part of the teams special teams unit will be a big miss if he is unavailable Sunday. Running back DJ Giddens (knee) was a new addition to the injury report missing practice on Thursday. Giddens who was a non/factor in his rookie year has seen a drop down the depth chart with the emergence of Seth McGowan at running back behind Jonathan Taylor. Giddens however can’t afford to miss time with injury as it could end up costing him his roster spot. Linebacker Austin Ajake (hamstring) was a full participant at practice. Shake looks like he should be healthy enough to contribute on Sunday. Wide receiver Keenan Allen )rest) was a full participant at practice. Allen was a full go after taking Wednesday off with a scheduled rest day. Quarterback Anthony Richardson (groin) was a full participant after missing Wednesday due to a groin injury. Richardson did not log a single snap in the season opener so it is unclear how he injured his groin but he has bounced back from it and looks to be healthy ahead of Sundays game against the Chiefs. Defensive tackle Grover Stewart (personal) missed practice due to an unknown personal reason, he should be back on Friday. Defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (ankle) and linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) both were full participants again on Thursday.
