title: Saints vs. Ravens: Quarterback Matchup
summary: The Saints are back on the road again following the loss in Detroit, and the matchup is not getting any easier. The Saints have to travel up to Baltimore and line up across from a two-time MVP in Lamar Jackson. Jackson has a new head coach in Jesse Minter and a new OC in Declan […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Saints are back on the road again following the loss in Detroit, and the matchup is not getting any easier. The Saints have to travel up to Baltimore and line up across from a two-time MVP in Lamar Jackson. Jackson has a new head coach in Jesse Minter and a new OC in Declan Doyle. Doyle was an assistant under Sean Payton from 2019-2022 and then went with Payton to Denver for the 2023 and 2024 seasons as well. He was promoted to OC under Ben Johnson last season with the Chicago Bears, but now he is serving as the play caller for Minter in Baltimore, and it seems like that was a great move. Baltimore and Jackson were unlocked last week in Indianapolis against the Colts. Jackson finished the game 17/25 for 324 yards, 13 yards per attempt, one passing touchdown, 40 rushing yards, and one rushing touchdown with no turnovers. If Doyle can make Jackson a more efficient passer of the football, this will definitely cause problems for the rest of the league, especially considering the balance that the offense has with Derrick Henry still being able to run the ball effectively. The Saints are going to have their hands full with Jackson at QB. He’s becoming a more patient passer, but he’s still just as dangerous as a runner. His speed and quickness are second to none, and his vision with the ball makes him as elusive as a running back in the open field. This will not be an easy challenge. Overall, the Saints defense did not play poorly against Detroit. The offense put them in some very tough situations, and in the third quarter, it did so rather quickly with back-to-back turnovers. Hopefully, those issues get cleaned up this week. That leads us into Tyler Shough. Shough is coming off one of the most impressive second-half performances the Saints have seen in quite some time. Shough finished the game last week with 410 passing yards on 35/56 completions for a completion percentage of 62.5%. He had three touchdowns, but he also had two interceptions and a fumble. It was literally a tale of two halves for Shough. It was not until the Saints went down 21-0 in the third quarter that this young, budding star turned the lights on and absolutely went off. Shough finished the second half 25/34 for a 73.5% completion percentage with three touchdowns, leading the Saints to score 30 points. That is a franchise-level performance for a half of football. But the Saints and this offense need to come out faster than this. In this game, on the road in Baltimore against a defense that will look to be aggressive, starting slow could potentially bury the Saints. The Saints did not fare too well against Aidan Hutchinson last week, and the Ravens added Trey Hendrickson over the offseason to bolster their pass rush. Not only that, but they also have a really good corner in Nate Wiggins who can match up with Chris Olave. Shough will have to be consistent from start to finish if the Saints are going to pull off this upset. Right now, the Ravens are favored by 8.5 points to win the game. It is a tall task, but upsets happen every day in the NFL. How do you think the Saints match up at the QB position, and do you think they can pull off this upset? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set for their Monday night game against the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026 | ESPN.com Giants fans who were trepidatious about the additions of Matt Nagy and Greg Roman as offensive architects […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set for their Monday night game against the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026 | ESPN.com Giants fans who were trepidatious about the additions of Matt Nagy and Greg Roman as offensive architects have to feel great about what they saw in Week 1. The Giants were the league’s second-best offense during the opening week of the season by EPA per play, trailing only the Bears. Their 58% success rate was second behind the Jaguars. The only reason they didn’t score more points was time; the Giants used more time per play than anybody else in the league and had only seven possessions in their 28-20 victory over Dallas. As a passer, Dart didn’t have a huge game working from under center, going 5-of-7 for 39 yards with a 2-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely. In all, though, the Giants looked comfortable majoring under center, something they ran only 20% of the time while Dart was on the field a year ago. It’s a positive sign for their offensive progress, although the Rams might offer a more imposing defense to Dart this week on “Monday Night Football.” Dart, Likely keys to impressive win: NFL Insider Jaxson Dart & the Giants are for real….completely different offense with Isaiah Likey out there. pic.twitter.com/W4IphKF45K — Chase Daniel (@ChaseDaniel) September 16, 2026 How this Giants star got on same page with Jaxson Dart and earned his trust | The Record The scene was common on the practice fields with the New York Giants all summer. Starting in West Virginia and continuing in New Jersey, seemingly every day of training camp, Jaxson Dart and Isaiah Likely would be standing together talking football. They would chat up different route concepts, the rules to follow for offscript plays and, above all else, gain comfort in the trust between them. Rams’ Aaron Donald returning vs. Giants? Here’s what Jaxson Dart thinks of facing him | NJ.com Dart said Donald’s “real impact on the game” — beyond his 111 sacks, eight first-team All-Pro selections and three Defensive Player of the Year awards — stems from how offenses must scheme around him. “For the longest time that I can remember, he’s one of the most dominant players that I’ve watched,” Dart said. “So getting the chance to go out there and compete against him, it’s going to be really cool, just to be on the same field as him. He’s a great player, and I’ve heard that he’s kept himself in really good shape. So it’s going to be a great competition. There’s countless clips of putting three offensive linemen on him and [Donald] still being able to make a play. So he’s an unbelievable player and has had an unbelievable career.” Dru Phillips tells The Post how he’s going to turn penalty-filled Week 1 into ‘learning point’ | New York Post Players always say they need to clean up whatever mistakes they made in one game before they hit the field for the next game. Dru Phillips is in that mode this week. The third-year cornerback was called for three pass interference penalties in the season-opening 28-20 victory over the Cowboys. Why it was so important for Giants to secure signature win early in John Harbaugh’s tenure | The Athletic Harbaugh’s resume gave him instant credibility throughout the organization and in the locker room. But the buy-in could fade if the results don’t follow the hard work. That’s why Sunday’s impressive start has made the Giants even stronger believers in Harbaugh’s methods. “I don’t think anyone would shy away from saying it was the hardest training camp of their career,” 10th-year veteran right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “I’ve been around Harbs (in Baltimore), and this was a physical-ass training camp. Now you know why you run that many plays in practice, why you hit as much, why you do those practices, why you lift as much as we do, how hard we work because you go out there on Sunday and, you really beat a team up like that.” NFL Take-o-Meter: What’s Real and Not Entering Week 2 | The Ringer [Extremely John Harbaugh voice] The New York GIANTS are legit contenders. I’ll admit it! I was overconfident that the Giants would stumble out of the gate. I (like an idiot) was high on the Cowboys offense and expected Dallas to experience some positive defensive regression after letting Matt Eberflus loose and replacing him at DC with football nerd icon Christian Parker. But Harbaugh’s new disgusting brothers in the booth— offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and assistant Greg Roman —took out a paddle and spanked the silver off the Cowboys’ pants for all to see. I’m a believer in the tone the Giants want to set and Skattebo’s ability to set it, but I am not buying fully in just yet. The only defense worse than Big Blue’s in Week 1 (again, by EPA per drive) was Parker’s disasterclass. Let’s see Harbaugh and his guys throw the same haymakers against the Rams with Sean McVay and Co. in a must-win spot coming off their Melbourne embarrassment. Daniel Jones lost a friend to suicide; now he advocates for others to ask for help | The Athletic Mission 34’s motto, “A New Type of Tough,” was painted on Jones’ cleats. The five-word slogan is aimed at those who may be struggling with their mental health, especially athletes, with the goal of helping them realize that toughness isn’t defined by a lack of vulnerability, the Bonners said. They believe, along with Jones, that there is strength — and life — in speaking up. Last November wasn’t the first time Jones teamed up with Mission 34, having represented the organization during his New York Giants days, and it won’t be his last. Jones considers it a worthy cause, and he’s keenly aware of the NFL spotlight he wields. September is National Suicide Prevention Month , If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or contact the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741. title: NY Giants DC Dennard Wilson: We’re chasing perfection
summary: The New York Giants have a lot to be happy about on both sides of the ball after Week 1. The offense was methodical and suffocating, while the defense played well against a tough opponent. But that was last week. Now Dennard Wilson’s squad is preparing to travel across the country to take on the […]
full_text: New York Giants pass rusher Kayvon Thibodeaux before a play against the Dallas Cowboys. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants have a lot to be happy about on both sides of the ball after Week 1. The offense was methodical and suffocating, while the defense played well against a tough opponent. But that was last week. Now Dennard Wilson’s squad is preparing to travel across the country to take on the Los Angeles Rams. The Giants’ defense will have to contend with an offense that was the best in the NFL a season ago, masterminded by a coach who has helped to revolutionize offensive football, and quarterback who’s bound for the Hall Of Fame. Oh, and the Rams are coming off of an embarrassing loss to open the season. If the Giants want to stun the NFL and get off to a 2-0 start to the year, they’ll need their defense to step up and make sure the offense doesn’t have to keep up in a shootout. In order to do that, Wilson is paying attention to the areas of improvement as well as what the defense did well against the Dallas Cowboys. On how the Giants’ defense can improve The Giants’ season got off to about as good a start as they could hope for against the Cowboys. The offense and defense both looked much better than expected and the Giants came away with a win after methodically suffocating the Dallas offense. But the Giants’ win wasn’t exactly dominant and left the coaches with areas of improvement on which to work, which is also a good outcome. The Giants were good, but still in a position where they can chase perfection. “We came out and played tough and played physical like we asked them to do,” Wilson said. “Were we perfect? No. We’re still chasing that. I think the guys tried to execute the game plan. They tried to execute it well. They believed in the game plan, and we got the results that we wanted. But there’s some things we need to clean up. First week, we got to get better and keep growing. And if we keep doing that, I think our defense will just keep getting better and better as the season goes.” While coaches always want to see perfect execution, teams also don’t want to peak at the start of the season. Getting an early win as proof that the team’s off-season work will pay off is great, but so too is having goals to chase. No coach wants their team to become complacent, and Wilson definitely has a list of things for his players to work on. In particular, the Cowboys were able to convert 8 of 11 third downs (72%). That would be a fantastic percentage and usually good enough to win a game — if the Giants’ own offense didn’t convert 90% of their own third downs. Getting better at getting off the field on third downs will be a point of emphasis this week as the Giants prepare for the Rams’ offense. “First and foremost, leveraging on route concepts,” Wilson said when asked how the Giants can improve on third down. “There were some plays where we were supposed to have outside leverage and we gave up outside leverage. A couple of those third downs were penalties.” Penalties were a big factor in the game for the Giants, and they were hit with four defensive pass interference penalties. While even wide receiver turned commentator Cris Collinsworth disagreed with some of the DPI calls, the fact remains that they were called and that needs to be cleaned up. “That’s the number one thing we need to correct going forward is the penalties,” Wilson said. “And when you look at the game, the penalties hurt us. All the penalties led to scoring points, right? So, we got to clean up that part of it. And then, on third down we just got to have a tighter game plan, be able to surround what they do offensively, and just go execute. And if we do that, we get them on a couple third downs, we get off the field, no penalties, we play an even cleaner game. So, we’re chasing that. That’s what we’re doing going forward. Those are two areas that we must get better at going into this game because this offense is an efficient offense. So, it’s eliminating the penalties, and being able to produce on third down and get off the field. “The teaching point is this,” Wilson added. “You don’t need to grab. We are in position at the top of the route. It’s just cleaning up our hands. We’re going to be physical. We’re going to challenge people. But at the top of the route, we have to understand how they’re going to call it. And it’s no excuse. When they get to the top of the route, we can’t grab. We can be in the pocket, understand where your leverage is, where your help is, and everything else but we have to clean that up. We cannot hurt our team and hurt our defense by getting penalties. And that’s something that we’re going to correct and it’s been pointed out. And it’s one thing that we’re going to get better at going forward.” Wilson’s defense strives to force low-percentage, tight window throws. The defense will take the next step once they can force quarterbacks into either forcing those throws or holding the ball. And it sounds like that’s an area of real emphasis for Wilson, as well as position coaches Donald D’Alesio and Addison Lynch. On the defense’s versatility The Giants have one of the — if not the — longest and most athletic defensive fronts in the NFL, and certainly the most invested. All told, the Giants have five first round linebackers, all of whom are between 6-foot-3 and 6-foot-5, 243 and 258 pounds, and run between a 4.40 and 4.58-second 40-yard dash. The length, athleticism, and versatility of the Giants’ linebacking corps is truly outstanding. And Wilson is only scratching the surface of how he can deploy all of those pieces. “I like the versatility in all those guys,” he said. “As we progress, Thibs might have a better matchup on a guard. He might have a better matchup on a tackle. It could be (inside linebacker) Arvell (Reese). It could be (outside linebacker Brian) Burns. So, we have flexibility. The guys do a good job because our defense is really, when they learn it, is exceptional. So, it’s just pieces. It’s just X’s moving across the board. So, I like it. It presents problems to other teams and we become a faster defense when they’re all up there. So, we’ll continue to keep sprinkling that in and expand the package.” Speed kills. And while the New York media is bringing back the “NASCAR Package” terminology from the Perry Fewell days, perhaps Steve Spagnuolo’s “Four Aces” is a better term. Or maybe “Royal Flush” is even more apt with the inclusion of Chauncey Golston with Brian Burns , Abdul Carter , Kayvon Thibodeaux , Tremaine Edmunds , and Arvell Reese . The addition of Edmunds and Reese has really changed the complexion of the Giants’ defensive front. Their length and athleticism make each fairly unique among off-ball linebackers in the modern NFL. Having two players like that is even more uncommon. “There’s really not a mismatch problem,” Wilson said. “When Arvell is on and playing the WIL or dime linebacker position. And then, Tremaine is another good athlete. So, it calms the defense a little bit. You can move them around. They can play different spots as well. So, it makes the defense even easier not to be able to have to substitute all the time for favorable matchups for the offense.” “It is unusual now, like in today’s game,” Wilson added. “Because you still have the ability to go dime and take one off or vice versa. But with us, with our flexibility and their athletic ability and their football intelligence, it’s a good thing for us that they can play every snap.” Generally egos can be a problem in a collection of elite athletes, particularly at positions that are known for racking up stats. However, the buy-in from all of the Giants’ front seven players is, as Wilson says, “huge.” “It’s not about individuals,” he said. “It’s not about all the stats. It’s us playing together because when we all play together and we excel on the football field, we’ll all get the results that we want. So, the buy-in is huge. There’s a bunch of…

title: NY Giants OC Matt Nagy: ‘Moment was never too big’ for Jaxson Dart
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Prior to the Week 1 game against the Dallas Cowboys, a Sunday Night Football prime time game against a division rival, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy wasn’t sure how quarterback Jaxson Dart and the rest of the offense would handle the moment. After Dart’s 23 of 29, 230-yard, 3 […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart talking with Matt Nagy. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Prior to the Week 1 game against the Dallas Cowboys, a Sunday Night Football prime time game against a division rival, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy wasn’t sure how quarterback Jaxson Dart and the rest of the offense would handle the moment. After Dart’s 23 of 29, 230-yard, 3 touchdown performance, and the offense’s efficiency, in a 28-20 victory, Nagy’s question has been answered. “He was calm, he was composed, he made plays when plays were needed. The moment was never too big for him,” Nagy said. “I wasn’t really sure going into it. We’re a young team and even in training camp, in our preseason we get excited. I love that part, but sometimes you wonder is the moment too big? I came out of that thinking and knowing with our guys the moment’s not too big.“ In a film review of Dart’s Week 1 performance , Big Blue View’s Nick Falato wrote that Dart put together an “elite performance” against the Cowboys. From his perch in the coach’s booth high above the playing field, Nagy saw a quarterback who was seeing the same things he was. “One thing as a coach that you look for is you look to see, me being up in the box, arere his eyes going to where my eyes are going?,” Nagy said. “In that game I’m telling you almost every play he went to where he was supposed to go which means he’s calm. He’s seeing things. “The moment wasn’t too big.” Nagy was also impressed by how smoothly Dart handled all of the pre-snap responsibilities. “There’s a lot of stuff that goes on on the headset and the communication between myself and the quarterback and whether it’s substitutions, formations, motion shifts, things that he’s doing within the play,” Nagy said. “I can’t tell everybody here enough of how well he managed that part of it. “There was a few times where I got to play in later than I should have and he fixed it. He made me right. I love that about him. That’s the teamwork part, but very cool, very calm, very collected.” Here are more takeaways from Nagy’s Thursday media availability. Mahomes-Kelce 2.0? OK, so comparing the Dart-Isaiah Likely connection to that of future Hall of Famers Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce with the Kansas City Chiefs, is hyperbole. There is no denying, though, that the Giants’ quarterback and his new tight end have quickly developed impressive on-field chemistry. That was evident against the Cowboys as Likely caught all eight of his targets against Dallas, two for touchdowns and the other six for first downs. It is a connection we saw grow throughout the spring and summer, and was a big part of why the Giants defeated the Cowboys. Nagy, of course, was part of the Kansas City coaching staff for much of the Mahomes-Kelce era. “I was there for the beginning stages of that, and I’ve seen it through throughout for many years. And what we have here with Jaxson and Zay is right there,” Nagy said. “I mean, it’s not there with them yet, but it’s at the beginning stages, it’s there. That’s the exciting part, is they’re just super, super talented people. And it’s going to take a little bit of time, but they were on the other night and I think you guys saw that. Nagy was particulary pleased by the 19-yard Dart-Likely hookup on a second quarter third-and-10. “That one throw that he [Dart] had to Zay on third down, he had some pressure in his face. He made a great throw, great accuracy,” Nagy said. “And then Zay made a great route and great catch, keeps the sticks moving. So, we’re building towards that. Those guys know it, but they’re not satisfied either.” ‘Worth two guys’ No one knew if wide receiver Malik Nabers was going to play until about two hours before Sunday’s game against Dallas. Nagy admitted being prepared for either scenario, even if he didn’t want to be. “I was a little bit stressed on that one. I had two different call sheets, one stuffed in my bag, and I never wanted to look at it, because I just did not want to see that one,” Nagy said. “But that’s right, that’s what’s real, and that’s okay. He came out and got that early catch, which was good, and now we’ll go from there. “But you certainly love to get him out there, and as I said last week, he’s worth two guys when he’s out there.” Three players in one Head coach John Harbaugh said on Monday that “Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do.” Sunday was an example of how different Ricard, by definition a 300-pound fullback, is. He played 37 snaps, aligning at fullback, tight end, slot receiver, and wide receiver. He also was used in motion more than just about any player in the NFL. pic.twitter.com/zoksIDkhpX — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 17, 2026 “What he allows us to do is he plays basically three different positions in one, whether it’s an O-lineman, whether it’s a tight end, or whether it’s a fullback. So, it’s a little bit of a chess piece,” Nagy said. “He’s super smart, so you can do different things formationally, personnel-wise. And so, it becomes a little bit of a back-and-forth with the defensive coordinator on what you’re doing personnel-wise with him. But then we’ve got to be able to protect that, too, and make sure we’re doing enough passes as well. “So, it’s been great for me to learn who he is from day one when he got here. He’s also really good at what he does. So, it’s one thing to be smart and be able to use him, but he’s really good at what he does, too.” Booth review Nagy had never called plays from upstairs in a regular season game before Sunday night. “I think the biggest thing is you rely on your prep and your coaching staff. I mean, I really, these guys here, I cannot say enough about the staff that we have and the knowledge that they have,” Nagy said. “So, we put it all together, and then they give me an opportunity. Now I’ve got to put my spin on it, when do I think things should come? And again, (senior offensive assistant) Greg Roman does such a phenomenal job, along with (offensive line coach) Mike Bloomgren and (assistant offensive line coach) Grant (Newsome), and all of our coaches on staff. They do a great job of working in that run game, and we put it all together.”

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Week 2 preview – Start/sit and more
summary: Welcome to Week 2! Week 1 was a scoreboard-spinning bonanza — the highest scoring opening week in the Super Bowl era, with teams averaging almost 25 points per game. Wow. That barrage of offense translated to a ton of fantasy points. Sixteen players scored two of more touchdowns last weekend. Hopefully your team was in […]
full_text: The Super Bowl MVP shines in his debut | Getty Images Welcome to Week 2! Week 1 was a scoreboard-spinning bonanza — the highest scoring opening week in the Super Bowl era, with teams averaging almost 25 points per game. Wow. That barrage of offense translated to a ton of fantasy points. Sixteen players scored two of more touchdowns last weekend. Hopefully your team was in on the fun, and wasn’t full of players who whiffed such as Matt Stafford, Drake Maye, Ja’Marr Chase, Jaylen Waddle, Kyle Pitts, Sr., and Colston Loveland. For some, seeing those names in print might make you wince. Remember, it’s just one week. Don’t panic…yet. You’re getting a slightly abbreviated column this week. Sorry about that. Stats of the Week : Chicago’s 59 points was the second highest scoring output ever in a season-opening game. The Bears had 291 rushing yards, averaged 7.5 yards per carry, and scored six rushing touchdowns. Chicago 59, Carolina 37 is a scorigami (first time ever for that final score), and at 96 points, the highest scoring Week 1 game in NFL history. The Jets and Giants are both 1-0 for the first time since 2009. Josh Allen now has nine career games with two of more rushing TDs plus two or more passing TDs. That’s five more than anyone else in NFL history. He’s also 20 th all time (among all players) in rushing TDs. On Sunday, Derrick Henry had his 26 th game with 100+ rushing yards and multiple rushing TDs. That broke a three-way tie for most all-time (Jim Brown, LaDanian Tomlinson). OK, Week 2, here we go! Bye Weeks: NONE Week 2 Rides, Fades and Sleepers For those who are familiar with this column, you know the drill. For everyone else: The Rides, Fades, and Sleepers is an analysis of players that I think are primed for an especially strong or poor performance, often as compared to consensus expectations. This isn’t a straight-up Start/Sit exercise. As a general rule, start your studs. I’ll rarely list the most obvious names at a position as “Rides” because those players are almost always expected to have strong performances. You don’t need me or anyone else telling you to start Jahmyr Gibbs . While this analysis is intended for season-long play, it works for DFS formats too. Half PPR scoring and Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) are used for the column. Each week, I’m picking a Ride, Fade ,and Sleeper of the Week . The rules: The Ride of the Week can’t be a truly elite option, the Fade can’t be someone who nobody is starting anyway, and the Sleeper must be an actual sleeper, from down in the rankings. This week, since the column is short, I’m doing two of each. Last week, my Ride of the Week (Chris Olave – 182 receiving yards) and Fade of the Week (Drake Maye – 1 TD, 3 INTs) delivered. My Sleeper of the Week (mike Washington, Jr.) was OK, but not worth a spot in starting lineups. *** Rides of the Week: D.J. Moore (vs. DET). If it ain’t broke…I might just pick “No. 1 wide receiver going against the Lions” as my Ride of the Week all season, or at least until they get their starting safeties back. This contest has shootout written all over it, and like Olave last week, D.J. Moore is primed for a big game against this unit. He had 100 yards and a long TD last week against Houston’s elite secondary, and should be able to build on that (and on his rapport with Josh Allen) against a defense that allowed the fifth-most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to opposing WRs last season. They’ll be lucky if they aren’t ranked worse than that by the time this season is done. Moore is listed as the RB13 this week and he’s Top-10 for me. Brock Purdy (vs. MIA). The extra rest from the Australia trip will do the 49ers good, although they might be itching to get back out there quickly after they dismantled the Rams so convincingly. This game shouldn’t be competitive, but that won’t stop Purdy from running it up early on an overmatched and very inexperienced Miami defense that just made Kirk Cousins look pretty good (although they did turn him over a couple of times, which kept the game closer than it should have been). He’s got enough healthy weapons to light up Miami this weekend. Fades of the Week: Drake London (@CAR). London was a sit for me last week, and as long as the Falcons’ QB options are the pu pu platter of Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa, I’m staying far away. The Panthers gave up 59 points last week, but most of the fantasy points went to Chicago’s quarterback and running backs. Look for Atlanta to hand the Panthers a lot of Bijan Robinson. It’s a good matchup for London, but I can’t get past the abysmal QB situation. Sam LaPorta (@BUF). LaPorta is always a volatile fantasy option, and in Week 1 he was just OK (5-48-0). His eight targets were encouraging, but this week’s matchup is a horrible one and he’ll probably need to find the end zone to give you a TE1 finish. The Bills were the single worst matchup for TEs last season (fewest catches, yards, and FPPG allowed), and they held Dalton Schultz in check in a Week 1 shootout (four catches for 35 yards) Sleepers of the Week: Quentin Johnston (vs. LV) is listed as the WR30 this week and for me that’s too low. No team suffered a bigger embarrassment in Week 1 than Jim Harbaugh’s Chargers. Mike McDaniel’s high octane offense struggled against an Arizona defense that everyone — and I mean EVERYONE — expected them to dominate. Ladd McConkey might miss this game. Look for a bounceback and a solid WR2 performance from Johnston in what now feels like a must-win game for the Chargers, who have a brutal schedule coming up. Carson Wentz (@CHI). Yeah I know, it’s Carson Wentz, who makes lots of mistakes and is now a career backup. I also know that he threw three TDs last week, has dangerous weapons at his disposal, and is facing a Bears’ defense that just allowed four total TDs to Bryce Young. Ben Johnson is serious about setting the points record, so this could be another shootout. Any QB playing against Chicago’s suspect defense warrants a look, and if you need a second QB in a Superflex this week, Wentz is a live play. Other Rides and Sleepers : Going beyond the obvious elite options at each position, here a few more Rides for me this week: QB: D. Prescott (vs. WAS), J. Daniels (@DAL), J. Dart (@LAR), P. Mahomes (vs. IND), B. Mayfield (vs. CLE), J. Love (@NYJ). RB: K. Walker III (vs. IND), J. Williams (vs. WAS), K. Williams (vs. NYG), C. Hubbard (@ATL), J. Mason (@CHI), J. Croskey-Merritt (@DAL), and if you need to dig deep: K. Black (vs. MIA) and G. Holani (vs. ARI). WR: G. Pickens (vs. WAS), C. Watson (@NYJ), G. Wilson (vs. GB), T. McLaurin and S. Diggs (@DAL), and if you need to go deep, D. Samuel, Sr. (vs. MIA), D. Vele (@BAL), and D. Wicks (@TEN). TE: D. Kincaid (vs. DET), D. Goedart (@TEN), I. Likely (@LAR), and if you need someone from down in the rankings, T.J. Hockenson (@CHI), C. Okonkwo (@DAL), and A.J. Barner (@ARI). Other Fades (among players who a lot of people might consider starting this week): QB: J. Burrow (@HOU – not expecting anyone to sit him, but that defense is going to bounce back, so temper expectations), D. Maye (vs. PIT), M. Stafford (vs. NYG), D. Jones (@KC), J. Brissett (vs. SEA). RB: B. Tuten (@DEN), Q. Judkins (@TB), J. Warren (@NE), M. Lloyd (@NYJ), T. Pollard (vs. PHI). WR: J. Waddle (vs. JAC), D. Adams (vs. NYG), R. Odunze (vs. MIN), D.K. Metcalf (@NE), B. Thomas, Jr. (@DEN), M. Harrison (vs. SEA), C. Tate (vs. PHI). TE: J. Johnson (@BAL), K. Pitts, Sr. (vs. CAR), B. Strange (@DEN). Good luck in Week 2! ***This column appears each Thursday here at Big Blue View. Each Monday, my Waiver Wire column appears here, and on Fridays you can find my weekly Prop bets of the week for the Giants. ***

title: How did Jaxson Dart get a mediocre PFF grade in the Cowboys game?
summary: quixotic – hopelessly impractical especially in the pursuit of ideals (Merriam-Webster) Shortly after I joined the BBV staff as a weekly contributor in 2022, Ed asked me if I’d be willing to write the weekly post on Pro Football Focus grades after each New York Giants game. It’s a somewhat thankless task, though I find […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect quixotic – hopelessly impractical especially in the pursuit of ideals (Merriam-Webster) Shortly after I joined the BBV staff as a weekly contributor in 2022, Ed asked me if I’d be willing to write the weekly post on Pro Football Focus grades after each New York Giants game. It’s a somewhat thankless task, though I find it personally educational to try to figure out why they gave a player the grade they did. I’ve tried over the years to explain what I know about how PFF grades and how they are determined, and I’ve even published a couple of pieces specifically on that topic. Judging by the reactions to my last piece after the Dallas game, none of it has had much effect. Many of you were incensed in particular that Jaxson Dart only received a PFF passing grade of 68.5, which is in the 60-70 range of grades that PFF regards as average, or expected, play. That for a night when he went 23-of-29 (79.3%) for 230 yards, 3 TDs, and no interceptions. I’m sure that Giants fans will take a stat line like that every week of the season. PFF looked at it and said, “at the upper end of average.” In general, you don’t want to know the details of how the sausage is made, but when you don’t like the taste of the final product, peeking behind the curtain can be a useful thing. PFF does give us some peeks behind the curtain. Generally, they emphasize that they grade process , not results . That makes sense for several reasons. Think of the two most recent unforgettable passing plays in Giants history: In the 2008 Super Bowl, Eli Manning made perhaps the most famous pass in Super Bowl history, hitting David Tyree deep downfield, the latter making the famous “helmet catch,” which kept the game-winning drive alive and led to spoiling the Patriots’ perfect season. I don’t know how PFF graded that throw. I do know that they credited Manning with one “turnover-worthy play” (TWP) in that game; that pass might or might not have been it. Manning heroically escaped pressure on that play to get the pass off, but let’s face it, he just put it up for grabs. If not for Tyree’s superhuman effort, Rodney Harrison might have intercepted that ball and it would have been lights out for the Giants. Four years later the Giants were in a similar situation, needing a TD to beat the Patriots in the Super Bowl. This time, it was the Manning-to-Manningham pass play that became part of history. Manning-to-Manningham had everything: Crucial situation, explosive pass play, unbelievable accuracy of ball placement in-bounds but between two defenders, plus an absolutely great catch by Manningham. We know that that pass received a grade of +2 from PFF, the highest grade it’s possible for them to give, because they used it to explain what a +2 grade is ( https://www.pff.com/grades ). All well and good, but it’s all the -1, -0.5, 0, +0.5, and +1 grades that make up most of a football game. This week PFF apparently noticed that Chicago Bears fans were mildly upset, to say the least, that their QB, Caleb Williams, received a passing grade of 64.0 after his 21-for-29, 269 yards, 2 TDs, and 0 INTs performance in a 59-37 win over Carolina. Pretty similar to Dart’s stat line, and a pretty similar PFF grade. At the heart of PFF’s grading system is an assumption that an NFL player shouldn’t get credit for the basic things he is supposed to do. If you’re a starting quarterback in the NFL you’re expected to complete easy passes. No participation trophy. If you go 20-for-20 and everything is a short pass where the receiver is wide open, they’re not impressed. It’s like not being impressed if the mailman shows up every day and actually puts the mail in the mailbox. The question they ask is: Don’t tell me about the result – how good was the process that led to that result? In the case of Williams, he dropped back 40 times, and 23 of those times he got a grade of 0. He had one terrible play for which he got a -1.5, 8 plays with a grade of +0.5, and 1 play with a grade of +1. No +1.5 or +2 plays. That’s how you wind up with an average overall grade. But you don’t care about Caleb Williams, you care about Dart. Fortunately the article gives us a peek – but only a peek – at how they viewed what Dart did on Sunday: Willams was only 12th-highest in positively graded plays. Trevor Lawrence and Lamar Jackson were the two highest. Sitting there at No. 3, though, is Jaxson Dart, who achieved a positive grade on 32.35% of his dropbacks. They also show us their rankings for negatively graded plays: Dart comes in sixth-lowest on this list. So put those two things together – third-highest in positively graded dropbacks and sixth-lowest in negatively graded dropbacks – and I think the result matches what most of you – and I – thought of Dart’s performance. Lots of good reps, not many bad reps. If PFF stopped there, I suspect that we’d all be pretty happy with it. But they don’t stop there. Positively graded plays go from +0.5 (nice) to +2 (wow!). Negatively graded plays go from -0.5 (oops) to -2 (omigod, what were you thinking?). The two extremes are what they refer to as “big-time throws” (BTT) and “turnover-worthy plays” (TWP). Both of those may or may not show up on the stat sheet. If Dart throws a beautiful pass deep downfield and the receiver drops it, it’s 0-for-1 on the stat sheet but it’s a BTT nonetheless to PFF because Dart went above and beyond what you expect of an average QB. Likewise if he throws the ball right into the midsection of a defensive back and the defender drops it, it’s 0-for-1 on the stat sheet but a TWP nonethless to PFF, i.e., the fact that the defender was inept doesn’t absolve the QB of his terrible throw. I don’t know how they exactly do the math to come up with the final grade, but those are the factors that go into it. They only show the detailed analysis for Williams, but they make it available for every other QB as well…for a $199.99 “PFF Pro” subscription. I don’t have that. So I’m going to try to guess at how they reacted to every Dart dropback from the film and compare it to what they actually said. The grades below are my guesses after watching the film. Remember, nothing wrong with a zero, it’s just an “as expected for an NFL QB” result. First Quarter: 10:49: Dart to Nabers, 9 yards (grade = 0) 9:43: Dart short to Ricard, incomplete, deflected (grade = -0.5) 7:32: Dart to Likely, 13 yards (grade = 0) 0:33: Dart incomplete to Nabers, almost intercepted (grade = -1) 0:29: Dart to Likely, 7 yards (grade = 0) Second Quarter: 14:13: Dart to Nabers, 7 yards (grade = 0) 5:01: Dart pulls it down, scrambles forward, sack but no yards lost (grade = -0.5) 4:19: Dart incomplete long to Fields, almost sacked (grade = 0) 4:14: Dart pressured, pass to Likely, 19 yards (grade = +1.5) 3:01: Dart short to Fields, 19 yards (grade = +0.5) 2:36: Dart sacked, -8 yards, fumbles, Runyan recovers (-2) 0:49: Dart to Nabers, incomplete (grade = 0) 0:45: Dart to Fields, 6 yards (grade = +0.5) 0:40: Dart to Nabers, 16 yards (grade = +0.5) 0:35: Dart to Mooney, 18 yards (grade = +1) 0:31: Dart to Likely, 5 yards (grade = 0) 0:20: Dart to Likely, 15 yards, TD (grade = +0.5) Third quarter: 13:41: Dart to Johnson, 9 yards (grade = 0) 11:25: Dart to Nabers, 16 yards (grade = 0) 9:55: Dart to Mooney, 9 yards (grade = 0) 8:28: Dart to Nabers, 13 yards (grade = +0.5) 6:59: Dart to Likely, 2 yards, TD (grade = 0) Fourth quarter: 12:10: Dart to Fields deep, incomplete (grade = -0.50) 11:16: Dart to Singletary, loss of 7 yards (grade = -1) 10:27: Dart to Nabers, 7 yards (grade = 0) 9:43: Dart to Singletary, 13 yards (grade = 0) 8:16: Dart to Singletary, 7 yards (grade = 0) 7:26: Dart to Singletary, 7 yards, TD (grade = 0) 4:34: Dart downfield to Nabers, incomplete (grade = -1) 4:30: Dart to Likely, 12 yards (grade = +0.5) 2:16: Dart to Likely, 5 yards (grade = +1) OK, so how did I do? PFF said: Positively graded plays: 32.35% of 34 dropbacks = 11 plays My score: 9 plays Negatively…

title: NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 2
summary: The New York Giants were ranked 22nd in the power rankings prior to Week 1. How high have they moved up? It was an exciting — high-scoring — first week of the 2026 season. Nine of sixteen games hit the over and there were 791 total points, an average of 49.4 points per game scored, which tied the post-merger […]
full_text: The New York Giants were ranked 22nd in the power rankings prior to Week 1. How high have they moved up? It was an exciting — high-scoring — first week of the 2026 season. Nine of sixteen games hit the over and there were 791 total points, an average of 49.4 points per game scored, which tied the post-merger record for Week 1 scoring. There were surprises, upsets, and plenty of action, as well as injuries, unfortunately. Here are my power rankings heading into Week 2. No. 1 — Baltimore Ravens ( last week 8 ) 📈 7 spots The Ravens start the Jesse Minter era with a 40-burger against the Indianapolis Colts. Declan Doyle’s offense had over 500 yards, 200 of which came on the ground. The Ravens did this on the road. It appears that Zay Flowers — who had five catches for 150 yards and a touchdown — avoided major injury after leaving the game with a hamstring strain. Derrick Henry might still be running — he averaged six yards per carry. It was an old-fashioned Ravens kind of win that showcased the potential of John Harbaugh’s former squad, and they vaunted themselves to number one in my rankings ahead of their home matchup against the Saints. No. 2 — Buffalo Bills (5th) 📈 3 spots The Bills went into Houston and defeated the Texans, 36-31. Josh Allen put the team on his back and willed them to victory — as he is one to do. He threw for 334 yards and rushed for two touchdowns, while connecting with new weapon DJ Moore for 100 yards and a score through the air. It’s even more impressive that the Bills did this with a short week ahead, as they host Detroit on Thursday Night Football. No. 3 — Seattle Seahawks (1st) 📉 2 spots I hate dropping Seattle after a commanding 13-10 win against the Patriots on Wednesday, but losing Sam Darnold and starting Drew Lock for the foreseeable future had an effect. Of course, though, the Seattle Seahawks remain a top-notch team due to their defense and the overall operation of Mike MacDonald. No. 4 — Los Angeles Rams (2nd) 📉 2 spots The Rams are looking to put the 27-7 beatdown by the 49ers behind them — Australia did not treat Sean McVay’s team well. They also lost Myles Garrett to a knee injury, and kind of just looked old. They host the Giants — a team with a ton of energy who is, in fact, no old at all — on Monday Night Football. They have extended rest and I expect them to be ready for the Giants, who aren’t an easy win anymore. No. 5 — Cincinnati Bengals (10th) 📈 5 spots The Bengals defense forced four turnovers and harrassed Baker Mayfield all game. If the defense is improved and can remain opportunistic, look out for Cincinnati and the Joe Burrow led Bengals. Dexter Lawrence had three pressures in the game. No. 6 — Chicago Bears (11th) 📈 5 spots The Bears scored 59 points against the Carolina Panthers and probably could have scored more. Now I am worried about the defense — they did surrender 37 points to Bryce Young — but Ben Johnson has Caleb Williams playing at a high level. Chicago is one of the most exciting teams in the sport, and they move up five spots in the rankings. No. 7 — Kansas City Chiefs (18th) 📈 11 spots Yeah, I was too low on the Chiefs. I bought into the Kenneth Walker addition, but I didn’t see them commanding the trenches as well as they did in their 31-10 slaughter of Denver. Steve Spagnuolo is still excellent, and his defense made Davis Webb’s offense look inept. A team with a run first/defensive mentality with Patrick Mahomes at quarterback is incredibly scary. No. 8 — San Francisco 49ers (16th) 📈 8 spots The 49ers punched their divisional rival in the mouth — looks like the extended week in Australia may have helped. Nevertheless, Raheem Morris has the now-healthy 49ers defense looking like a top-five unit, while the offense continues to thrive despite injuries. Brock Purdy is an underrated quarterback, and I expect to see another beatdown this week against Miami. No. 9 — Jacksonville Jaguars (15th) 📈 6 spots Jacksonville easily handled the Cleveland Browns, beating them 34-10 as Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdowns. Liam Coen’s unit cruised to victory and will now face a tougher task in Denver, against a team that slid far down the rankings after their abysmal performance. No. 10 — Houston Texans (7th) 📉 3 spots Houston faced Josh Allen and failed to contain the star quarterback in a back-and-forth battle. DeMeco Ryans still has a top-three defense in the league, despite allowing 36 points. I expect the Texans to bounce back, but the Bengals pose a tough test; at least Houston is home again. No. 11 — New England Patriots (3rd) 📉 8 spots The Patriots had one of the worst — most anticlimactic — opening games against a team that beat them in the Super Bowl. A.J. Brown was injured, Romeo Doubs disappeared, and Drake Maye played one of his career worst games. New England hosts Pittsburgh. No. 12 — Philadelphia Eagles (6th) 📉 6 spots The Eagles won, but slid six spots down the rankings — my bias against Philadelphia or objective analysis of an offense that looks concerning? The latter! Sean Mannion struggled against the revamped Washington defense, and the offensive line did not look great. The Eagles won, 24-22, but it was in a very unconvincing fashion. No. 13 — Detroit Lions (13th) SAME A failed two-point conversion by Tyler Shough and the Saints’ offense spared the Lions from a brutal overtime collapse. Shough, who was contained through the first three quarters, threw for over 400 yards, and the Lions could not cover Chris Olave through the game, who went for 182 yards. They’re ranked in the exact same spot as last week. No. 14 — Denver Broncos (4th) 📉 10 spots Denver was dominated by the Kansas City Chiefs and now faces a hot Jacksonville team. The playcalling of Davis Webb is already in question, and the defense was gut-punched by Kenneth Walker. They dropped ten spots with that performance, but I expect them to stabilize. No. 15 — Minnesota Vikings (17th) 📈 2 spots The Vikings continue to be a resilient team under Kevin O’Connell. Kyler Murray was injured in the first half, and Carson Wentz finished the game with an epic come-from-behind victory against Green Bay. The final score was 39-22, and Brian Flores’ defense turned it on in the second half, forcing a pair of turnovers and sacking Jordon Love four times. The Vikings will likely start Carson Wentz on Sunday against the Bears in Chicago. No. 16 — New York Giants (22nd) 📈 6 spots We heard all off-season about the run-first mentaltity centrailized around heavier personnel packages and under-cneter looks, and WOW was it effecitve against the Dallas Cowboys. The Giants ran the ball at will agaisnt Dallas, and limited Dak Prescott to just two possessions in the second half. Multiple 10+ play drives with four touchdowns, including three Jaxson Dart touchdowns through the air. The chapter of medocrity might be over. It’s a new and exciting time in New York for Big Blue. No. 17 — Dallas Cowboys (9th) 📉 8 spots Dallas’ offense was sloppy against the Giants and their defense had several miscommunications. Still, it was the Giants commanding the trenches on offense that led to the poor defensive mishaps, for Christian Parker could not get his guys off the field. Sure, Dallas was a mess, but that doesn’t take anything away from the Giants. I expect that Dallas will see better days this season. Their defense has talent, but they’re not quite playing in unison yet. No. 18 — Green Bay Packers (14th) 📉 4 spots The Packers were up 22-10 in the third quarter but Minnesota forced a fumble, interception, and a pair of turnover on downs in the fourth quarter that ended the game with a 39-22 Vikings’ win. The Packers will look to get right in their second consecutive road game against the Jets. No. 19 — Los Angeles Chargers (12th) 📉 7 spots The Chargers did one of the most Charger things ever — lose as a massive home-favorite. Jacoby Brisset and the Arizona Cardinals defeated Jim Harbaugh’s Chargers, start-to-finish. The Chargers have two new coordinators,…

title: NY Giants news: Aaron Donald, ‘Pancake’ Patrick Ricard, more headlines
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants hit the practice field for the first time this week to prepare for their clash with the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL Projection Model is buying the Giants offense and selling Patriots panic | The Athletic Buying the Giants offense. Maybe the […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants hit the practice field for the first time this week to prepare for their clash with the Los Angeles Rams. Why NFL Projection Model is buying the Giants offense and selling Patriots panic | The Athletic Buying the Giants offense. Maybe the Dallas Cowboys’ problematic defense isn’t any better than last year, but the New York Giants absolutely destroyed them from wire to wire Sunday night; it was the kind of performance that often predicts future success. Perhaps the most impressive aspect of the offense was quarterback Jaxson Dart’s play. Dart made some nice throws, took what the Cowboys gave him, and used his legs effectively. I’m not sure I was fully bought into the Dart experience within a Matt Nagy and Greg Roman offense, but the poise and accuracy he showed in prime time has me reconsidering that stance. Outside of Dart, the other reason the model likes the Giants more today than it did before the season is that they looked better than expected in the trenches. The Giants’ offensive line completely dominated the Cowboys’ front, delivering 0.7 EPA per dropback and a 51 percent success rate on the ground. The model still has concerns about New York’s defense, but it’s buying the offense being better than expected and believes the Giants will be a factor in the NFC playoff race. title: Scouting Jets kicker Blake Grupe
summary: After final cuts, the Jets claimed a few players, including kicker Blake Grupe. Despite being on the 53-man roster, Grupe was inactive for the team’s opener, as Jason Sanders was elevated from the practice squad and handled the kicking duties, but he may get an opportunity in due course. Today we take a look at […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JANUARY 04: Blake Grupe #10 of the Indianapolis Colts kicks a field goal during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images After final cuts, the Jets claimed a few players, including kicker Blake Grupe. Despite being on the 53-man roster, Grupe was inactive for the team’s opener, as Jason Sanders was elevated from the practice squad and handled the kicking duties, but he may get an opportunity in due course. Today we take a look at Grupe in more detail. The 27-year old Grupe is listed at 5’7″ and 156 pounds and was undrafted out of Notre Dame in 2023. Having won the Saints’ job as a rookie, he kicked for them for two and a half seasons before being released in November, then ended last season with the Colts but failed to win their placekicker role in training camp. Background Grupe was originally a walk-on at Arkansas State, having been unranked as a high school recruit. He redshirted his first season in 2017, but then took over as the team’s kicker early in the 2018 season. Having made 14 of 21 field goals in his first season, Grupe showed a dramatic improvement in 2019 and was named as an all-Sun Belt Conference first teamer after making 19 out of 22 field goal attempts. He was just 11 of 18 in 2020 but bounced back to make 20 of 25 in 2021, earning second-team all-conference recognition. Ahead of the 2022 season, Grupe transferred to Notre Dame and he made 14 of 19 field goals for them, but was perfect on 49 extra points. Grupe’s NFL career began as he was picked up by the Saints as an undrafted free agent and made a game-winning kick in his first ever preseason game. He built on that to win the kicker job and had a solid first season that saw him make 30 of 37 field goals and all 40 of his extra points. In 2024, he had another good year as he made 27 of 31 field goals, although he did also miss two extra points. Last season didn’t go so well for Grupe initially, as he missed eight field goals in the first 12 games and was released by the Saints in November. However, the Colts claimed him following an injury to Spencer Shrader and he excelled down the stretch as he was 11 of 11 on field goals and 10 for 10 on extra points over the last five games. He was hoping to hold onto the job in preseason but missed a couple of kicks, including a 36-yarder. The Jets claimed Grupe off waivers following final cuts, after the Colts had opted to stick with Shrader as their full-time kicker. Now let’s break Grupe down in a variety of categories, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Grupe is the smallest kicker in the NFL based on listed weight and there are only currently two players in the league who have a lower listed weight than he does. He did not work out at his pro day. In high school, Grupe played soccer and baseball. Leg Strength Despite his diminutive size, Grupe has good power, and has creditable numbers of 19 made field goals on 27 attempts from beyond 50 yards. He has made a 60-yard field goal at the NFL level and it should have been a game-winner but the Colts’ defense gave up a late score to lose. Grupe’s leg strength on kickoffs is difficult to judge. As a rookie, he put up some of the best numbers in the NFL on kickoff metrics, with 76 touchbacks on 85 attempts. However, the change in rules has not been good to him as his numbers dropped precipitously in his second season and were among the worst in the league last year. This may not reflect on his leg strength, though. Perhaps he has been instructed to lay his kicks short of the end zone and his coverage units haven’t been pulling their weight. If this is a concern, punter Austin McNamara could kick off instead, as he was continuing to work on this in camp, having done it at times last year. Accuracy With an 82 percent success rate on field goals at the NFL level, Grupe has hit the all-important 80-percent benchmark in his career so far. However, he’s been a little inconsistent and streaky with that. 2025 in particular was a tale of two seasons for Grupe, who missed 6 of 11 kicks from beyond 40 with the Saints to lose his job, but then was perfect on 21 kicks in five games with the Colts. In college, he was below 80 percent overall and only exceeded 80 percent in one of his five seasons. Clutch As noted above, Grupe had a game-winner in his first ever preseason game and hit a go-ahead 60-yarder in a game with the Colts, albeit that this ended up being a loss. Otherwise, he hasn’t had a lot of significant success in clutch situations. He had a 42-yard game-winner with 77 seconds on the clock in a 2021 game, hit a game-winning extra point with 32 seconds left in a 2019 win over Coastal Carolina and made an overtime field goal in 2018, although again this ended up being a loss. His first three games at the NFL level were all high pressure situations as each was decided by three points or less. He handled the pressure well initially but missed a key go-ahead field goal attempt in week three. He also missed a 48-yarder as time-expired as Arkansas State lost their season finale 24-22 to Texas State in 2021. Tackling Grupe only had one tackle in his college career, but has been credited with three at the NFL level. However, his lack of size is detrimental in this area. Intangibles/Miscellaneous Grupe has shown good character to start off as a college walk-on and then win a couple of kicking competitions. He was respected in New Orleans for his ability to bounce back from tough stretches and was even named as a team captain. He was good academically, finishing his degree in the spring before his redshirt junior season and then moving on to do a masters. He was a two-time member of the Arkansas State athletic director’s honor roll and was an academic all-district 6 selection in 2020. He has limited experience of kicking in cold weather climates at the NFL level, although a couple of his 2025 games were in heavy rain and windy conditions and he mostly fared well under these conditions. Grupe hasn’t had major injury issues during his NFL career but did deal with a minor groin issue during his rookie season. Over the course of his NFL career, Grupe has been a teammate of several current Jets: Demario Davis, Adonai Mitchell, Kene Nwangwu and Jack Heflin. Grupe has never punted at the NFL, college or high school level and has yet to be involved in a fake field goal. Conclusions For now, the Jets seem to prefer Sanders, despite his preseason struggles and an embarrassing miss in the opener. Aside from that miss, Sanders did a good job, but the Jets won’t tolerate too many more mistakes before they give Grupe a shot instead, assuming Grupe is kicking well in practice. An inflection point may come after week three, at which point the option of elevating Sanders from the practice squad may have been fully exhausted. Grupe has some good leg talent, and a decent track record, but we’ve seen recently how difficult it is to get someone you know you can rely on. In light of their recent history, it seems unlikely the Jets will stick with Sanders all year, so Grupe should get a chance at some point but we’ll have to wait and see. If he does, hopefully we get the 2025 Colts version and not the 2025 Saints version.

title: New York Jets Week 1 Game Balls: Geno Smith, Demario Davis, Qwan’tez Stiggers
summary: The Jets emerged victorious in Week 1 over the Tennessee Titans. Let’s hand out some game balls to celebrate the top performers in the win. Geno Smith: Smith was very efficient in his first Jets start in almost a decade. After a quiet first half, Smith shredded Tennessee in the final two quarters to help […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets warms up prior to the game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets emerged victorious in Week 1 over the Tennessee Titans. Let’s hand out some game balls to celebrate the top performers in the win. Geno Smith: Smith was very efficient in his first Jets start in almost a decade. After a quiet first half, Smith shredded Tennessee in the final two quarters to help the Jets put the game away and turn it into a laugher. Most importantly, he avoided major negative plays. The Jets’ 2026 success depends in no small measure on Smith avoiding sacks and turnovers. Through one game he has done the job. Breece Hall: Hall’s first game after receiving his new contract produced over 100 rushing yards. Just as significant was his sky high 59.1% success rate on rushing attempts. Through his career, Hall has been viewed as a homerun threat who can be inconsistent on a play to play basis. This was just one game, but Breece was able to put up 102 yards on 22 carries with a long of just 13 yards. He was consistently ripping off solid gains in this one. We will need to watch to see whether this is the start of a new trend. Offensive Line: The guys up front deserve a lot of the credit for the respective success of Smith and Hall. The quarterback was not sacked and was only hit once during the game, while the Jets ran for 152 yards total. The Jets completely controlled the line of scrimmage on the offensive side of the ball. Demario Davis: The opening chapter of Davis’ third stint with the Jets was a success. He led the team in tackles with 8. His true impact on the defense went beyond that and is difficult to quantify. Watching the game, things were just more stable with Davis on the field. He was always in the right spot to clean things up. Tennessee’s offense wasn’t very threatening, but we saw none of the self-inflicted errors from a year ago. I think Davis’ presence had a lot to do with that. Will McDonald: There were plenty of Jets standouts in this game who gave a game ball worth performance, particularly on defense. I’m going to single out McDonald. He gets plenty of criticism. There is a lot of focus on what he’s not as a player. For this week let’s appreciate what he is, a credible NFL pass rusher. He had a sack and generated consistent pressure through the second half. I thought he was the team’s most consistent pass rusher through the game. Qwan’tez Stiggers: Whether or not Stiggers develops as a defensive back, it is becoming clear that he is likely at a minimum to have a long NFL career as a top special teamer. He was in the middle of three big Jets special teams plays in Week 1, directing a Titans blocker into the return man to prevent a punt return, recovering a fumbled kickoff, and downing another punt at the 2 yard line.

title: Why Eagles fans shouldn’t panic if Eli Stowers needs more time to develop
summary: Eagles assistant GM, Jon Ferrari, was recently on the New Heights Show with Jason and Travis Kelce to talk about some of the more misunderstood officiating calls — and about how the Michigan game clock got so messed up. But, notably, he ended up talking about how challenging blocking as a tight end, outside the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Eli Stowers #87 of the Philadelphia Eagles lines up against the New England Patriots during an NFL preseason football game at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Eagles assistant GM, Jon Ferrari, was recently on the New Heights Show with Jason and Travis Kelce to talk about some of the more misunderstood officiating calls — and about how the Michigan game clock got so messed up. But, notably, he ended up talking about how challenging blocking as a tight end, outside the tackle, can be. “Fans don’t understand how hard it is to block in the NFL, especially when you’re outside the tackle, how hard it is to block. There’s a lot of space. So, you have to be aware of blindside blocks, meaning blocking backward toward you’re own endline. When you’re flexed, you have to be aware of a crack back block, where you block inside, you can’t block high or low. And then, you have to be aware of blocks in the back, so you’ve got to get him on the side. You have to check a lot boxes to legally block, especially in the run game when you’re blocking outside in, and it’s really hard.” Ferrari went on to explain the different rules for a blindside block and a crack block, and how many limitations there are for how and where they can hit a defender, and why that nuance takes time to learn. “That’s why it’s so hard. You’ve gotta think about exactly where you are, what direction you’re traveling, where the opponent is, what is he looking at — there’s so much to think about in those blocks, which obviously we know come on you in a second.” Immediately, Ferrari’s comments put some of rookie tight end Eli Stowers’ development into perspective. Throughout training camp, the coaches talked about their second-round pick having to learn new aspects of his position, specifically as a blocker, which now seems like a longer process than just one offseason. “Tight end’s a position that requires a lot of versatility,” Eagles OC Sean Mannion explained in mid-August. “I know Eli’s put a lot of work into improving as a blocker, and along with that entire position group, there’s a huge commitment to being productive in both areas.” Stowers ended up being placed on injured reserve as he dealt with quadriceps and hamstring injuries leading up to the regular season opener, and will miss at least four weeks. Some have suggested the Eagles made the move to divert attention from the fact that the rookie wasn’t ready to contribute just yet. Even if the tight end does need more time to develop, that shouldn’t be a disqualifying reflection on Stowers or his potential.

title: Eagles News: Jeffery Simmons says the Titans “just need to make Jalen Hurts be a quarterback”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Not sure why the Tennessee Titans, who are seven-point home underdogs on Sunday, are giving Jalen Hurts and the Eagles any bulletin board material. Especially after Philly’s starting quarterback is coming off a strong Week 1 showing. But, hey, the Birds […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks to pass against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Not sure why the Tennessee Titans, who are seven-point home underdogs on Sunday, are giving Jalen Hurts and the Eagles any bulletin board material. Especially after Philly’s starting quarterback is coming off a strong Week 1 showing. But, hey, the Birds will take it. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Titans star takes shot at Eagles’ Jalen Hurts before Week 2: ‘Make [him] be a QB’ – NJ.com “We just need to make Jalen Hurts be a QB,” Jeffery Simmons said on Wednesday. “Stop his runs, make sure Hurts doesn’t get out of the pocket and make plays.” The Eagles could use these comments as bulletin-board material. What Simmons said could be taken as a jab at Hurts. Hurts has developed into a good pocket passer, but his running ability makes him even more dangerous. Hurts will have to escape Simmons’ pressure for Philadelphia’s offense to have success against the Titans. With left guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve, second-year player Drew Kendall will likely start on Sunday. Simmons could take advantage of that matchup to get after Hurts. Eagles Film Review: A very good defensive performance against the Commanders – BGN The Eagles’ defense was very good against the Washington Commanders. It wasn’t an elite performance, and the final two drives left a slightly sour taste, but the unit held Jayden Daniels to 18 completions on 34 attempts for 164 yards and limited Washington to 4.4 yards per play. Given the number of new pieces in the secondary and how difficult Daniels was to defend, I came away impressed. However, this defense has an offense problem. The Eagles’ defense played 67 snaps while the offense ran only 53 and gained just 10 first downs. Washington possessed the ball for 10:02 in the fourth quarter alone and put together touchdown drives of 67 and 63 yards. You could see the defense tiring. Jalen Carter looked exhausted by the end, and the pass rush dropped off. This is becoming a familiar problem. The defense can play exceptionally well for long stretches, but asking it to keep returning to the field eventually has consequences. The advanced numbers tell an interesting story. The Eagles generated pressure on 47.4% of Washington’s dropbacks despite blitzing on only 23.7%, but Daniels was sacked just once. That matches up to the film. The rush affected him and remained disciplined, but it rarely arrived quickly. I think the Eagles were deliberately cautious because they did not want to create huge escape lanes for Daniels. Game Review – PHI 24, WAS 22 – Iggles Blitz OL – Not a good showing. Penalties. Sloppy blocks. Missed assignments. WAS blitzed on more than 50 percent of plays and that certainly made things tough. You also factor in a lack of game tape on a new scheme. That made it challenging to prepare. Still, the OL should have played better. Landon Dickerson wasn’t healthy and it showed. He really struggled in pass protection. He didn’t have the quickness or lateral agility to get the job done. He got some movement in the run game, but also had his share of problems on run plays. He’s now on IR. Cam Jurgens had a couple of early penalties, but I thought he was solid overall. Tyler Steen was mostly good, but he has stuff to clean up as well. Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata were sloppier than you would want from players of their caliber. Mailata did have one highlight play. Five thoughts on the Eagles offense: What the numbers say about Jalen Hurts vs. zone coverage, Makai Lemon’s usage – PHLY Eagles Blocking woes aside, Lemon was not billed as a twitchy gadget player coming out of USC and is probably better utilized working the middle of the field as a slot receiver tasked with finding soft spots against zone coverage. There’s a conundrum with that, though: Lemon is a willing, but limited blocker in an offense that utilizes a heavy dose of condensed sets that will make him an important part of the run game. There were a handful of examples of him struggling in the run game in his debut, which is understandable given the transition to the league and the fact that he’s 5-foot-11, 192 pounds. Nick Cross drove Lemon into Saquon Barkley’s running lanes a couple times on Sunday and, in general, he’s not the conventional dirty-work receiver most iterations of the Kyle Shanahan-Sean McVay systems often deploy. Watching through each of the 25 routes Lemon ran against Washington, my general conclusion is that he’s still a work in progress doing most of the things the Eagles asked of him. He’s not going to consistently win against man coverage from the slot or the outside and probably shouldn’t be on the field quite as much on early downs. The best-case scenario right now is probably getting him the ball on underneath routes tied to play-action, something the Eagles didn’t utilize much against Washington and putting him in fewer blocking situations from condensed formations. Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026 – ESPN Under center: 34% of offensive snaps. The Eagles didn’t morph into an offense from the 1980s overnight, but this 34% under-center rate was the seventh highest of any Hurts start. And the quarterback run game that faded out of the offense during the 2025 season completely evaporated. Hurts had seven carries in this game against Washington — five scrambles and two kneel-downs. There wasn’t even a tush push, as the Eagles ran Saquon Barkley, threw the ball or punted on various third- or fourth-and-2 opportunities. Barkley produced 42 yards on a third-and-2 attempt, running away from Leo Chenal, through the second level and into the open field on outside zone. His other 14 carries produced 41 yards and just five successful runs. That’s a solid performance, but it’s not the sort of 2024 Barkley the Eagles were hoping to unlock by moving toward an outside zone-heavy scheme. The same held in the passing game from under center. Hurts dropped back five times from under center. Those plays produced three incompletions, a sack and a 64-yard completion to Dontayvion Wicks on a pretty deep ball where cornerback Mike Sainristil lost track of the throw and nearly came to a complete stop in coverage. Averaging 12.8 yards per play from under center looks great in the aggregate, but the Eagles weren’t consistent in their first game under Mannion. And as the game wore on, the offense felt more like the tired, disappointing one we saw for most of 2025 than the dynamic 2024 attack. The Eagles picked up one first down in the third quarter, and it took great individual efforts to get the offense going, notably from Hurts converting a third-and-18 with his legs. It’s Week 1, and we’ll see how the offense operates in the games to come. Will we see more big plays, or will the offense struggle to move the ball consistently? Eagles Week 2: Hurts’ legs, A.J. Brown’s absence and replacing Landon Dickerson – The Athletic Jalen Hurts’ mobility was a major factor in Week 1. It would make sense for the Eagles to lean into Hurts’ legs this season. I’m not prepared to say it will be a prominent part of the offense because Hurts started last season averaging 44.8 yards per game in the first four games, then he reached 40 yards once the rest of the season. Yet Hurts is at his best when he can be a “triple-threat…

The reasoning for Porter Jr.’s absence is not yet known and head coach Mike McCarthy said before practice that Porter Jr. was scheduled to do more work today than in yesterday’s practice. Porter Jr. was listed as a limited participant, but his designation was changed from a back injury to non-injury related/conditioning. Linebacker Patrick Queen backed Porter Jr., regardless of whether the contract or injury is the main reason why he hasn’t played or fully practiced. “Joey, whatever he’s going through, whether it’s injury or contract, I respect it,” Queen said on Thursday, per Chris Adamski of The Trib.
