title: Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026
summary: Teams such as the Commanders, Eagles, Ravens, Chiefs, Giants and Raiders are going under center more -- and out of the shotgun less and less. Will this trend stick?
full_text:
A trend that had been a popular topic of conversation over the summer in buildings around the NFL was even more prevalent in Week 1 than I would have expected.

 During the offseason, organizations that have a track record of operating out of the shotgun or pistol with mobile quarterbacks made plans to move that QB under center. The Commanders, Eagles and Ravens hired new offensive coordinators in David Blough, Sean Mannion and Declan Doyle, respectively, who come from offensive trees built around under-center play. And the Vikings signed Kyler Murray , who had spent the vast majority of his college and pro careers working in the shotgun, and spent training camp working on his ability to read the field, take drops and throw from under center.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Some of these organizations committed more aggressively than others in Week 1, and in the Vikings' case, the plans were thrown off by a first-quarter concussion to Murray. On a leaguewide basis, though, teams took snaps from under center at the highest rate since 2012.

 Why are NFL teams shifting back toward getting under center? Who benefited the most in Week 1? And will this trend stick? Coaches will talk about their philosophies during the offseason, but now that offenses had to show their cards in Week 1, the move under center is one of the more dramatic changes we've seen from NFL offenses in years. Let's cover how we got here and what might be next.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 How did we get here? 
 Why the return to under center? 
 What's missing from the approach? 
 Which teams have leaned in? 
 What's next for this trend? 

 
 

 The path to shotgun (and back) 
 Let's go back to 2007 and the 16-0 Patriots, who produced one of the best offenses in league history with a spread attack that looked little like the league's other 31 attacks. Though the NFL had seen the "run and shoot" and K-Gun in the 1990s, those were perceived to be short-lived fads from a relatively small number of coaches.

 But in '07, more than 74% of Tom Brady's dropbacks came from the shotgun, a figure that was nearly double the league average. The Patriots ran more than 49% of their snaps out of shotgun, a figure that would have been even higher if they hadn't been blowing teams out in the second half and running out the clock for most of the season. Consider that in 2001, Brady's first year as a starting quarterback, the Patriots had been in the shotgun just under 14% of the time.

 The league as a whole was still primarily operating from under center in 2007. Even as the Patriots tore up the NFL, the other 31 offenses were in shotgun only about 26% of the time. Getting out from under center was more of a move for obvious passing situations like third-and-long or as part of a two-minute drill. On first-and-10 in 2007, NFL offenses were in shotgun only 15% of the time. The Patriots were there on 40% of their snaps.

 

 Within five years, the league had shifted. During the 2012 season, NFL teams were under center just 54% of the time, down from 74% in 2007. And in 2013, the pendulum really swung. NFL teams took more snaps out of the shotgun or pistol (which had gained a foothold in the league after traveling with Colin Kaepernick from Nevada to San Francisco and being installed by Mike Shanahan and his staff of future head coaches in Washington for Robert Griffin ) than they did from under center. That disparity continued to rise in the years to come, with both scoring and offensive efficiency gradually rising alongside.

 By 2023, the shotgun craze peaked. Teams ran 71% of their offensive snaps from the shotgun or pistol and just 29% from under center, nearly one-third of where it had been in 2007. At the same time, though, offensive efficiency had cratered. Teams were scoring just under 22 points per game, down three points from the high-water mark of 2020. Vic Fangio-style defenses were spreading around the league, squeezing big plays away from offenses and daring them to run the ball. Teams grew more experienced dealing with some of the problems those three- and four-wideout sets presented.

 And as a result, in the past few years, we've seen a shift back toward the football of years past. We've watched offenses lean into bigger personnel groupings with multiple tight ends and/or a fullback on the field, something I wrote about during the offseason in my piece on the Rams and their surprising shift to 13 personnel in the middle of the 2025 season. In part, that's to push defenses out of nickel alignments and back to their base defense with four defensive backs, which would allow offenses to get back to tormenting linebackers with the passing game. The Seahawks exploited those base defense looks  during last season's run to the Super Bowl, and perhaps as a result, defenses were  more aggressive  about staying in their nickel defense against 12 and 13 personnel looks in Week 1 of the 2026 season.

 We've also seen the league get under center more often. After a decade of heading toward the shotgun, the under-center rate took a small step forward from 29% in 2023 to 30.5% in 2024. In 2025, that rate rose more dramatically to 35%. And in Week 1 of 2026, NFL offenses were under center 42.5% of the time .

 We're suddenly back where we were in 2013 (42.2%) in terms of under-center rate. And as you might have noticed, that decision came with plenty of scoring. Teams averaged 24.7 points per game in Week 1, tying with 2012 for the highest-scoring opening week since the 1970 merger. Correlation isn't necessarily causation, but offenses went under center at the highest rate in more than a decade and didn't exactly suffer for their choice.

 OK, so now you know how we got to what we saw in Week 1. But what benefits are teams hoping to realize from moving under center? How does it fit what defenses are showing? And what are the trade-offs?

 

 

 

 The 'why' of going under center 
 If you ask NFL coaches why offenses are going under center, one answer invariably comes up: They want a more diverse and unpredictable run game. There are advantages to operating out of the shotgun, and we'll get to them in a minute, but one of the disadvantages comes with what teams are able (or unable) to do on the ground. In the shotgun, running backs line up to the side of the quarterback, which both limits the types of run concepts offenses can run and makes the side to which they'll ultimately run more predictable. Offensive architects have gotten more creative with motion to try to disguise some of those concepts, with blockers motioning in one direction pre-snap before immediately turning around and attempting to kick out a defender post-snap, but there are concepts where the timing just doesn't really work from shotgun.

 Take last season's Seahawks, for example. Under center, Seattle ran all kinds of concepts, including inside zone and outside zone, power, counter, duo and a handful of other run schemes. When the Seahawks were in the pistol or shotgun, though, their run game (and the play-action attack that resulted) was almost always built around counter. If you can nail down what a team's going to run by where the running back lines up, you can limit some of its offensive creativity.

 Under center, the RB lines up directly behind the quarterback, which allows offenses to retain the ability to run to either side without needing to realign or shift personnel. It also helps create the timing needed to run outside zone concepts consistently and effectively. When Washington drafted Griffin in 2012 and attempted to mesh a Shanahan-style zone-rushing attack around the zone-read concepts the rookie had run at Baylor, the coaches installed the pistol to keep the back -- usually Alfred Morris  -- directly behind Griffin as opposed to lining him up alongside him. Morris and Griffin combined for 2,428 rushing yards during their shared rookie campaign, but once Shanahan started working with more traditional QBs, he moved…

title: Top moments, highlights as Bills dominate Lions in Highmark Stadium opener
summary: The Buffalo Bills hosted the Detroit Lions in their first game at their new home, Highmark Stadium. Here are all the highlights from Bills vs. Lions in Buffalo.
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills opened Highmark Stadium in style, blowing past the Detroit Lions 41-31  on Thursday night.

 

 Buffalo scored a touchdown on its first four drives, jumping out to a 27-7 lead and cruising the rest of the way. Detroit never cut its deficit to single digits once Buffalo went up 14-0 with 3:42 left in the first quarter. The Bills put up 446 total yards, averaged 6.5 yards per play and scored a touchdown on all five of their trips to the red zone.

 The catalyst of the Buffalo's dominant offensive display? Quarterback Josh Allen , who put together a virtuoso performance. He threw for 248 yards and three touchdowns, while running for 69 yards and two scores. Running back James Cook III added 135 yards on the ground and a touchdown.

 Allen has accounted for nine touchdowns this season -- five passing and four rushing -- and hasn't turned it over in the Bills' first two games. He's the third player all time with at least nine combined touchdowns with no turnovers over his team's first two games of a season, according to Elias. The other two players went on to win the MVP.

 Lions quarterback Jared Goff had 327 passing yards and four touchdowns, while running back Jahmyr Gibbs added 113 total yards and a score. Wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown had nine catches for 142 yards and two touchdowns.

 Here are the top moments from Buffalo's victory.

title: Josh Allen opens the Bills' new stadium with a 5-TD outing in a 41-31 win over the Lions
summary: — Forget the official name of the Buffalo Bills' new stadium. It’s Josh Allen’s house.

title: Bills open new stadium with impressive performance over Lions
summary: Josh Allen accounted for five touchdowns as Buffalo moved to 2-0 in the debut of the new Highmark Stadium.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- In the debut of the new Highmark Stadium, the  Buffalo Bills gave the home crowd something to cheer about as they opened things with a 41-31 win over the Detroit Lions  on Thursday.

 The Bills celebrated the opening of their new stadium with everything from an appearance by Hall of Famer Bruce Smith to bands, and then the fireworks really began. With Josh Allen accounting for two touchdowns in the first quarter, the Bills raced to a 21-0 lead early in the second quarter and never looked back.

 Allen accounted for five touchdowns in the game -- his fourth career game with at least three passing touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns. Kordell Stewart, who did that twice, is the only other player in NFL history with multiple such games.

 While Allen picked apart the Lions' injury-ravaged secondary -- a busted coverage left Joshua Palmer wide open for a 43-yard touchdown reception in the first quarter --  James Cook III  ran all over the Lions' defense for 135 yards, including 101 in the first half, and a touchdown. It all led to some lopsided statistics that will undoubtedly be noted by future opponents.

 The Bills had 11 first downs in the first quarter, their most since Week 9 of 2020 against the  Seattle Seahawks . And the Bills' emphasis on a vertical attack, established in their season-opening triumph over the Houston Texans , continued. In the first half, Allen was 3-of-5 for 84 yards and two touchdowns on passes of at least 15 air yards. The biggest hiccup for the Bills' offense was the loss of wide receiver  DJ Moore  in the second quarter because of a shoulder injury. 

 Here are the most important things to know from Thursday night for both teams:

 

 

 

 Buffalo Bills (2-0) 

 What to make of the QB performance: Allen made the Lions' defense pay whenever it sent the blitz. In the first half, the Lions blitzed on 11 of 23 dropbacks, and Allen was 7-of-10 for 98 yards, with two touchdowns and a sack. Allen had just one game last season with multiple touchdowns against the blitz.

 Most surprising performance : With defensive tackle Ed Oliver being a last-minute scratch after injuring his hip during pregame warmups, second-year defensive tackle Deone Walker was pressed into an increased role, and he responded. He had five of the Bills' eight quarterback pressures in the first half and finished with seven total -- after having six pressures in 200 pass-rush plays last season. QB Jared Goff was 2-of-3 for 25 yards with two sacks on those plays. Walker also had three batted/defended passes.

 Stat to know: Cook, who had 13 rushes for 57 yards in Week 1, had 83 rushing yards before first contact in the first half against the Lions -- that's more than the Lions had in total rushing yards in the first half (57). He finished with 104 rushing yards before first contact, his third career game with 100 or more such rushing yards. -- Judy Battista 

 Next game:  vs. Los Angeles Chargers  (1 p.m. ET, Sept. 27)

 

 

 

 Detroit Lions (1-1) 
 It was a humbling experience for the Lions. By halftime, Detroit trailed 27-10, allowing Allen to throw three touchdowns and run for another as the defense couldn't get a stop.

 But the Lions showed life in the second half with WR Amon-Ra St. Brown , who had 142 receiving yards on nine catches and two touchdowns, scoring a 2-yard touchdown on the opening drive of the third quarter to cut the deficit to 10.

 Coach Dan Campbell was heated entering the locker room, as he couldn't contain his emotions on live television -- saying that "the little s--- is killing us." Detroit was playing without two of its starting offensive linemen,  Christian Mahogany (hip) and Blake Miller (knee), who were both ruled out ahead of the contest, and the Lions are hoping they'll return for Week 3.

 What to make of the QB performance: It was a disastrous start for the offense as Jared Goff was sacked twice and had just 2 passing yards in the first quarter. But Goff helped stabilize the unit as the game progressed, finishing 26-of-38 with 327 passing yards and four touchdowns. He also hit 40,000 career passing yards in 153 games, which is the sixth fewest a QB has needed to hit that benchmark in NFL history. The Lions are still working out the kinks under first-year offensive coordinator Drew Petzing while working to get healthy, but they have put up 62 points in the first two games.

 Most surprising performance: The lack of involvement for WR Jameson Williams . Coming off a strong training camp, Williams seemed poised for a breakout season as the WR2 but is off to a slow start. He was targeted just four times, finishing with two receptions for 33 yards in Buffalo. In Week 1, Williams finished with four catches for 45 yards with a dropped pass, despite nine targets.

 Trend to watch: Detroit's defense has allowed at least 30 points in back-to-back games. The secondary continued to struggle against Allen and the Bills' offense. This stretch marks Detroit's first time allowing 30 points in its first two games of a season since 2021 -- the first games of the Campbell era in Detroit. The Lions have allowed 30 or more points in five of their past eight regular-season games.  -- Eric Woodyard 

 Next game:  vs.  New York Jets  (1 p.m. ET, Sept. 27)

title: Chiefs' rookies eager for more success after opener
summary: Mansoor Delane, R Mason Thomas, Emmett Johnson, Peter Woods and Kahlil Benson must do it again vs. Indy.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- The  Kansas City Chiefs ' locker room was filled with similar scenes after Monday night's 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos .

 Kenneth Walker III , who produced 191 all-purpose yards and two touchdowns, hugged fellow running back Emmett Johnson , a rookie. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and tight end Travis Kelce each dapped up, hugged and expressed congratulations to Kahlil Benson , who started at left tackle and became the first undrafted rookie on offense to start in Week 1 for coach Andy Reid. In the back corner of the locker room, defensive end George Karlaftis praised rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas .

 "My guy balled out!" Karlaftis shouted, referencing Thomas. "He f---ing balled out."

 The Chiefs, who have one of the NFL's youngest rosters, had 11 rookies experience their first victory. Many in the group contributed to the Chiefs' success, too. But a few minutes after he exited the locker room, Thomas acknowledged just how quick the NFL can be from one week to the next, especially since most of the Chiefs' rookies in college didn't experience as short of a turnaround from "Monday Night Football" to the next opponent, the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC), in six days.

 In less than 30 hours from their season-opening victory, Reid delivered a short message Wednesday morning during the team's first meeting in preparation of facing the Colts: He wants an encore from the rookies.

 "[General manager] Brett [Veach] did a nice job of bringing the guys in," Reid said of the rookies. "The thing I mentioned to them is there's tape out there now. Whatever hiccups you had, you've got to fix those. You know these other coaches are pretty creative people and [opposing] players study."

 The Chiefs are hoping to get similar production from their rookie class against the Colts for them to move to a 2-0 record.

 Two of the rookies (Benson and cornerback Mansoor Delane ) are expected to start again. Alongside them, four other rookies -- Johnson, Thomas, defensive tackle Peter Woods and receiver Cyrus Allen -- will hope to show incremental progress in their respective rotational roles.

 "There's a lot of room for improvement," said Johnson, who had 10 touches for 68 all-purpose yards against the Broncos. "Going out there and playing free was good for me, trusting what I do in practice. But I've got to keep getting better. There's a lot more football left."

 The rookie who is expected to have the biggest spotlight against the Colts is Benson, who is expected to be in the lineup again in place of starting left tackle Josh Simmons , who has missed almost a month with a lower back injury. Benson survived several pass-blocking reps against Nik Bonitto , the Broncos' best pass rusher, allowing only one pressure in 15 matchups, according to Next Gen Stats.

 "The only thing I said to him was right before the game," Mahomes said of Benson. "I said, 'I believe in you; You're out there for a reason.' A lot of times, it's the NFL, and sometimes you make it bigger than what it is. But you're still playing a game that you've loved since you were a kid."

 The Chiefs are eager to see how much Benson can polish his footwork and blocking techniques against Arden Key and Laiatu Latu , the Colts' top edge rushers.

 "It's one thing to do the right thing in practice or against a bag," Reid said Wednesday. "It's another thing to do the right thing when it's live and it counts."

 In holding the Broncos to just 10 points, the first player to make a highlight in the game was Delane, the Chiefs' top draft pick. Delane, in just his third snap, played perfect coverage on receiver Courtland Sutton to intercept quarterback  Bo Nix 's intermediate pass.

 "That's not something that I was super surprised by," Woods said of the interception. "I mean, it's Mansoor Delane. It's what I said he would do from the first time [I spoke after the draft]. I'm super excited for him for the season, as well as R Mason."

 Delane did aggravate a right shoulder injury at the end of his 5-yard return when he stumbled and fell to the turf, landing on his shoulder. He did not return to the game, but coach Andy Reid said the rookie, who was a full participant in Wednesday's practice, is on track to play against the Colts.

 This offseason, the Chiefs felt they needed to add more youth, speed and athleticism to their roster to return to the postseason. Reid, Veach and longtime defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo accomplished their objective.

 In March, the Chiefs traded cornerback Trent McDuffie , a two-time All-Pro, to the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for a package of four draft picks. The Chiefs also traded up three spots with the Cleveland Browns , moving from the ninth pick to the sixth, to select Delane in the NFL draft in April. The first-round pick the Chiefs received from the Rams was used to acquire Woods, who on Monday recorded two tackles, one pressure and a pass deflection. Thomas, who was selected with the 40th pick, finished Monday with a sack and two pressures.

 "Shoutout to Coach Veach," Thomas said, laughing. "That [performance] is what we want to do [as rookies]. We want to play fast, physical and who cares if you make mistakes if you can learn from them. We've got some ballers."

 The rookie who could see his usage increase the most against the Colts is Johnson, the fifth-round pick. Against the Broncos, the Chiefs relied heavily on Walker, who finished with a game-high 26 touches. Johnson demonstrated that he can be an effective ball carrier, a player who showcased his juke moves against the Broncos to break a handful of tackles.

 The rookie is confident he can get better at a rapid pace because his coordinator (Eric Bieniemy) and position coach (DeMarco Murray) each had notable NFL careers.

 "I don't know how much better it can get, honestly," Johnson said, smiling. "Having guys who played this position in the league, having them as coaches, I learn so much every single day. When they're saying something, I've got to make sure I'm listening. I definitely want to dominate this game at a high level."

title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why you should use 49ers, Eagles in Week 2
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and picks including the 49ers and other cautious picks.
full_text:
Welcome to 2026 ESPN NFL Survivor ! The rules are simple: Pick one NFL team each week to win its game. If that team wins (or ties), you advance to the next week. If that team loses, you are out. Survive all 18 weeks and you can take home a share of the $25,000 grand prize. The catch is that each team can be chosen only once.

 While the rules are simple, the game theory is not. Depending on the size of your group or what platform you play on, the optimal selections could change drastically. Smaller groups will likely end well before Week 18, so optimizing win probability each week is paramount. However, the larger the group, the more you need to focus on saving strong teams for later, as your season is more likely to last all 18 weeks.

 

 ESPN's game requires just one team each week, so that will be the strategic focus of this column. Last week, the most-selected team on ESPN Survivor was the Los Angeles Chargers . Its upset loss to the Arizona Cardinals knocked out 21% of the field and served as the biggest Week 1 betting upset since the Tampa Bay Buccaneers stunned the New Orleans Saints in 2018.

 Outside of the Chargers, virtually all the other popular selections won, including this column's top choice, the Jacksonville Jaguars , who dominated the Cleveland Browns  34-10.

 This week, seven teams are favored by at least 6.5 points, the most in any September week since 2021. Public opinion is consolidating among two teams: the San Francisco 49ers and the Buccaneers.

 The 49ers are the biggest favorites, laying 13.5 at home against the Miami Dolphins . That is the largest point spread this early in the season since 2021.

 For contests where you only need to select one team each week, I would suggest burning the 49ers now. The win equity offered by the 49ers is unmatched by other teams this week. Recently, we've seen smaller favorites struggle early in the year. Over the last five seasons, teams favored by 6 to 9.5 points have won just 60% of the time in September compared to 78% of the time in later months. Meanwhile, double-digit favorites are 11-1 in September in that span.

 

 However, that doesn't mean there aren't other strong plays. The Buccaneers have their easiest game all season with limited future value. The Chargers project to be underselected compared to how large a favorite they are, and they are also running out of usable weeks. The Philadelphia Eagles , Kansas City Chiefs and Baltimore Ravens also make some sense as contrarian plays.

 My estimated exposure for multiple contests is 50% 49ers, 25% Eagles, 20% Buccaneers, and 5% Chargers. Make sure to monitor the injury report for the Raiders and Chargers, as there are several key injuries on both sides that could affect that line, which could have me pivot to the Chiefs.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. San Francisco 49ers (vs. Miami Dolphins ) 

 This is the most lopsided matchup on paper all season according to ESPN Analytics, so it's hard to pass up on the "free square" in single-pick contests. The trickier decision will be handling the 49ers in bigger contests. On Splash Sports' flagship contests, saving the 49ers for Week 9 on a double-pick week against the Raiders is very valuable, though they have difficult matchups in Weeks 12-16. That said, they do not play on a holiday slate, adding to their appeal in Circa.

 
 Chance to win: 92% (ESPN Analytics), 95% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: 49ers -13.5 (-950 moneyline) 
 Future value: 10th (60% average win probability) 
 ESPN Selection: 23% 
 

 2. Philadelphia Eagles (at Tennessee Titans ) 

 

 The Eagles are coming in a little under the radar this week despite facing the team with the worst record in the NFL over the past three seasons. Yes, it's a road game, but the Eagles are 30-13 on the road under Nick Sirianni, the best record in the NFL. The Titans looked miserable in Week 1, getting outgained by 172 yards against the Jets, and now they face a much tougher opponent in the Eagles. This is the easiest Eagles game all season according to ESPN Analytics and second-easiest according to Mike Clay, so while they have future value, I don't feel obligated to save them like the Ravens. However, in the Circa contest, I would downgrade the Eagles significantly as they play on both holiday slates.

 
 Chance to win: 69% (ESPN Analytics), 80% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Eagles -7 (-310 moneyline) 
 Future value:  Seventh (62% average win probability) 
 ESPN Selection: 12% 
 

 3. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (vs. Cleveland Browns ) 

 The Buccaneers are the second-biggest favorites, and this is their largest favorite role all season on paper. For those who like to save the best teams for later, the Buccaneers are the easiest choice against the second-worst team in the NFL per ESPN Analytics. However, they are also shaping up to be very popular, which is scary for a team that has failed to cover a spread in 10 straight games dating back to last season. The Buccaneers will certainly be in my Survivor portfolio, but if selection keeps trending high, I plan to be slightly underweight.

 
 Chance to win: 79% (ESPN Analytics), 82% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Buccaneers -8.5 (-410 moneyline) 
 Future value: 19th (52% average win probability) 
 ESPN Selection: 27% 
 

 4. Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Las Vegas Raiders ) 
 

 As disappointing as the Chargers were in Week 1, that loss arguably makes them a more appealing pick in Week 2, especially in more casual pools. ESPN Analytics downgraded them from 6th to 15th in its power rankings, meaning the Chargers do not have much future value. The Raiders looked good last week against the Dolphins, but this is a much more difficult spot against the Chargers off a loss. Historically, 0-1 teams that are similar-sized favorites against 1-0 team have been great outright bets. Just monitor injuries to Ladd McConkey and Brock Bowers as both are pivotal players to each team's offense. Downgrade the Chargers in Splash Sports, as two of their easiest remaining games happen in Weeks 14 and 16.

 
 Chance to win: 69% (ESPN Analytics), 81% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Chargers -6.5 (-298 moneyline) 
 Future value: 23rd (49% average win probability) 
 ESPN Selection: 3% 
 

 5. Kansas City Chiefs (vs. Indianapolis Colts ) 
 

 If I have a large number of entries, I would consider the Chiefs instead of the Ravens for a small sprinkle. The Ravens are trending to be more than twice as popular of a pick, and the Ravens have the highest average win probability for the rest of the season according to Mike Clay's model. The Chiefs are an especially sneaky pick in the Splash Sports contest, as one of their toughest stretches all season happens from Weeks 12-16, all double-pick weeks.

 ESPN Selection: 2%

title: Career-defining season for Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell?
summary: O'Connell has had tremendous regular-season success, but is this the season it extends into the playoffs?
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- Kevin O'Connell has produced one of the most unique résumés in NFL history. He is the only head coach to deliver multiple seasons of at least 13 victories, as he did for the Minnesota Vikings in 2022 and 2024, without winning a playoff game.

 That distinction, via Elias Sports Bureau, neatly encapsulates the enigmatic nature of O'Connell's tenure with the Vikings, which moved to a fifth season Sunday with a 39-22 victory over the Green Bay Packers . 

 O'Connell has demonstrated many of the key attributes of successful NFL coaches, from his work with veteran quarterbacks to his empathetic personality to -- most importantly -- a clear aptitude for winning. Yet he has failed to translate those qualities into a serious run at the Super Bowl, failing to get past the wild-card round. 

 In 2022, the Vikings allowed 431 yards and 28 first downs to the New York Giants in a 31-24 loss, leading to the firing of defensive coordinator Ed Donatell a week later. In 2024, the Vikings were overwhelmed on both sides of the ball in falling to the Los Angeles Rams  27-9.

 In either case, that bottom line looms over a series of unique circumstances he has encountered during that process. 

 With two significant complications removed -- the Vikings fired general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah in January and demoted 2024 first-round pick J.J. McCarthy to third-string QB this summer -- will O'Connell take the step this season from a good coach to a great one?

 Can he do so after the inauspicious loss of new quarterback Kyler Murray , who suffered a concussion on the 11th play of his debut game Sunday and remained in the protocol as of Friday morning? Or is O'Connell destined to become this generation's Marvin Lewis or Jim Mora, two coaches who had long and successful careers without making a playoff run? 

 Sitting in his office this summer, O'Connell said he felt "incredibly confident" about "how to be the best version of myself for this organization" after four years "learning different aspects of what it takes to win" and understanding how to maintain it.

 "I'm really excited about what a lot of those things mean for me personally," O'Connell said, "but also for a building that I have so much confidence in from top to bottom -- where we are now in 2026 from the team we've put together, getting a chance to work with [new general manager Nolan Teasley] and his staff and my coaching staff every day."

 The numbers on O'Connell's résumé are clear. His .638 winning percentage is the best in team history, and he is tied for the NFL's fifth-most wins since 2022 despite using nine different quarterbacks. The four coaches ranked ahead of O'Connell benefited from using one primary quarterback over that period. One longtime AFC executive said: "He would have his pick of jobs if they ever fired him."

 Speaking generally at training camp last month, Vikings owner/president Mark Wilf said "we try to be patient as an ownership" in pursuit of postseason wins but added: "Patience isn't infinite." O'Connell's contract extends through the 2029 season, and Wilf said he is evaluated annually on the "totality" of his performance -- not playoff success alone. 

 "Coach O'Connell knows the expectations as well as anyone," Wilf said, "and that's to win, and win championships. And we're thrilled with coach O'Connell and everything he's brought here, most importantly the culture he's brought."

 The historic binaries of O'Connell's résumé, amid the circumstances that produced them, prompt further digging as he moves forward in his fifth season. Three aspects in particular merit closer inspection: his work with quarterbacks, the impact of Adofo-Mensah's rocky tenure and the culture the coach has built.

 
 

 The quarterback whisperer 

 O'Connell himself flinches when he's referred to as a "quarterback whisperer." The moniker implies a Midas touch that elevates any quarterback he works with, a power that no NFL coach can realistically possess. 

 O'Connell has coaxed a career year from Sam Darnold , elevated Kirk Cousins into a fourth-quarter marksman, suctioned two wins from journeyman Josh Dobbs and gotten 1,110 passing yards in three starts from career backup Nick Mullens . But his work with young quarterbacks does not compare favorably. 

 Since the start of the 2023 offseason, the Vikings have drafted two quarterbacks and kept one undrafted rookie on their roster. Of the 97 quarterbacks who have started at least one NFL game since then, McCarthy, Jaren Hall and Max Brosmer rank No. 71, No. 90 and No. 94 in career QBR, respectively. 

 

 An AFC coach suggested that it's better to think of O'Connell as "a really good playcaller" who can give quarterbacks a decisive advantage if they understand and accept his concepts. 

 ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky said on "NFL Live" this summer that "the quarterback needs to let the star of the offense be Kevin O'Connell," and further explained his point in a telephone conversation. 

 "There are certain guys that just have a high-end level of play design, playcall and the setup of that playcall," Orlovsky said. "I played for one of them in Houston, Gary Kubiak. I had never been around a coach that could watch film, know exactly how the team and quarterback could attack the defense, but then in the game within a drive or two, know exactly what wrinkle might be needed and know how to get that wrinkle set up. I think Kevin has that.

 "Sometimes quarterbacks, because they are highly competitive and incredibly egotistical, think they can make whatever throw. For quarterbacks with this type of playcaller, you've just got to get into that rhythm of believing he's got it."

 In an interview this summer, Murray joked that O'Connell can coach "football for dummies" because of how clearly he articulates his concepts and provides answers. That reputation was a factor in the months leading up to the 2024 draft, setting into motion a series of events that could be career defining for O'Connell's time in Minnesota.

 
 

 Adofo-Mensah and the McCarthy saga 

 The Vikings drafted McCarthy with the No. 10 pick in the 2024 draft when Adofo-Mensah was still the GM. Five months later, as McCarthy was recovering from a season-ending right knee injury, O'Connell said on the "The Rich Eisen Show" that "organizations fail young quarterbacks before young quarterbacks fail organizations."

 Four days before the Vikings opened the 2026 season against the Packers, O'Connell demoted McCarthy to the No. 3 quarterback position after Murray won the starting job, making McCarthy eligible to play only if both Murray and backup Carson Wentz were injured in Week 1. 

 So did O'Connell and the Vikings fail McCarthy? Or was McCarthy destined to be a draft bust all along? 

 ESPN spent recent weeks asking those questions. Publicly, the Vikings have not conceded McCarthy's future. Teasley has said that McCarthy's story is "not written," and O'Connell referred to him as "a guy that we want to pour into every single day." But team and league sources produced this collective assessment:

 As ESPN has previously reported, the Vikings put the top of the 2024 quarterback class into two tiers . The first group included the top three picks of the draft in Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels and Drake Maye -- prospects they believed could elevate a roster and were worth giving up additional draft assets to acquire. The second tier -- McCarthy, Michael Penix Jr . (No. 8) and Bo Nix (No. 12) -- would need a more fulsome team around them to succeed. In the case of McCarthy, who was 21 at the time, the Vikings thought he might need multiple years before it was time to play him, sources said.

 

 O'Connell pushed hard to trade up from No. 11 to No. 3 to select Maye, but the New England Patriots turned down Adofo-Mensah's offer . Despite recent speculation that O'Connell opposed drafting McCarthy with a trade up to No. 10, multiple sources said he supported it alongside a development plan that…

title: Saints QB Tyler Shough expects less jitters vs. Ravens
summary: The 26-year-old starter is the first to say he and his New Orleans team will fight through the adversity.
full_text:
METAIRIE, La. -- The New Orleans Saints and Baltimore Ravens could either be headed for an offensive shootout or a defensive battle when they play Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 The identities of both teams are yet to be determined after just a week, but it's clear they both have the ability to put up major offensive numbers after combining for 71 points and 975 net yards of offense in their respective Week 1 games.

 It was a fast start for the Ravens, who beat the Indianapolis Colts 41-23 after leading 31-13 in the first half. But in the Saints' game, New Orleans fell into a 21-0 hole before rallying to lose to the Detroit Lions , 31-30 in overtime .

 So what version of the Saints' offense will show up in Baltimore? The answer depends on Saints quarterback Tyler Shough .

 

 "There was a lot to clean up just as a whole offensive unit, especially myself. I wish I would have just kind of gone through my operation and had cleaner feet earlier on," Shough said Wednesday. "My feet were too quick and I was trying to be too perfect."

 The 26-year-old quarterback had a significant amount of pressure placed on his shoulders compared to last season, when he sat behind Spencer Rattler for half the season until he was ready to start as a rookie.

 By the time Shough made his first start in Week 9 in 2025, the one-win Saints were already long shots to make the playoffs. Simple signs of growth from the second-round pick were considered a win.

 The Saints expect more in Year 2, both from Shough and themselves.

 "This year we're not going to take moral victories," Saints edge rusher Chase Young said. "Our job is to go back to the drawing board and look through our mistakes and correct them."

 Shough has said he doesn't get rattled easily, but there was an early disconnect from the offense in Detroit in Week 1. The QB ran into defensive walls, took five sacks and missed open receivers.

 His teammates kept their confidence in him though. Saints wide receiver Devaughn Vele said Shough's body language never changed, showing his maturity in handling adversity.

 "He was still saying, 'Hey, we're just going to take it play by play.' Those kind of guys, those are the ones that you can get behind and help you stay positive and continue to make those plays. I think that's why we're able to create that spark in that second half," said Vele.

 Wide receiver Chris Olave said he wanted Shough to know how much he believed in his QB's abilities. Olave kept telling him he knew he could play like he's the league's best passer.

 

 "Let's just drive confidence into him. We all know what he can do, but it's going to be adversity sometimes," Olave said after the game. "We're just going to need other people to pick him up. ... We all know he can do it, so he bounced back."

 Shough said that belief encouraged him to play fast and free.

 "I just kind of took that pressure off myself, just played football and that's part of it. I'm still pretty early when it comes into that aspect of it," Shough said. "I had a lot of fun being able to have some adversity. ... It was good to be able to build off that and the whole offense. We just were not on the same page and we were able to just get things going."

 The third quarter of the loss to the Lions went as poorly as possible for Shough, who turned the ball over on two straight series to give the Lions a 21-0 lead.

 Perhaps feeling like there was nothing to lose, Shough stepped up on his next play, threw a 47-yard pass to Olave and got better from there, leading scoring drives on four of the Saints' next five possessions.

 New Orleans finished a two-point conversion away from beating the Lions in overtime, capping off Week 1 with 30 points, 410 passing yards and 469 total yards of offense.

 "Once you get things going and get a rhythm, that big play to Chris, that's an obvious game-changing moment where you can go out there and make a big play," Shough said.

 

 The Saints can't afford a slow start against the Ravens, who stifled the Colts' passing attack early, allowing only 166 total passing yards and 88 passing yards in the first half.

 "We've just got to play better in the first quarter, simple as that. It's not a time on task thing, it's a design and execution thing for all of us," Saints coach Kellen Moore said.

 New Orleans will need to figure out how to get its run game going as well and rely less on Shough, who had 56 pass attempts against the Lions. Moore said he "feels good" about running back Alvin Kamara 's chances to play after missing the last month with a knee injury.

 The Saints utilized a running back by committee approach against the Lions, with free agent addition Travis Etienne Jr . rushing nine times for 46 yards, slightly more than Kendre Miller (nine attempts for 30 yards).

 Kamara could be another pass catcher for Shough. Olave had 10 catches for a personal best 182 receiving yards, but Vele and tight ends Noah Fant and Juwan Johnson combined for the team's three receiving touchdowns.

 "He's a difference-maker at every position, to be honest. His physicality, his speed, his one-cut ability, his presence just in the huddle ... He's got the experience and then they have to respect all that stuff," Shough said of Kamara. "So having him, Trav, Juwan, Noah, there's a lot of weapons you can put in the backfield."

title: Why the Jets feel their tight end room 'is a weapon'
summary: New York deployed its tight ends in a myriad of ways, including a rushing TD by first-round pick Kenyon Sadiq.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When rookie Kenyon Sadiq scored the first touchdown of the  New York Jets ' season, the first to congratulate him were fellow tight ends Jeremy Ruckert and Mason Taylor .

 Call it a lucky "13" celebration -- and a glimpse into the future.

 Ruckert and Taylor delivered key blocks on the play, a 3-yard run on an end around -- one of 11 plays the Jets ran out of the 13 personnel grouping (one back, three tight ends, one wideout). It's a growing trend in the NFL, and the Jets -- with four tight ends on the roster -- like to believe they're on the cutting edge.

 "I think that room is a weapon for us," coach Aaron Glenn said Monday.

 

 For years, the tight end position was a black hole in the Jets' offense. From 2016 to 2025, their tight ends ranked 31st in receptions, 32nd in receiving yards and 31st (tied) in touchdown receptions.

 This spring, they drafted Sadiq with the 16th overall pick -- one of three first-round selections -- essentially announcing their intention under new offensive coordinator Frank Reich to become a tight-end-heavy offense.

 Sadiq joined Taylor (second round, 2025) and Ruckert (third round, 2022) in the room. Jelani Woods , a third-round pick of the Indianapolis Colts in 2022, crashed the party with a strong training camp, prompting the Jets to keep four on the roster.

 Reich has leaned toward the traditional 11 grouping (one back, one tight end, three receivers) throughout his career as a playcaller, but he vowed in training camp to adjust to his current personnel.

 "The whole group is super talented and super versatile," Reich said.

 It wasn't lip service.

 On the opening possession of their 23-10 win over the Tennessee Titans , the Jets used 13 personnel on three plays -- matching their total for the entire 2025 season. They marched 60 yards in eight plays, a rarity for the Jets, who had only one first-possession touchdown drive in 2025.

 By the end of the day, they had used multiple tight ends on 27 of their 63 plays, including both touchdowns, according to Next Gen Stats. They rolled out four tight ends on one play in the third quarter -- about as common as a lunar eclipse. Most teams don't have four tight ends on the roster; the ones that do typically don't deploy them at the same time.

 

 It's worth noting that the fifth player in the grouping was  Andrew Beck , a hybrid player listed as a fullback but practices with the tight ends. Quarterback  Geno Smith  said Beck is really a tight end, making that a five-tight end play -- perhaps unprecedented.

 "I don't think I've ever been on the field with five tight ends," said Smith, in his 14th season.

 The personnel package appeared to confuse the Titans, who got caught with 13 men on the field for the next play -- a 4-yard touchdown run by  Breece Hall  out of 12 personnel.

 "I thought that was pretty fun to see," Glenn said.

 While Taylor, Ruckert and Woods are traditional tight ends, Sadiq is a chess piece because of his versatility. He's the key to the operation, capable of playing anywhere in the formation. On Sunday, he lined up at tight end (18 snaps), split out wide (four), in the slot (two) and in the backfield (two).

 On his touchdown run, Sadiq went in motion toward Smith, took the handoff and burned rubber around the left end, reaching a top speed of 20.08 mph -- tied with Mark Andrews (2025) for the fastest max speed on a rushing TD by a tight end since Next Gen Stats began tracking in 2016.

 "It was awesome, something you just dream of," said Sadiq, who joined Pro Football Hall of Famer Ozzie Newsome (1978) as the only two tight ends in history to score a rushing touchdown in their first game. "I have so much gratitude for all the guys. Mason and Jeremy were really the big reason why I scored there."

 Reich knew immediately what he had in Sadiq, who recorded one of the fastest 40-yard dash times (4.39 seconds) for a tight end in the history of the scouting combine. Reich was so excited on draft night that he was almost hyperventilating during a welcome-to-the-team phone call with Sadiq.

 "It's exciting and it opens doors for all of us," Taylor said after Sadiq's arrival.

 

 The plans were temporarily put on hold, as Sadiq underwent hernia surgery in the spring and missed most of OTAs and then training camp after a setback in late July. Reich downplayed Sadiq's potential impact in the opener, saying the rookie would need time to get up to speed.

 He exceeded those expectations.

 "Coach Reich, he's going to have a hell of a time scheming for our offense," Taylor said. "We have a bunch of skill in that room -- not just him, but, I mean, he's smooth, he's quick and he's as athletic as hell."

 The tight ends combined for only six receptions for 23 yards in Week 1, but their production should increase as they settle into the offense. The Jets are part of the "13" craze sweeping the league, started last year by the Los Angeles Rams . In Week 1, there were 160 snaps of 13, the most since at least 2007.

 "That's an improved group," Glenn said of his four tight ends, "and each week we're giving them more and more on their plate so we can try to take advantage of who they are."

title: Inside the saga around Joey Porter Jr.'s future with Steelers
summary: The future of Pittsburgh's No. 1 cornerback with the team he grew up around remains unclear. Here's what we know.
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- After navigating through nearly two feet of snow dumped on the city by Winter Storm Fern, cornerback Joey Porter Jr . slipped in the PNC Champions Club at Acrisure Stadium through a side door on Jan. 27 and took a seat next to his dad, Joey Porter Sr., facing the stage.

 In front of the pair, the Pittsburgh Steelers  introduced Mike McCarthy as the team's next head coach, two central figures in the organization's future staring at each other face to face as the past looked on.

 A legacy player and the team's first 2023 second-round pick, Porter was the perfect bridge for the organization as it transitioned from Mike Tomlin to McCarthy.

 Nine months later, Porter's future with the team he grew up around is unclear and becoming less certain by the day. After lengthy and contentious negotiations, ones that continued until just hours before kickoff against the visiting Atlanta Falcons in Week 1, the Steelers and Porter's side failed to agree to a contract extension prior to the start of the 2026 regular season.

 

 Porter, meanwhile, was inactive for the season opener, instead watching the game from the sideline in a gray sweatshirt and gray Steelers shorts. McCarthy decided to hold Porter out against the Falcons because he hadn't completed the ramp-up period in his return to practice. The cornerback was placed on the physically unable to perform list and missed all of training camp with an aggravated back injury he reported to the team following a mobility workout on the first day on July 28.

 While the plan was to increase Porter's workload this week, the cornerback left Thursday's practice with an athletic trainer during the media viewing window. Before his early exit, Porter stretched with the team and did a rep of a ball-security drill. Unlike Wednesday's practice report in which he was listed as a limited participant with "Not Injury Related -- conditioning" as his official injury, Thursday's report listed a back injury. Porter, the team said, was cleared of the previous back injury earlier in the week, though McCarthy declined to give specifics on Porter's timeline or availability for Sunday's Week 2 game at the New England Patriots (1 p.m. ET, CBS).

 "I'm with Joe, whatever he's doing -- whether it's injury, whether it's contract, whatever it is, I respect it," Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen said after Thursday's practice. "I'm behind him 100%. I tell him every single time, 'I respect how you go about your business every single day.'"

 Thursday night, some close to the situation sensed a fracture in the relationship between Porter and the organization.

 "I don't know if he ever puts on a Steelers uniform again," a source with knowledge of the situation told ESPN.

 That leaves the Steelers and their homegrown talent in limbo, a place that seemed unlikely when Porter arrived at Acrisure Stadium to greet his new coach in January.

 The two sides have been here because of a significant difference between the Steelers' view of Porter's value and how Porter values himself. The core issue is the structure of the contract, sources told ESPN, and the Steelers' organizational precedent that doesn't fully guarantee a healthy portion of the contract was considered a sizable hurdle.

 Many of the Steelers past deals for key players fully guarantee only the first year. That was the case for Porter's draft mates, Keeanu Benton , Darnell Washington  and Nick Herbig , whose four-year extensions this summer guaranteed 2027 for injury only. Porter wants stronger guarantees, sources said. Pittsburgh has broken precedent in the past. For example, Pittsburgh guaranteed $108 million for T.J. Watt in the summer of 2025. While Porter doesn't have the megastar cachet of Watt, he's still a high-level cover corner.

 The sides simply did not get close to bridging that guaranteed gap, which sources say made any talks about a per-year average on a deal moot. "It never even got that far," a source said.

 Porter believes that he deserves a contract commensurate with his impressive skill set. However, Porter hasn't been voted to a Pro Bowl or All-Pro team during his three seasons, and each of the 10 highest-paid corners on a per-year average have at least one Pro Bowl or All-Pro nod. All but one ( Dallas ' DaRon Bland ) are former first-round picks.

 

 As a second-round selection, Porter isn't in the same boat as Christian Gonzalez and Devon Witherspoon , who have reset the market with their own extensions this offseason. Though the pair were drafted in the same class as Porter in 2023 and are also up-and-coming cornerbacks, Gonzalez and Witherspoon already had their fifth-year options picked up, a contract clause attached only to first-round picks. While Porter has the opportunity to hit free agency a year earlier, the Patriots and Seattle Seahawks were motivated to get extensions done to alleviate the 2027 cap hit that comes with the fifth-year guarantees.

 With a year still left on his rookie deal, Porter also isn't in the same position as Le'Veon Bell was in 2018, when the running back held out and refused to sign his second consecutive franchise tag with Pittsburgh. Unlike Bell, Porter is still under contract. Not only do the Steelers have control of Porter's rights this season, but the team could also franchise tag him before he's able to hit free agency in 2027.

 The emergence of cornerback Asante Samuel Jr . is a factor, too. With Porter out, the Steelers are comfortable with Samuel as a starter.

 A 2021 Los Angeles Chargers second-round pick, Samuel landed with the Steelers late last season once he was cleared to return to football activities following spinal fusion surgery. He gave the secondary an immediate boost in 2025, leading to him signing a one-year, $4 million deal to return to the Steelers. He was a standout during training camp and the preseason. Listed as a co-starter alongside Porter on the depth chart, he played all 60 defensive snaps in Porter's absence against the Falcons on Sunday.

 The Steelers could trade Porter, though the team has neither made nor received any serious inquiries about the cornerback. One NFL executive believes the Steelers could get a second-round pick in exchange for Porter and a quality Day 3 draft selection.

 Before the season opener, Porter was hopeful that his future remained with the organization. But sources have described Porter as "disappointed" a deal couldn't be made and "frustrated" by the situation. Because of that, Porter requested a trade, per ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter and NFL Network national insider Ian Rapoport , a possibility that seemed inconceivable nine months ago. The notion of a trade was not surprising to multiple sources who first brought up the possibility to ESPN in August, when the Steelers hadn't made a formal offer and gave the full impression they wanted Porter to play out his rookie deal.

 Adding to that emotion is Porter's history with the Steelers.

 "I'm from here," Porter said on Sept. 1. "My family lives here. My cousin went to high school here, so they know I'm a hometown kid."

 Porter's dad was a linebacker for the Steelers from 1999 to 2006 and had 98 sacks in 13 seasons. He eventually returned as a defensive assistant in 2014 and remained as a coach with the team through 2018. Last year, Porter was inducted into the team's Ring of Honor, and he's a constant presence at games and occasionally pops into some practices at the team facility.

 

 Though he was born in California, Porter grew up running around the Southside practice facility with Tomlin's sons and went to high school at North Allegheny in Wexford, Pennsylvania -- a suburb of Pittsburgh. As a 5-year-old wearing his dad's jersey, Porter was hoisted up by his father as confetti rained down on Ford Field after the Steelers celebrated their Super Bowl XL title in Detroit on Feb. 5, 2006.

 As a teenager, Porter was a ball boy at Steelers training camp, scrubbing footballs after…

title: Titans remain patient with Cam Ward despite 'rough' opener
summary: Tennessee didn't score a touchdown until its last drive in coach Robert Saleh's debut.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- When Robert Saleh signed to become the next coach of the Tennessee Titans in January, one thing was clear:  Cam Ward 's development into a franchise quarterback was the key to his success.

 There was optimism for Ward after he showed growth over the final six games of his rookie season last year, with 10 of his 15 touchdowns and only one of his seven interceptions coming over that stretch.

 But Ward's season debut under Saleh on Sunday against the New York Jets  wasn't what they imagined in the 23-10 loss , but Saleh is still confident in the Titans' plans to get the best out of the second-year quarterback.

 "I thought he did a lot of good things in the game early that showed the progress that he's been making," Saleh said of Ward, who finished the game 19 of 32 passing for 140 yards and was sacked three times. "He had a rough game, but it's not all on him. There were opportunities where we've got to be better for him as a staff; his teammates have got to be better for him, and then obviously he's got to be better for his teammates with regards to delivering a football."

 

 The Titans wanted to see improved pocket presence and accuracy from Ward as he entered his second season, but both issues surfaced Sunday. 

 "I'm sure there are times where Cam says he wishes he would have stood in there, just like there are times he feels he could gotten out," quarterback coach Shea Tierney said. "It's a feel thing. You just continue educating him and have him make the best decision. We do drills every day for that."

 Ward missed throws to  Wan'Dale Robinson  on a screen and Tyjae Spears on a swing route. Rookie receiver Carnell Tate was wide open on a crossing route, but Ward was unable to find him either. Ward still believes he's a "very good quarterback." But he isn't running from the fact he needs to play better to prove it.

 "I'm very critical of myself. I want to be a great player," Ward said. "That comes whether it's from myself or the coaching staff, it's what can I do to be the best I want to be and for the team for us to be the best. There are key plays that myself and the staff think that I helped, but there are plays where I could have helped even more. That means continuing to take coaching from myself and from [offensive coordinator Brian Daboll] and [Tierney] and getting back to the drawing board and making something happen."

 The Titans staff believes Ward's improvement will come with more time on task. Allowing Ward to accumulate more practical experience will require patience the organization hasn't shown in the past. This is the same franchise that has fired a general manager or coach every year since 2022.

 That patience is going to be tested considering the success of fellow second-year quarterbacks Tyler Shough , who won Offensive Rookie of the Year with the New Orleans Saints last season, and Jaxson Dart , who had three passing touchdowns in Giants' season-opening win over the Dallas Cowboys last Sunday night. Sure, they're in different situations, but it's natural for team ownership to get frustrated that quarterbacks selected after Ward have had a higher degree of statistical success.

 

 Saleh is committed to allowing time for the process to carry out. He pointed out how Ward has had seven coordinators over the last seven years and stressed the importance of building a foundation for the young quarterback with stability around him. Despite Sunday's performance, Saleh is fully committed to Ward and feels the quarterback's growth is going to happen throughout the year.

 "We're fully committed to Cam because we believe in him," Saleh told ESPN. "You've got to let these young men grow. You would hate to be on the other side of it where you give up on a young man, and he goes to another team, and he wins a Super Bowl. We believe he has the right mindset, and we're going to give him every opportunity to grow."

 Saleh has seen this movie before. The Jets selected Zach Wilson with the second overall pick in the 2021 draft when he was the head coach. Wilson, like Ward, led his team to three wins as a rookie. The Jets gave Wilson two seasons to show he can develop into a franchise quarterback. His 18 interceptions to 15 touchdowns and 4,022 passing yards in 22 starts didn't cut it, so the Jets acquired future Hall of Famer Aaron Rodgers in a trade with the Green Bay Packers .

 Unlike when he was in New York, Saleh has a proven quarterback developer in Daboll, but the Ward and Daboll duo failed the first test in the opener.

 When asked to assess the performance, Daboll refused to place all of the blame on Ward either.

 "It takes all 11," Daboll said. "There's certainly plays that I wish I had back. I'm sure there's plays that Cam wishes he had back -- and the 10 other guys out there as well. So we got to do a better job with that. That starts with me."

 

 The Titans have done a lot to create a launching pad for Ward. They selected Tate with the No. 4 overall pick in the draft. They signed Robinson in free agency. Titans general manager also signed veteran quarterback Mitchell Trubisky to be Ward's backup and a veteran presence to help him grow.

 Trubisky has experienced what Ward is going through, having been the No. 2 overall pick by the Chicago Bears in 2017. He spent four seasons in Chicago as a starter before signing with the Buffalo Bills  as a backup, where he first played for Daboll.

 Trubisky mentioned how this era is different than the old-school days when quarterbacks were given time to develop and grow into the franchise role. A highly-drafted quarterback is usually thrown into the fire and asked to produce right away. Trubisky's advice to Ward is to focus on what he can control and not lose sight of who he is.

 "You've got to go back to what made you get drafted that high and know that you're a talented quarterback," Trubisky told ESPN. "Continue to believe in yourself and just know that it's a process. This is not an easy league. There are no easy games. There's going to be bumps along the way."

 There were plenty of bumps for Ward and the Titans in the opener, where their lone touchdown came on their ninth and final drive trailing 23-3.

 "I'm just continuing to try and get better," Ward said. "How can I get better from last Sunday to this Sunday? It's going to be a process." 

 Ward's next opportunity will come against last year's NFC East champions in the  Philadelphia Eagles  on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, FOX ) at Nissan Stadium. 

 "I have great coaches around me who continue to push me to that level that I want to play at," Ward said. "And when the tide turns, I'm pretty sure it's going to be a different story."
